stem: A superstar footballer was granted a 'super-injunction' at the High Court in London, to prevent details of an alleged extra-marital relationship between him and a young model from being published. The football player's lawyers had not applied for an injunction at the Court of Session in Edinburgh, and a Scottish newspaper has now published details of the alleged affair.
ask: Does the High Court in London's ruling have force in Scotland?

options.en: The High Court in London's ruling has no force in Scotland
The High Court in London's ruling has force in Scotland, because it is impossible to seal the Scottish and English border
The High Court in London's ruling has no force in Scotland, unless copies of the Scottish newspaper were sold in England
The High Court in London's ruling has no force in Scotland, unless copies of the Scottish newspaper were sold in England and Wales
The High Court in London's ruling has force in Scotland, because it is part of the United Kingdom

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The High Court in London's ruling has no force in Scotland, unless copies of the Scottish newspaper were sold in England and Wales. If the football player's lawyers had not applied for an injunction at the Court of Session in Edinburgh, this means that the High Court in London's ruling has no force in Scotland, unless copies of the Scottish newspaper were sold in England or Wales. In CTB v News Group Newspapers Ltd [2011], Mr Justice Eady granted a temporary injunction at the High Court in London, preventing the naming of Manchester United footballer Ryan Giggs in the media. The injunction was initially intended to prevent details of the case, an alleged extra-marital relationship between Giggs and an aspiring model, from being published in an English newspaper. The ruling of the court was based on Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the "right to respect for private and family life." Giggs' lawyers, however, had neglected to apply for an interdict (Scottish injunction) at the Court of Session in Edinburgh. Scottish newspaper 'The Sunday Herald' subsequently published details of the story. The Herald's editor asserted that the newspaper was not sold in England or Wales and that Giggs' name and photo were exclusive to the print edition and had not been posted on the newspaper's website. This meant that the Mr for England and Wales subsequently confirmed that no legal action would be taken against the Herald for contempt of court. Lead case: CTB v News Group Newspapers Ltd [2011] EWHC 1232 (QB). Statute; rule; constitution: Article 8 ECHR, Article 10 ECHR.

stem: The question for the court was whether a breach of the Betting and Lotteries Act 2012 (fictitious) conferred on bookmakers a right to sue for damages on the ground that the occupier of a dog-racing track had failed to provide space for them to carry on bookmaking. The Act was silent as to the consequences.
ask: Which option best states the main issue to be considered where a claim is based on breach of statutory duty?

options.en: The main issue is, whether from the provisions and construction of the statute, the express intention can be understood to create a public law remedy
The main issue is, whether from the provisions and construction of the statute, the express intention can be understood to create a private law remedy
The main issue is, whether from the provisions and construction of the statute, the intention can be understood to create a private law remedy
The main issue is, whether from the provisions and construction of the statute, the intention can be understood to create an implied public law remedy
The main issue is, whether from the provisions and construction of the statute, the implied intention can be understood to create a public law remedy

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best option. Where a claim is based on breach of statutory duty, the main issue is, whether from the provisions and construction of the statute, the intention can be understood to create a private law remedy. The question of whether a statute creates a duty in private law may sometimes be difficult and is likely to be as much dependent upon the apparent policy of the statute as upon the particular language which it uses. The general principles for the tort of breach of statutory duty were spelt out by the House of Lords in Cutler v Wandsworth Stadium Ltd and have been followed ever since. Lord Justice Du Parq, in the course of his judgment, had this to say: "...To a person in the science or art of legislation it may well seem strange that Parliament has not by now made it a rule to state explicitly what its intention is in a matter which is often of no little importance, instead of leaving it to the courts to discover, by careful examination and analysis of what is expressly said, what that intention may be supposed to be.... trust, however, that it will not be thought impertinent, in any sense of that word, to suggest respectfully that those who are responsible for framing legislation might consider whether the traditional practice, which obscures, if it does not conceal, the intention which Parliament has, or must be presumed to have, might =-лу

stem: Your client is facing a charge of blackmail.
ask: Since he does not fully understand what blackmail actually consists of, he asks you to advise on what the prosecution must Which of the following must the prosecution prove to gain a blackmail conviction?

options.en: The defendant made a warranted demand with menaces with a view to make a gain for himself or another, or with intent to cause a loss to another

The defendant made a warranted demand by the taking or carrying away of one person by another with menaces, whether he intended to make a gain for himself or another or with intent to cause a loss to another

The defendant made a warranted demand by the taking or carrying away of one person by another with menaces, and he intended to make a gain for himself or another or have intent to cause a loss to another
The defendant made an unwarranted demand with menaces with a view to make a gain for himself or another or with intent to cause a loss to another

The defendant made an unwarranted demand by the taking or carrying away of one person by another with menaces, and he intended to make a gain for himself or another or with intent to cause a loss to another

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The defendant made an unwarranted demand with menaces, with a view to make a gain for himself or another or with intent to cause a loss to another. This offence is created by section 21(1) of the Theft Act 1968. Sections 21(1) and (2) of that Act provide: (1) A person is guilty of blackmail if, with a view to gain for himself or another or with intent to cause loss to another, he makes any unwarranted demand with menaces; and for this purpose a demand with menaces is unwarranted unless the person making it does so in the belief: (a) that he has reasonable grounds for making the demand; and (b) that the use of the menaces is a proper means of reinforcing the by the person making the demand. Where the defendant believes that his demands are warranted, he cannot be held to be undertaking blackmail, as it is a central issue in blackmail for the demands to be unwarranted.

stem: A man exchanges contracts to purchase a property from a woman. The contract specifies that completion of the transaction will take place within two weeks. After exchange, the woman changes her mind and decides that she no longer wants to sell. She believes that, since completion of the transaction never took place, the man has no interest in the property.
ask: Which statement best describes the legal position?

options.en: The woman remains the legal and equitable owner of the property
The woman remains the legal and equitable owner of the property but the court could award damages to the man for breach of contract
The man is the legal owner of the property because the completion date has passed, but the woman remains the equitable owner
The man is the legal and equitable owner of the property
The woman remains the legal owner of the property but the man is the equitable owner

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The woman remains the legal owner of the property but the man is the equitable owner. Legal ownership of land does not pass until the transfer has been registered at Her Majesty's Land Registry (HMLR), and in this case, no transfer deed has been executed. However once contracts have been exchanged, equitable ownership of the land passes to the buyer. The woman holds the property on a constructive trust for the benefit of the man.

stem: A man bought lunch for his work colleague every day for the whole of last week. The following Monday, the man's colleague promised to buy him lunch in return.
ask: She has reneged on her promise and the man is quite miffed and wants something done To what extent can the man enforce his colleague's promise?

options.en: The man can enforce this promise, because there is consideration on both sides of the agreement
The man can enforce this promise, because his colleague's acceptance of his offer contained an implied promise that she would return the favour
The man cannot enforce this promise as his consideration, buying his colleague lunch, is past
The man can enforce this promise, because the conduct of the parties shows that there was a material agreement
The man can enforce the promise, because both parties must have contemplated that his colleague would return his kindness

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The man cannot enforce this promise as his consideration, buying the woman lunch, is past. Since the man had bought lunch for the woman, and she had therefore received the benefit before she had made her promise to return the compliment, the consideration was past and her promise is therefore unenforceable. Lead case: Re McArdle [1951] 1 All ER 905.

stem: A man and woman have agreed to act as trustees of a trust which contains a range of property, including land. Under the trust, the beneficiary is entitled to the income of the trust for 15 years, after which time the remainder will pass to her two children. The trustees have no experience in administering and managing a trust, and would, therefore, like to delegate the selection and management of trust investments to more experienced individuals.
ask: To which of the following persons would you advise them to delegate their powers?

options.en: A man who used to work as an independent financial adviser before the discovery of a number of financial irregularities in his practice
A real estate investor with a financial background
A man who runs a successful auction website
A friend to whom the trustees often turn for advice
One of the trustee's sister, who is a bank manager

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. A real estate investor with a financial background. In selecting an agent, the trustees must exercise such care and skill as is reasonable in the circumstances, pursuant to Section 1 of the Trustee Act 2000 (the Act). Choosing someone who has a dishonest track record would not be reasonable, especially where a central asset management function is involved, giving the agent access to the trust property, pursuant to Section 15 of the Act. A trusted friend (despite his successful business credentials) may lack the relevant experience required to choose and manage investments, and even a bank manager may not have the appropriate skills required (added to which is the potential conflict of with a financial background- assuming he indeed possesses the relevant experience and qualifications for this purpose.

stem: You are advising a firm of solicitors incorporated as a limited liability partnership (LLP). They wish to admit a new member to the LLP. The introduction of new members is not dealt with in their partnership agreement. Some of the membership is opposed to this particular person being admitted as a new member.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: In the absence of express provision in the partnership agreement, no new members may be admitted to the LLP after formation, and the LP must amend their partnership deed to deal with this issue
In the absence of express provision in the partnership agreement, a new member may be admitted only with the approval of 50% or more of the existing members
In the absence of express provision in the partnership agreement, a new member may be admitted only with the approval of 75% or more of the existing members
In the absence of express provision in the partnership agreement, a new member may be admitted only with the unanimous approval of all the existing members
In the absence of express provision in the partnership agreement, a new member may be admitted with no consent from existing members required

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. In the absence of express provision in the partnership agreement, a new member may be admitted only with the unanimous approval of all the existing members. Under Section 5(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Regulations 2001 (the Regulations), the mutual rights and duties of an LLP and its members are governed by an agreement between the members. In the absence of an express provision in the partnership agreement or in general law, the default provisions contained in Section 7 of the Regulations apply. Under Section 7(5), no person may be introduced as a member or voluntarily assign an are very general, and an LLP should always have a detailed partnership agreement that structures the operation of the LLP in accordance with the needs of the business and its members.

stem: A woman alleges that the government's policy allowing night flights at the nearby airport has caused her persistent sleep deprivation. She alleges her sleep deprivation constitutes a violation of the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention). The government argues that to close the airport to all night flights would undermine the UK's economy.
ask: Which option best describes the best advice to give to the woman?

options.en: Deprivation of the right to a private life is a breach of the woman's Convention rights and the court would be compelled to overturn the decision of the elected government
Deprivation of sleep constitutes inhuman or degrading treatment under the Convention and the court would be compelled to overturn the decision of the elected government
Although the woman has a right to a private life under the Convention, the court would be very reluctant to overturn the decision of the elected government
Although the woman has a right not to be tortured under the Convention, the court would be very reluctant to overturn the decision of the elected government
Although the woman has a right not to be treated in an inhuman or degrading manner under the Convention, the court would be very reluctant to overturn the decision of the elected government

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Although the woman has a right to a private life under the Convention, the court would be very reluctant to overturn the decision of the elected government. In Hatton v United Kingdom Application No 36022/97, (unreported) 8 July 2003 confirms how courts should approach questions such as these. In Hatton's case the applicants lived near Heathrow airport. They claimed that the government's policy on night flights at Heathrow violated their rights under Article 8 of the Convention. The court emphasised 'the fundamentally subsidiary nature' of the Convention. National authorities have 'direct democratic legitimation' and are in principle better placed than an may reasonably differ widely, 'the role of the domestic policy maker should be given special weight': see paragraph 97. A fair balance must be struck between the interests of the individual and of the community as a whole.

stem: A partner in the property department has been advising a client in relation to the purchase of a new home for occupation by the client's family, which is to be secured by a first legal mortgage over the property. The client has obtained advice from an independent financial adviser and has decided to take out a repayment mortgage with a particular building society. The client has asked the partner to make the arrangements for him to enter into the mortgage.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes what the partner should do?

options.en: The partner may make the arrangements for the mortgage, provided he does not receive any commission for doing so from the building society
The partner may make the arrangements for the mortgage, provided he does not receive commission for doing so from the building society which is more than £20

The partner may make the arrangements for the mortgage, because these may reasonably be regarded as a necessary part of the legal work that the partner is carrying out in relation to the client's house purchase
The partner may make the arrangements for the mortgage, because these may be construed as incidental to the legal work that the partner is carrying out in relation to the client's house purchase
The partner may not make the arrangements for the mortgage, because no exclusion or exemption applies

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The partner may make the arrangements for the mortgage, because these may be construed as incidental to the legal work that the partner is carrying out in relation to the client's house purchase. Arranging a regulated mortgage contract (defined as a first legal mortgage on land in the UK, which relates to a property for residential use by the borrower) constitutes a specified investment for the purpose of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA). The necessary exclusion would not apply here, as the partner could easily suggest to the client to ask his Independent Financial Adviser (IFA) to arrange the mortgage on his behalf. The activity will therefore -ГГ from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)), unless the arranging is complementary and incidental to the provision of legal services. This latter requirement would seem to be satisfied - arranging the regulated mortgage contract could be construed as incidental to the legal work the partner is carrying out in relation to the client's house purchase. The partner may receive commission for doing the arranging, provided he accounts for it (even if under £20) to the client - hence options A and B are both inaccurate.

stem: Your client calls you and says she is very upset with her young son and is going to give him a smack if you do not come and see her right away to discuss her will.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: You must report your client to the appropriate authority because of the risks to her son
You must not report your client to the appropriate authority in any circumstances
You should report your client to the appropriate authority, because it is better to err on the side of caution when a child's well-being is at stake
You should report your client to the appropriate authority, because the potential threat to her son's well-being is sufficiently serious to justify a breach of confidentiality
You should not report your client, because you would be in breach of your duty of confidentiality and the circumstances are not sufficiently serious to warrant the breach

explanation.en: The best answer is E. You should not report your client, because you would be in breach of your duty of confidentiality. 04.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct requires a solicitor to keep the affairs of clients confidential, except where disclosure is required or permitted by law or by your client. There may be exceptional circumstances involving children where you should consider revealing confidential information to an appropriate authority. There might be situations, for example, where an adult discloses abuse by himself or herself against a child but refuses to allow any disclosure. You must consider whether the threat to the child's life or health, both mental and physical, is sufficiently serious to justify a breach of the duty of does not appear to justify deciding to breach confidentiality because of the risks to the child, as the nature of the threat is not serious to the child's life or health and there are many things that can be done before that, e.g. going and seeing your client as she asked, telephoning her, writing to her etc. Therefore, the best answer is E.

ask: You have been asked to advise a client who is accused of being part Which of the following is the most accurate statement of the necessary elements for the offence of riot?

options.en: There must be at least 12 people present together who use or threaten unlawful violence for a common purpose
There must be at least 20 people present together who use or threaten unlawful violence for a common purpose
There must be at least 12 people present together who threaten violence for a common purpose
There must be at least 20 people who are together and threatening unlawful violence
There must be at least 12 people present together who use or threaten unlawful violence simultaneously for a common purpose

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The offence of rioting is defined in section 1 of the Public Order Act 1986. Where 12 or more persons who are present together use or threaten unlawful violence for a common purpose and the conduct of them (taken together) is such as would cause a person of reasonable firmness present at the scene to fear for his personal safety, each of the persons using unlawful violence for the common purpose is guilty of riot. It is immaterial whether or not the 12 or more use or threaten unlawful violence simultaneously (therefore E is incorrect).

stem: Before his sudden death, an 82 year-old man expressed a desire that his 24 year-old live-in nurse be allowed to spend the rest of her days living in his luxury £2,000,000 villa near Brighton. His executors drafted an agreement with the nurse to this effect and that she pays a £1 per year obligation, which was expressed to be 'in consideration' of the man's wishes. The man's children are not impressed with the arrangement and now argue that there was no contract, because the nurse had not provided sufficient consideration.
ask: How would you advise the man's children?

options.en: There was no contract, because the nurse had provided insufficient consideration
The actual 'consideration' was the payment of £1
The agreement to pay £1 to live in the villa is totally inadequate in terms of its relationship to its value
Since the agreement stated that it was 'in consideration' of man's wishes, this is proof of sufficient consideration
Past consideration is no consideration, so it is not valid and cannot be used to sue on a contract

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The actual 'consideration' was the payment of £1, even though the payment of £1 could in no way be regarded as anything approaching a commercial rent for the property. While the statement that the agreement was 'in consideration' of the testator's wishes, this does not necessarily constitute 'consideration' in its technical contractual sense. Rather, it is merely expressing the motive for making the agreement. The actual 'consideration' was the payment of £1. Lead case: Thomas v Thomas (1842) 2 QB 851. Comment: In Thomas v Thomas, the court pointed out that consideration must be 'something which is of some

stem: A settlor executes a trust instrument by which she declares a trust over her share portfolio, with the income to be distributed by her trustee amongst her nieces and nephews as her trustees see fit.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the?

options.en: The settlor has created an inter vivos charitable trust
The settlor has created a testamentary charitable trust
The settlor has created an inter vivos discretionary trust
The settlor has created a testamentary discretionary trust
The settlor has created an irrevocable trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The trust is inter vivos because it takes effect prior to the settlor's death. As the trustees are given discretion as to how to apply the trust income, the trust would be termed a discretionary trust.

stem: Three men are solicitors who agree to set themselves up to practise together. They contribute equally to the running of shared office premises and support staff (owned/employed by a limited company of which they are all members and directors) and meet regularly to discuss various issues of management of the office and their brand in general. They bill their clients separately to each other and payment of invoices goes directly to each of them.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The three men are trading as a partnership
The three men are not trading as a partnership, because they are not carrying on a commercial business
The three men are not trading as a partnership, because they are not carrying on their business in common
The three men are not trading as a partnership, because they are not carrying on their business with a view to profit
The three men are not trading as a partnership, because they are not carrying on their business in common with a view to profit

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The three men are not trading as a partnership, because they are not carrying on their business in common with a view to profit. The three men are clearly in business together, as they are practising as solicitors with a view to making money. Although they share marketing, office and staff expenses and all have an equal say in how those elements of their enterprise are managed, their finances are kept separate to each other and they all invoice their own clients directly. They are not carrying on business in common and are not intending to make a common profit. They could more aptly be described as three separate sole proprietors who simply share incidental expenses. stem: A married couple, where the wife was the sole earner, complained that the UK income tax regime had the effect of taxing comparable couples in a discriminatory way on grounds of sex and marital status. First, married couples where the husband was the sole earner were taxed more heavily than married couples in which the wife was the sole earner. Second, married couples were taxed more heavily than co- habiting couples who were not married.
ask: Which option best describes the available remedy, if any, afforded to the married couple under the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA)?

options.en: The married couple can find redress under the HRA, as the right not to be discriminated against is a fundamental human right
The married couple need not find redress under the HRA, as fundamental rights such as the right to marital equality cannot be governmentally waived
The married couple cannot find redress under the HRA; it only protects individuals from being discriminated against in respect of their European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)
The married couple can find redress under the HRA, as far as equal taxation goes, but not in respect of marital equality
The married couple may not find redress under the HRA, as far as equal taxation goes, but may do so in respect to marital equality

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option C is correct. The tax measure giving extra advantages to a wife who is the earner in the family has an objective and reasonable justification in positively encouraging married women to work. Married couples are not necessarily in a similar position to co-habiting couples for the purposes of taxation. Article 14 of the Convention only protects people from discrimination who are less favourably treated compared to others in a similar position. Accordingly, there is no violation of Article 14. The UK has not signed on to Protocol 12, which would extend the right not to be discriminated to all legal rights. Currently, Article 14 (Prohibition of Discrimination), as read into UK law by the HRA,). -г

stem: A lorry driver stopped to allow a 13 year old girl to cross a main road. He held out his right hand to warn traffic coming along to stop and with his left hand signalled for her to cross, but as she passed the front of the lorry she was struck and injured by a car being driven at excessive speed as it overtook the lorry. The car driver had failed to see the lorry driver's outstretched hand.
ask: Which below answer best states the legal position?

options.en: The girl cannot be said to have been contributorily negligent, because an ordinary child of 13 could not be expected to have done any more that she did to avoid the accident
The girl can be said to have been contributorily negligent, because an ordinary child of 13 could be expected to have done more that she did to avoid the accident

The girl can be said to have been contributorily negligent, because she was negligent in moving past the front of the lorry into the open road without pausing to establish whether there was any approaching traffic

The girl can be said to have been contributorily negligent, because she was negligent in moving past the front of the lorry into the open road without pausing to establish whether there was any approaching traffic and her damages would be reduced by one third
The girl can be said to have been contributorily negligent, because she failed to go through the proper mental processes and relied unquestioningly on the lorry driver's signal

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. A judge should only find a child contributorily negligent if they are of such an age as can reasonably be expected to take precautions for their own safety. At the age of the girl, it was reasonable for her to rely on the driver's signal, whereas it might not have been for an adult. Lead case: Gough v Thorne [1966].

stem: Your client is aggrieved that his necessary medical treatment is not freely available on the National Health Service (NHS). He wishes to challenge the local NHS trust's authority to decide the matter. Other complainants are considering following the judicial review process regarding the same matter.
ask: Which of the following is the best states the availability of judicial review?

options.en: Judicial review is available to challenge any Act of Parliament with which an individual does not agree
Judicial review can only be initiated by a public body
Judicial review is available to anyone who feels a public body has acted in an unlawful manner
Judicial review is inextricably linked to human rights
Judicial review is only related to acts of the government

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Judicial review can be initiated by an individual (or a group) who feels that a public body has acted against their authority. Judicial review is, at times, linked to human rights, but this is not an essential part of the process. The process is against a public body and not specifically against the government, with little recourse against primary Acts of Parliament. Acts of Parliament can only be the subject of judicial review where there is a human rights element.

stem: A man and woman make an offer to purchase a brand new house from a local builder for £100,000.
ask: The builder tells them that, in addition to the purchase price, they will have to make a regular payment of £25 per year for the property and, provided that they do this, they will be able to use the property as their own for the Which of the following statements best describes the interest that the man and woman will acquire in the property?

options.en: They will acquire a leasehold interest in the property for 99 years and at the end of that time will become the freehold owners
They will become the freehold owners because they are purchasing a house
They will acquire a leasehold interest in the house for 99 years
They will acquire a legal easement for 99 years giving them the right to enter the house and use it
They will acquire an interest under a trust of land allowing them to occupy the property for 99 years

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. They will acquire a leasehold interest in the house for 99 years. As their interest in the property is only for a limited duration and they are required to pay rent, the interest is not capable of being a freehold. The fact that they are purchasing a house as opposed to a flat is irrelevant, as it is possible for houses to be disposed of by way of a lease. The fact that they are acquiring an interest in the land which allows them to use it "as their own" implies that they are not being granted an easement, where the grantee has no dominion over the land subject to the easement.

stem: A dog breeder placed an advertisement in the classified advertisements section of a newspaper, which stated: 'Jack Russell puppies for sale - £150 each'. A man responded to the advert, sending payment for one dog. The dog breeder declined to sell the dog to him and returned the man's payment.
ask: Which option best states the legal position?

options.en: An advertisement in the classified section of a newspaper, such as was used by the dog breeder, constitutes the acceptance of an offer
An advertisement in the classified section of a newspaper, such as was used by the dog breeder, constitutes a unilateral offer
An advertisement in the classified section of a newspaper, such as was used by the dog breeder, constitutes a bilateral offer
An advertisement in the classified section of a newspaper, such as was used by the dog breeder, constitutes an invitation to treat
An advertisement in the classified section of a newspaper, such as was used by the dog breeder, constitutes the communication of the acceptance of an offer

explanation.en: ParA You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The dog breeder's advertisement was not an offer to sell but an invitation to treat. Advertisements such as the one in the scenario are treated in the same way as the display of goods with price tags. If the courts were to treat such generalised advertisements as offers, this would lead to the absurd situation whereby, everyone who replied to the advertisement would be accepting it, and would therefore be entitled to a Jack Russell puppy. Lead Case: Partridge v Crittenden [1968] 2 All ER 421.

ask: A private company limited by shares has issued 100 ordinary shares of £1 each to three members, who each paid £100 to the company when the shares were issued to Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Creditors of the company would be able to claim against the three members directly for any debts that the company could not meet itself
Creditors of the company would be able to claim against the three members directly for any debts that the company could not meet itself up to the value of £100 each
The company would be able to claim against the three members for any debts that the company could not meet itself
The company would be able to claim against the three members for any debts that the company could not meet itself up to the value of £100 each
Neither the company nor the company's creditors would be able to claim against the three members for any debts that the company could not meet itself

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Neither the company nor the company's creditors would be able to claim against the three members for any debts that the company could not meet itself. As the company has a separate legal personality, its creditors have no ability to claim against the members in respect of the debts of the company. The members are only liable to contribute in respect of any proportion of the value of any of their shares which remains unpaid, and this liability is to the company and not its creditors. As the members in this case have all fully paid for their shares, they have no further liability and the company would not be able to claim anything from them.

stem: A newly elected Member of the Welsh Assembly is about to take her seat. She wishes to propose legislation by way of introducing a Bill. She seeks advice regarding the extent, if any, of Welsh law-making powers in devolved areas.
ask: Which option best advises the Assembly Member?

options.en: The Welsh Assembly can make laws on subjects in all of the areas for which the Assembly Government has responsibilities, without needing agreement from the Westminster Parliament

The Welsh Assembly can make secondary legislation on subjects in all of the areas for which the Assembly Government has responsibilities, which can be amended by Westminster parliamentary primary legislation in terms of its effect in Wales

The Welsh Assembly can make primary legislation on subjects in all of the areas for which the Assembly Government has responsibilities, which can be amended by Westminster parliamentary primary legislation in terms of its effect in Wales

The Welsh Assembly can make primary and secondary legislation on subjects in all of the areas for which the Assembly Government has responsibilities, which can be amended by Westminster parliamentary primary legislation in terms of its effect in Wales
The Welsh Assembly can make laws on subjects in all of the areas for which the Assembly Government has responsibilities with agreement from the Westminster Parliament

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best option. The Welsh Assembly can make laws on subjects in all of the 20 areas for which the Assembly Government has responsibilities, without needing the Westminster Parliament's agreement. The areas include agriculture; education; the environment; health; housing and local government. The subjects that the Assembly can pass laws on are set out in Schedule 7 to the Government of Wales Act 2006.

stem: A brewery worker, reasonably, but mistakenly, thought a man was about to steal a crate of beer from his boss's wagon.
ask: The worker struck the man on the back of the neck, and the blow caused him to fall under the wheels of the wagon, injuring the Is the brewery likely to be vicariously liable for the worker's actions?

options.en: Yes, because the worker was protecting his employer's property, and therefore acting in the course of his employment
No, since it was an unauthorised tortious act by the worker, so he was not acting in the course of his employment
Yes, because the worker was acting in self-defence and the fact that he used a greater degree of force than was necessary does not absolve the brewery of liability
No, because the worker's action was personal and not permitted or linked with his employment
No, because the worker's violence in reaction to the supposed theft wasn't made to protect the brewery's property, but borne of malice

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The brewery would be liable as the worker's was protecting his employer's property and therefore acting with the brewery's implied permission. Where an employee takes emergency measures with the intention of benefiting his employer in cases where the latter's property appears to be in danger, the employer will tend to be liable even though the acts of the employee are excessive. Lead case: Poland v Parr & Sons (1927) 1 KB 236.

stem: A man found a wallet containing cash in the street and, seeing no one nearby, picked it up and took it home. He decided to put an advert in the local paper, to the effect that if no one claims the wallet in one week, he will consider it to be his. Three days later, the man sees a message in a local shop about the lost wallet, but chooses to ignore it, as he has had no response from his advert. He asks your advice as to whether or not this
ask: is definitely theft?

options.en: When he picked the wallet up, he did so innocently; therefore it is not theft
The issue of appropriation is crucial and, as he has now acted in a way that is contrary to the owner's rights, he has now committed theft
Placing an advert to find the owner means he has done all he needs to do to prevent the offence of theft from arising
Unless the owner contacts him, directly, he has no obligation to hand the wallet back
As it had cash in it, the man should have been aware that it had not simply been discarded and therefore he is guilty of theft

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The issue of appropriation is crucial and, as he has now acted in a way that is contrary to the owner's rights, he has now committed theft. Although answers C, D, and E are all evidentially important, the central point is that the man has appropriated the wallet and is using the property in a way that is against the will of the owner; therefore, he is guilty of theft under Section 3 of the Theft Act 1968. The fact that the man 'found it' is irrelevant.

stem: After a particularly grievous terrorist attack in London, a suspect was arrested and held in police custody, with neither access to legal advice nor legal representation. During this period the suspect confessed to the attack.
ask: Amnesty International (Amnesty) now wishes to bring a claim against the UK Government for breaching the suspect's rights afforded under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Which option best advises Amnesty?

options.en: An advocacy organisation like Amnesty does not have a claim under the Convention or the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA)
Amnesty does not have a claim, because the policy of denying terrorist suspects access to legal advice is a well-established custom
Amnesty has a claim if it made an application as part of a class action suit with other similarly treated suspects
As an advocacy organisation, Amnesty has a claim under the Convention or the HRA
Amnesty does not have a claim because the complainant must be a natural person

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option A is correct. An advocacy organisation like Amnesty does not have a claim under the Convention or the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA). Only victims may assert a claim; advocacy organisations may not. As per Section 7(7) of the HRA, the term "victim" has the same meaning as under Article 34 of the Convention. UK decisions carry forward the thinking enunciated in case law of the European Court of Human Rights on the matter of "standing". Class action suits are not allowed. However, advocacy organisations may challenge the actions or decisions of public authorities, if their own member's rights are infringed on.

stem: Your client's employer failed to properly maintain the fork lift truck that your client regularly uses to perform his duties. One day, the brakes fail and the truck crashes into a wall. Your client is physically unharmed but is shaken up as a result of the incident. He is fine after a couple of days.
ask: Can your client claim damages from his employer for psychiatric injury?

options.en: Yes, because transient shock is a recognised psychiatric injury
Yes, because employers' liability is strict in such cases
No, because it is not foreseeable that the claimant would suffer psychiatric injury as a result of the incident
No, because no physical injury was suffered
No, because a psychiatric injury claim requires a recognised psychiatric injury; transient shock will not suffice

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. No, because a psychiatric injury claim requires a recognised psychiatric injury; transient shock will not suffice. Where a duty of care is established, the recovery of damages is contingent on causation of a recognised psychiatric illness. In McLoughlin v O'Brien Lord Bridge stated: "...the first hurdle which a plaintiff claiming damages of the kind in question must surmount is to establish that he is suffering, not merely grief, distress, or any other normal emotion, but a positive psychiatric illness..." Similarly, in Page v Smith [1996] AC 155, it was stated that: "the ordinary emotions of anxiety, fear, grief or transient shock are not conditions for which the law gives compensation..." is physically unharmed so he did need to prove the existence of recognised psychiatric injury to claim damages from his employer.

stem: A patient is in a persistent vegetative state and is being kept alive by artificial feeding techniques and the use of antibiotics. There is no hope of the patient making a recovery. Doctors are unsure if they can terminate life support.
ask: Which option best states the courts' approach to such cases?

options.en: Doctors may discontinue life-sustaining treatment to a patient in a persistent vegetative state and with no hope of recovery where they act out of a compassionate motive
Doctors may not discontinue life-sustaining treatment to a patient in a persistent vegetative state and with no hope of recovery, unless the patient has given his explicit prior consent to do so
Doctors may discontinue life-sustaining treatment to a patient in a persistent vegetative state and with no hope of recovery, because a doctor's duty to his patient is absolute
Doctors may discontinue life-sustaining treatment to a patient in a persistent vegetative state and with no hope of recovery, even though they know that this will cause the patient to die
Doctors may discontinue life sustaining treatment to a patient in a persistent vegetative state and with no hope of recovery, if they do not know that this will cause the patient to die

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is D. A decision to discontinue treatment in these circumstances is considered to be an omission rather than an act. Discontinuation would not be the substantive cause of the patient's death; rather it would fail to continue to prolong his life. Lead case: Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993] 1 AlI ER 821 HL

ask: Your client wants to appeal a decision of the High Court directly to the Supreme What is the function of the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom?

options.en: The final court of appeal for all civil and criminal cases in England and Wales and civil cases in Scotland and the arbiter of disputes in relation to devolution and laws made by the governments/assemblies of England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland

The final court of appeal for all civil and criminal cases in England, Wales and Scotland and civil cases in Northern Ireland and the arbiter of disputes in relation to devolution and laws made by the governments/assemblies of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland

The final court of appeal for all civil and criminal cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and civil cases in Scotland and the arbiter of disputes in relation to devolution and laws made by the governments/assemblies of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland
The final court of appeal for all civil and criminal cases in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
The final court of appeal for all civil and criminal cases in England, Scotland and Wales

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is C. The final court of appeal for all civil and criminal cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and civil cases in Scotland and the arbiter of disputes in relation to devolution and laws made by the governments/assemblies of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. The Supreme Court is the final court of appeal for all civil and criminal cases, focusing particularly on civil and criminal cases of the greatest public and constitutional importance. The Supreme Court also hears cases from the highest courts of Scotland and Northern Ireland - the Court of Session and Court of, respectively. Criminal cases in Scotland, however, still have the High Court of Justiciary as their highest appellate court. The Supreme Court is also the arbiter of disputes in relation to devolution and laws made by the governments/assemblies of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Like the House of Lords before it, the Supreme Court is unable to overturn Acts of the Westminster Parliament, due to the principle of parliamentary sovereignty. However, it can still make declarations of incomnstibilit undar Cartion Aoftha Lamon Dinhtr interpret and apply the law in accordance with the rules of statutory interpretation.

stem: Your client's mother phones you in a bit of a panic as her son has been charged with a public order offence. She is unable to provide a lot of details but tells you that your client is due to stand trial in the crown court.
ask: Which of the following could be the offence that your client is charged with?

options.en: It must be a racially aggravated offence
It could be any public order offence at all
It can only be riot as this is the only offence that is indictable
It could be riot, violent disorder or affray
It could be either riot or violent disorder as these are more serious

explanation.en: The best answer is D. Riot, violent disorder and affray are all potentially indictable and could result in an appearance before the crown court. More information about the offence would be required.
