stem: A celebrity had multiple images of his private life published by a national newspaper, some of which included images of his children. The images were supplied to the newspaper by the children's former au pair. The celebrity wishes to know if any law may have been breached.
ask: Which of the following options best describes the legal issues a court would consider in these circumstances?

options.en: The court would consider whether there was a breach of trust and/or unauthorised disclosure of personal information in violation of the right of secrecy guaranteed by the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)
The court would consider whether there was a breach of contract and/or unauthorised disclosure of personal information in violation of the right of equality guaranteed by the Convention
The court would consider whether there was a breach of confidence and/or unauthorised disclosure of personal information in violation of the right of privacy guaranteed by the Convention

The court would consider whether there was a breach of the duty of care and/or unauthorised disclosure of personal information in violation of the right of confidentiality guaranteed by the Convention
The court would consider whether there was a breach of confidence and/or unauthorised disclosure of personal information in violation of the right of confidentiality guaranteed by the Convention

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option C is correct. The questions the court would consider are whether the au pair had committed a breach of confidence and whether there was a reasonable expectation of privacy (and a violation of it), under Article 8 of the Convention (i.e. the new and the traditional approaches). While there remains no general tort of invasion of privacy as such, non- personal information continues to be protected by the traditional equitable claim for breach of confidence. The law took a new direction when it was required to give added protection in cases where personal information was misused or wrongfully disclosed in violation of the right of privacy which was guaranteed Article 8 of the Convention. Under the Human Rights Act 1998, effect had to be given to the right to privacy (guaranteed by Article 8 of the Convention) and the right to freedom of expression (guaranteed by Article 10 of the Convention). These values are as much applicable in disputes between individuals, or between an individual and a non-governmental body such as a newspaper, as they are in disputes between individuals and a public authority. The traditional equitable claim for breach of confidence has been transformed in order to extend protection to private information (regardless of whether it is confidential) so as to give effect to Article 8 of the Convention.

ask: A settlor makes a gift of "£100,000 to the vicar of my local church to build and maintain a suitable tomb for me, to decorate the same with flowers, in so far as my trustees may legally do so." Which of the following best explains the legal position regarding the gift?

options.en: The settlor has made a valid gift
The settlor's money will be held for him on resulting trust, because there is no beneficiary to enforce the trust
The settlor's money will be held for him on resulting trust, because the trust promotes vague and uncertain purposes
The settlor's money will be held for him on resulting trust, because there is no perpetuity period
The settlor's money will be held for him on resulting trust, because the trust merely promotes a purpose

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the correct answer. The settlor has made a valid gift. Normally, a trust cannot exist unless there is at least one beneficiary to enforce it (Morice v Bishop of Durham). The law does not allow trusts to merely promote a purpose, unless that purpose is charitable (Leahy v AG for NSW). Nor does the law permit trusts that promote vague, uncertain purposes (In re Astor's ST). In Re Endacott, however, the Court of Appeal accepted that there were certain 'troublesome, anomalous and aberrant cases' that allowed exceptions and could not now be overruled. One of the four exceptions mentioned were trusts for the erection or maintenance of monuments or graves. The exceptions could not be held in In re Hooper to imply the permitted perpetuity period of 21 years.

stem: You are a solicitor investigating title to an unregistered car park on behalf of a client and the seller's solicitor has deduced title to you and the good root of title makes reference to the land using measurements from fixed points on the ground. The good root of title does not include a plan. In all other respects, the title is satisfactory.
ask: Which statement best describes the position?

options.en: The description of the property is inadequate and you should raise a requisition requesting the delivery of all pre-root documents until one containing a plan is produced
The description of the property is inadequate but you are prevented from raising a requisition requesting the delivery of all pre-root documents until one containing a plan is produced
The description of the property is adequate, but you may raise a requisition requesting the delivery of all pre-root documents until one containing a plan is produced
The description of the property is adequate and you are prevented from raising a requisition requesting the delivery of all pre-root documents until one containing a plan is produced
The title is defective and you should advise your client not to proceed with the purchase

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The description of the property is adequate and you are prevented from raising a requisition requesting the delivery of all pre-root documents until one containing a plan is produced. A verbal description of the property containing measurements is sufficient to enable the property to be identified and therefore title has been deduced sufficiently. You would not be permitted to require production of pre-root documents based solely upon the lack of a plan.

stem: A mail order company receives money from customers buying items from its catalogues before the items are sent to the customers. The company realises it is in danger of insolvency and segregates all its customer prepayments into a distinct bank account, with money being moved from the account only once the item is sent to the
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position on liquidation of the?

options.en: The money will be returned to the company's customers on liquidation, because an express trust has been created
The money will be distributed among the company's creditors on liquidation, because an express trust has been created
The money will be returned to the company's customers on liquidation, because a constructive trust will be imposed by the court
The money will be distributed among the company's creditors on liquidation, because a constructive trust will be imposed by the court
The money will be distributed equally by the court between the company's creditors and the company's customers on liquidation, because no trust will apply

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The money will be returned to the company's customers on liquidation, because an express trust has been created. The company's intention is clearly to create a trust over the prepayments by customers. The company, as legal owner of the bank account, is a trustee; the customers are the beneficiaries in the period between making a prepayment and receiving their items. In general, the English view is that the court prefers to uncover an express trust, rather than impose a constructive trust in order to reverse unjust enrichment by the company's creditors. See Re Kayford [1975].

stem: Three persons are the directors of a private company limited by shares. The company carries on a business as a property development company and the directors are authorised by the company's articles of association to purchase commercial land for the purposes of investment to make a profit or for the operational needs of the company. One of the three directors sees land that she wishes to buy for herself for future investment. She then buys the land on the company's name. She plans the company to hold title to the property until she can afford to buy it from the company at the same price.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position with respect to that?

options.en: The director has acted outside of her powers and the transaction is void against third parties
The director has acted outside of her powers but the transaction is not void against third parties
The director has not acted outside of her powers; however, the transaction would be voidable against third parties
The director has not acted outside of her powers and the transaction is not void against third parties
The director has acted outside of her powers unless the act is subsequently ratified by a resolution of the board of directors

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The director has acted outside of her powers but the transaction is not void against third parties. The director's powers to acquire land on behalf of the company can only be used where this is to generate a profit for the company or for the company's own use. If the director acquires the property for any other purpose, she has acted outside of her powers. Although a third party would be able to rely on the director's acts, the director would be in breach of her statutory duty to the company to act within her powers and would be liable to it for any loss caused.

stem: A radical preacher was tried and convicted by a domestic court for incitement to murder after making inflammatory speeches against 'non-believers'. His appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) was subsequently dismissed. He seeks to make an application to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), based on the fact that the context in which his words were spoken was, at the time, perfectly acceptable political and religious rhetoric. You are instructed to represent him, but you have concerns that the application will fail for lack of substantiation.
ask: Which option best states the evidentiary ground on which the ECtHR may declare an individual's application inadmissible?

options.en: The ECtHR may declare any individual application inadmissible if it considers it to be "obviously unmeritorious"
The ECtHR may declare any individual application inadmissible if it considers it to be "manifestly ill-founded"
The ECtHR may declare any individual application inadmissible if it considers it to be "evidently inconsequential"
The ECtHR may declare any individual application inadmissible if it considers it to be "unmistakably trivial"
The ECtHR may declare any individual application inadmissible if it considers it to be "unquestionably frivolous"

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. According to Article 35 § 3 of the Convention, the ECtHR may declare any individual application inadmissible if it considers it to be "manifestly ill-founded". Applications can be declared inadmissible on this ground both by Committees - i.e. without the application being communicated to the respondent government - or by Chambers. A Chamber may do so either before or after communication of the case to the respondent government. This ground of admissibility constitutes an important means for the ECtHR to weed out unmeritorious - indeed also frivolous - applications. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 35 § 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

stem: A post office employee left a manhole covered by a small tent, with a paraffin lamp as a warning to pedestrians and motorists. A 10 year old boy entered the tent with his eight year old friend, took the lamp, and they entered the manhole.
ask: Once inside the manhole, the eight-8 year old dropped the lamp, triggering an explosion (which was unique in its fashion because the paraffin had unusually vaporised), badly injuring How would you advise the injured boy's parents?

options.en: The boy cannot recover damages, because the injury he sustained was of a kind which was not foreseeable
Although it might have been foreseeable that the boy would enter the tent out of curiosity, it was not to be expected that the injuries would be as serious as those which he in fact sustained
The boy was clearly up to no good, and since the boy was a trespasser, the defence of ex turpi causa non oritur actio applies
The post office is likely to be liable for the boy's injuries, since he is a child; therefore, the post office must prove that it wasn't responsible for the accident
The accident was caused by a recognised danger and that made it foreseeable, even though the way in which it happened might have been unexpected

explanation.en: E is correct. Although the manner in which the accident occurred was unexpected, the post office would still be liable, even if the accident occurred in a way which could not have been foreseen, because the act was caused by a recognised danger. Lead case: Hughes v Lord Advocate [1963] UKHL 8.

stem: The defendant attacked someone whilst in a state of sleep induced automatism. There is no evidence of external cause and a doctor's finding indicates that a sleep disorder was the reason- an internal cause. The trial judge has ruled that a defence of insanity can be raised.
ask: Which option best advises the defendant as regards to the burden of proof where a defendant raises insanity as a defence?

options.en: The prosecution must prove that the defendant is sane on the balance of probabilities, or satisfy the jury so that they are sure of the defendant's guilt
The prosecution must prove that that the defendant is sane beyond reasonable doubt, or satisfy the jury so that they are sure of the defendant's guilt
The defence must prove on the balance of probabilities the elements of insanity
The defence must prove beyond reasonable doubt the elements of insanity
The defence must prove the elements of insanity beyond reasonable doubt, or satisfy the jury so that they are sure of the defendant's innocence

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best option. The defence must prove on the balance of probabilities the elements of insanity. The only exception to the rule recognised by common law that it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the defendant's guilt is with regard to the defence of insanity; since the presumption of mental capacity is usually sufficient to prove that the accused acted consciously and voluntarily (there is a rebuttable presumption that everyone is sane). Where a defence of insanity is raised, the defendant must discharge the full legal burden in order to be acquitted. In other words, the legal burden of proof placed on the defence is that every person of the age of discretion is. In such a case, the burden is on the defence to establish insanity at the time of the offence on the balance of probabilities. This was reaffirmed in the case of Kebilene [1999].

stem: A man is the freehold owner of an industrial estate and disposes of one of the warehouse units on a long lease to a woman. Unfortunately, the man's solicitors mistakenly fail to include an express right in the lease for the woman to use the roads in the estate to drive goods vehicles up to the warehouse to be unloaded. A public footpath connects the rear of the warehouse to the public highway, but this is not wide enough to take the woman's vehicles.
ask: Which of the following options best describes the interest that the woman will acquire over the estate roads?

options.en: The woman will have an implied easement of necessity over the estate roads, because she has no other means of vehicular access and this is required to use the warehouse
The woman will have an easement implied by common intention over the estate roads, because the man intended to grant an easement in any event
The woman will have no implied easement over the estate roads, because an alternative means of access exists via the public footpath
The woman will acquire an easement to use the estate roads via the Doctrine of Lost Modern Grant
It is not possible to include easements in leases and, therefore, a separate Deed of Easement would be required in any event

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The woman will have an implied easement of necessity over the estate roads because she has no other means of vehicular access and this is required to use the warehouse. Notwithstanding that an alternative means of access exists via the footpath, it was intended at the time of the grant of the lease that vehicular access (necessary for the proper enjoyment of the warehouse) would be granted over the estate roads and, therefore, an easement of necessity over the estate roads would be implied to give effect to the common intention of the parties: Thorburn v Holland [2002] All ER (D) 220 (Apr).

stem: A toy manufacturer has been negotiating a deal over its new soft toy with a large toy retailer. It recently received a letter of intent from the retailer saying how much of a pleasure it had been to meet with the toy manufacturer's representatives, how impressed they were with the product and that the retailer wished to purchase a large quantity of the toys. The toy retailer have not yet stipulated the exact quantity of the toys required, how much they are prepared to pay, or when they require them.
ask: Did the toy retailer's letter of intent amount to a legally binding promise?

options.en: Yes, because the consequences of any decision by the toy retailer to repudiate its moral responsibility are matters a court cannot turn a blind eye to
No, but once the toy manufacturer signs the letter and sends it back to the retailer by first class post, it becomes a binding agreement
Yes, because letters of intent are legally binding, so the retailer cannot go back on the deal
No, because there was not enough detail to show that the toy retailer was thinking of entering into an agreement, and it did not contain enough detail about the terms of any contract
No, because letters of intent are of minimal commercial importance and entirely devoid of legal effect

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. There was not enough detail to show that the toy retailer was thinking of entering into an agreement, and it did not contain enough detail about the terms of any contract. Letters of intent are not normally legally binding, and the facts of the scenario show that the retailer was only thinking of entering into an agreement. It did not contain enough detail about the terms of any contract to be legally binding. Lead case: British Steel v Cleveland Bridge (1981) 24 BLR 94. mercius portunice and entirely BUS CUIE

stem: A testator settles his 'valued employees and his personal secretary' with 'equal gifts of no more than £10,000 each out of a total fund of £100,000.' The testator only had one personal secretary during his entire career.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The employees and the personal secretary would each receive a total of £50,000
The employees would receive the entire £100,000
The personal secretary would receive the entire £100,000
The personal secretary would receive £10,000, but the employees would receive nothing
The entire trust power would be invalid

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The entire trust power would be invalid. 'Equal gifts' require a fixed trust so that the trustees can know between how many people the fund is to be divided in order to achieve equal shares. However, the category of 'valued employees' would appear to be so vague and insufficiently certain, under the complete list test, as to be incapable of effect. It is true that a trust made up of many different powers can remain valid if the one offending, or void, power contained in the trust is simply removed. However, it would be contrary to the intention of the trust to grant the entire £100,000 to the testator's personal secretary; therefore, it would not be permissible to allow the trust to be valid in relation to the secretary's

stem: A man and woman are the directors of a public company limited by shares. The two directors execute a contract by which the company agrees to purchase a guaranteed level of haulage services from a supplier. Halfway through performance of the contract, the company goes into liquidation and the supplier is faced with losing 50% of the income from his contract with the company. The supplier notes that the two directors have signed the contract and he seeks to bring proceedings against them personally for the outstanding money due.
ask: How would you advise the two directors of the company?

options.en: The company is liable under the contract and the two directors are personally liable as directors in the event of the company's liquidation, as they signed the contract
The company is liable under the contract and the two directors are not personally liable as directors in the event of the company's liquidation, even though they signed the contract
The company is not liable under the contract and the two directors are personally liable as directors in the event of the company's liquidation, as they signed the contract
The company is not liable under the contract and the two directors are not personally liable as directors, even though they signed the contract
The company is liable under the contract until the point of dissolution and the two directors are liable after that, as they signed the contract

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The company is liable under the contract and the two directors are not personally liable as directors in the event of the company's liquidation, even though they signed the contract. The two directors signed the contract in their capacity as directors of the company, and in that respect, they were acting as the company's agent. In the same way that debts of the company do not accrue to the members beyond their agreed level of liability due to the company having a separate legal personality, directors are not liable for the acts of the company provided that they act in good faith.

stem: The new British Prime Minister has just moved in to 10 Downing Street. He has been invited to Buckingham Palace for his first weekly meeting with the Queen. He seeks advice from the Permanent Secretary regarding how the Queen may express her views to the Prime Minister on governmental matters.
ask: Which advice should the Permanent Secretary give to the Prime Minister?

options.en: l The Queen may overrule, argue and advise
The Queen may encourage, advise and observe
The Queen may advise, warn and encourage
The Queen may warn, revise and observe
The Queen may not express an opinion on governmental matters

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The Queen may express her views privately to the Prime Minister at their weekly audience where she may advise, warn and encourage.

stem: The Abortion Act 1967 (the Act) stipulated that a pregnancy should be terminated by a registered medical practitioner. Subsequent advancements in medical techniques meant that non-registered medical practitioners, such as nurses, were perfectly competent to perform these procedures.
ask: The minority of the House of Lords (as then constituted, now the Supreme Court) found that a nurse's involvement was unlawful under the Act, because, in their opinion, the plain and ordinary words of the Act clearly and explicitly stated that only a registered medical practitioner could carry out Which rule of statutory interpretation did the minority use in this example?

options.en: The golden rule
The literal rule
The mischief rule
The purposive approach
The unified common approach

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The minority employed the literal rule in this example. The Literal rule applies the plain, ordinary, literal meaning of a statute, with barely any interpretation. In this case the minority construed the statute according to the words used by Parliament irrespective of the unsatisfactory result. Lead case: Royal College of Nursing v DHSS [1981] 1 AlI ER 545.

stem: You represent a client who has been charged with a particularly horrendous murder and confesses to you that he is guilty.
ask: The client then tells you that he still wishes to Which of the following statements best describes what you should do in respect of whether you should reveal this information?

options.en: Your duty of confidentiality to the client would prevent you from revealing this information
Your duty of confidentiality to the client is overridden by the interests of justice and you would therefore be required to reveal this information
Your duty of confidentiality to the client requires you to continue to defend your client's innocence to the court
Your duty of confidentiality to the client requires you to suggest to the court that another person, who was with the client at the time of his arrest, is guilty of the offence
Your duty of confidentiality to the client requires that you refrain from acting any further on the client's behalf

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Your duty of confidentiality to the client would prevent you from revealing this information. You may continue to act for your client, so long as you do not mislead the court by putting in a spurious defence protesting the client's innocence or suggesting that someone else is guilty - i.e. by advancing a positive case. It is not misleading the court to require the prosecution to prove its case.

stem: A building landlord seeks a tenant for one of its empty floors. He finds a charity looking for office space and draws up an agreement giving the charity the right to occupy the floor for three years, with the right to exclude all others, including the landlord, from the floor. The landlord writes in a clause to state that the charity will not pay any rent, as it is a start-up charity with minimal funds. The landlord writes 'LICENCE' at the top of the document and inserts a paragraph to the effect that the agreement is specifically meant to take effect as a licence.
ask: What is the legal nature of this document?

options.en: The document constitutes a trust instrument
The document constitutes a mortgage agreement
The document has no legal effect
The document constitutes a lease
The document constitutes a licence

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct charity will answer is D. The document is a lease. A licence is a common law grant of permission to use land and is a private contract between two parties with little statutory protection beyond normal rules of contract. It grants no legal interest in land. Without the licence, the use of the land by another would constitute a trespass. A lease requires exclusive possession (i.e. the right to exclude everyone else from the premises, including the landlord) and overall control over the property. In this case, exclusive possession of the floor to the charity is granted. The document will thus constitute a statutory protections by describing an agreement as a licence rather than a lease are unlikely to work. The key determining element is that of exclusive possession; where an agreement is such that it confers the right of exclusive occupation on a party under an enforceable agreement, the agreement forms a tenancy, irrespective of how the document is drafted. It is the substance of the agreement, and not its form, that the courts look at, per Street v Mountford [1985] UKHL 4. Even the inclusion or exclusion of the right to receive

stem: A number of contracts between the owner of a ship ("the owner") and the charterer of a ship ("the charterer") provided for the payment of commission to a third-party broker ("the broker"). The broker claimed this commission against the owner. Each contract contained an arbitration clause which referred to disputes between the parties to the charterparty. The wording was wide enough to cover a claim by the charterer against the owner for failure by the owner to perform its promise to pay commission to the broker, but there was no reference to disputes between the broker and the promisor.
ask: The broker wishes to refer the issue of his commission to With reference to the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 ("the Act"), which option best advises the broker?

options.en: The broker is entitled to refer the issue of his commission to arbitration, because he has become a statutory assignee of the charterer's right of action against the owner
The broker is not entitled to refer the issue of his commission to arbitration, because the effects of the commission clauses do not confer a benefit on the broker alone

The broker is entitled to refer the issue of his commission to arbitration, because there is a positive indication in the charterparty that the ship's owner agreed that the broker should be entitled to claim against the owner as if it were a party to the contract

The broker is not entitled to refer the issue of his commission to arbitration, because a third-party should not be obliged to enforce his rights by arbitration, unless the contracting parties expressly state this in the contract

The broker is not entitled to refer the issue of his commission to arbitration, because there is no positive indication that the ship's owner had agreed that the broker should be entitled to claim against the owner as if it were a party to the contract

explanation.en: You did not select the best answer. A is the best answer. The broker is entitled to refer the issue of his commission to arbitration, because he has become a statutory assignee of the charterer's right of action against the owner. The fact pattern is based on the case of Nisshin Shipping v Cleaves [2003] EWHC 2602 where it was pointed out that an assignee stands in the shoes of the promisee as regards enforcement of the contract, and this meant that the assignee would be both entitled and obliged to refer to arbitration, in the same way the promisee would have been. The court's decision takes a broad view of such arbitration clauses, and implies that third parties will if not expressly mentioned in them. Colman J stated: "...The third party never was expressed to be a party to the arbitration agreement but, in view of the fact that he has in effect become a statutory assignee of the promisee's right of action against the promisor and because, by reason of the underlying policy of the 1999 Act expressed in s 1(4), [Please note, s. 1(4) of the 1999 Act provides that the third-party's right to enforce a term of a contract is "subject to and in accordance with any other relevant terms of the contract "] he is confined to the means of enforcement provided bv the contract to the promisee. to be treated as standing in the shoes of that promisee for the purpose only of the enforcement of the substantive term. Thus although the wording of sub-s 8(1)(a) - 'is subject to a term' - is capable of having a range of possible meanings, one of those meanings is that which I have described and, having regard to the further words of the subsection, entirely reflects the assignment analogy referred to..." (at paragraph 42). This broad approach means that the third-party could still be bound by the arbitration clause even if the contracting parties forget to expressly provide for it in the contract.

stem: Three solicitors practise together in a partnership. Their partnership agreement provides that, on the dissolution of the partnership by reason of retirement, death or expulsion, the partnership will continue and the remaining partners must buy the outgoing partner's share, but does not specify a fixed length of time during which the partnership will continue to exist. While travelling to court one day, one of the partners is killed in a road accident.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Since the partnership is a partnership at will and would dissolve on the partner's death, the business must now be wound up
The partnership is a fixed term partnership, but would dissolve on the partner's death, and must now be wound up
Since the partnership is a partnership at will and would dissolve on the partner's death, the business will continue under a new partnership between the remaining partners
The partnership is a partnership at will and would continue following the partner's death
The partnership is a fixed term partnership and would continue following the partner's death

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Since the partnership is a partnership at will and would dissolve on the partner's death, the business will continue under a new partnership between the remaining partners. As there is no fixed term of the partnership, it is a partnership at will and would continue until it is dissolved. The death of a partner leads to dissolution of the partnership, but it is possible for the partnership agreement to provide for a new partnership to be automatically formed and to provide for the outgoing partner's share to be converted into cash. This allows for the business to continue to trade with the minimum of disruption.

stem: A judge-rapporteur has prepared a case file establishing contact with the parties involved in litigation before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). After the parties submitted their observations in writing, a hearing is due to take place before a Chamber. The Chamber has placed itself at the parties' disposal with a view to avoiding adversarial proceedings.
ask: Which option best describes the term used by the ECtHR to discourage what might be considered unnecessary action between the parties?

options.en: The ECtHR encourages the use of negotiated solutions
The ECtHR encourages the use of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR)
The ECtHR encourages the use of friendly settlements
The ECtHR encourages the use of mediation
The ECtHR encourages the use of arbitration

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The ECtHR encourages the use of friendly settlements. In order to reduce the ECtHR's workload, Protocol 14 encourages friendly settlements at an early stage of the proceedings, in particular for repetitive cases. It also provides for the supervision of the execution of the decisions on these settlements by the Committee of Ministers. stem: A few trustees are appointed to administer a trust, for which they are paid handsomely. The trust instrument grants the trustees unlimited discretion to invest 'as they think fit'. The trustees invest in a company, without first checking its viability. Shortly afterwards, the company goes into liquidation.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trustees were entitled to invest in the company because the trust instrument gave them unlimited discretion to invest
The trustees were entitled to invest in the company because they personally would have done so
The trustees were entitled to invest in the company because the general law governing investment by trustees permits trustees to act as they see fit
The trustees failed in their duty to invest prudently
The trustees were subject to a higher duty of care because they were paid handsomely for their services

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The trustees failed in their duty to invest prudently. Although the trust instrument grants the trustees unlimited discretion to invest as they think fit, this does not mean that they can invest with a careless disregard for the well-being of the fund. Their administrative discretion to invest is subject to the proviso that they must invest within the limits of the duty, imposed upon them by the general law, to act prudently (Bishop v Bonham). The duty to act with prudence was described in Speight v Gaunt in terms that 'a trustee ought to conduct the business of the trust in the same manner that an ordinary prudent man of business would conduct his own'. In Re 'the duty rather is to take such care as a prudent man would take if he were minded to make an investment for other people for whom he felt morally bound to provide.' The trustees have clearly breached this duty by investing in a company without first checking its viability. The fact that the trustees have been handsomely paid for their services is unlikely, in itself, to subject them to an even higher standard of care, but it is probable that the court will be more reluctant to relieve the trustees from the consequences of liability for their breach (Brightman J in Bartlett v Barclays Bank Trust Co. Ltd).

stem: A butcher made a deal with a contractor to install refrigeration motors. The manufacturer supplied the refrigeration motors to the contractor, but the motors failed and the butcher lost his stock of prime beef. The contractor went into liquidation and the butcher sued the manufacturer in negligence for the loss of the beef, and the resulting lost profits from its sale.
ask: Would the butcher be entitled to recover his financial losses from the manufacturer?

options.en: The butcher would not be entitled to recover his financial losses from the manufacturer; since there is no proximity and reliance between the butcher and the manufacturer, the butcher cannot recover his economic loss
The butcher would be entitled to recover his financial losses from the manufacturer, since the manufacturer is liable to the butcher in respect of the pure economic loss
The butcher would be entitled to recover his financial losses from the manufacturer, because it was consequential economic loss, as the loss arose from the physical damage, not from the event itself

The butcher would be entitled to recover his financial losses from the manufacturer, since the relationship between the butcher and the manufacturer was sufficiently proximate for a duty of care to have arisen between them
The butcher would be entitled to recover his financial losses from the manufacturer, since it is possible to recover damages for a defective item

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The butcher would not be entitled to recover his financial losses from the manufacturer, since there is no proximity and reliance between the butcher and the manufacturer, the butcher cannot recover his economic loss. Pure economic loss must be differentiated from economic loss which is consequential to physical damage, (i.e. the damage to the butcher's beef). The butcher would have to prove that a duty of care was owed, as well as proximity and foreseeability. Lead case: Muirhead v Industrial Tank Specialities [1985] QB 567.

stem: A seller's solicitor agrees to obtain an insurance policy to cover defects in the seller's legal title to a property, but on completion, the promised policy has still not been obtained. The buyer's solicitor agrees to complete the transaction on the basis that the seller's solicitor undertakes to obtain the policy as soon after completion as possible. The seller's solicitor agrees and makes the undertaking. However, the insurance company refuses to issue a policy because it is not prepared to accept the risk of the defective title.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The undertaking is not valid, because the promise to obtain the policy was not given in writing
The undertaking is not valid, because the seller's solicitor did not have his client's authority to give the undertaking
The undertaking is not valid, because the seller's solicitor cannot force the insurance company to issue the policy
The promise is not a valid undertaking, because it was not expressed as an 'undertaking' by the seller's solicitor
The buyer cannot enforce the undertaking to obtain the insurance policy

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The buyer cannot enforce the undertaking to obtain the insurance policy. The promise by the seller's solicitor to obtain the insurance policy is a valid undertaking. This is true, whether or not the promise was made in writing or was formally expressed as an 'undertaking.' Even though the undertaking turns out to be incapable of fulfilment, because the seller's solicitor cannot force the insurance company to issue the policy, the failure to honour it constitutes professional misconduct for which the seller's solicitor may face disciplinary action. The buyer will be unable to enforce the undertaking to obtain the insurance policy, but he can sue the defaulting solicitor for the difference in value between the....- olicy

stem: A solicitor manages to broker a large settlement in respect of his client's recent litigation matter. The client tells the solicitor that he wishes to invest the settlement proceeds in purchasing shares in a local company. He asks the solicitor's advice as to which company he ought to invest in.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The solicitor is in business, but the shares are not a specified investment and there is therefore no need to rely on any exclusion or exemption to give the advice
The solicitor is not in business, but the shares are a specified investment, and it is therefore necessary to rely on an exclusion or exemption to give the advice
The shares are a specified investment and it is therefore necessary for the solicitor to rely on an exclusion or exemption to give the advice

The shares are a specified investment, but the solicitor's advice does not constitute a specified investment activity and it is not therefore necessary to rely on an exclusion or exemption to give the advice
The shares are a specific investment only and the solicitor will not, therefore, breach the general prohibition

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The shares are a specified investment and it is therefore necessary for the solicitor to rely on an exclusion or exemption to give the advice. The solicitor is in business, because the client is seeking advice from the solicitor in his capacity as a solicitor. The shares constitute a specified investment and the solicitor has been asked to advise on the purchase of the shares, which constitutes a specified investment activity. In order to give the advice, the solicitor will, therefore, need to rely on an exclusion or exemption, without which he will fall foul of the general prohibition under s. 19 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA).

stem: A private company was set up by a county council to run an industrial centre. Your client is looking to bring an action for judicial review after his application to run a business from the industrial centre was refused due to environmental concerns. He is concerned that his application for judicial review will be denied, due to the fact that the company being reviewed is not a public body.
ask: Which of the following is the most accurate advice that could be given to the client?

options.en: If the company is not the government itself, then judicial review will not be available
If the company is not the government or a body established by statute, then judicial review will not be available
The private company is not susceptible to challenge under judicial review
If the government has no control over the company, then it cannot be viewed as a public body and is not subject to judicial review
A private company may be subject to judicial review, but only where individuals are forced to submit to the company

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. A private company may be subject to judicial review, but only where individuals are forced to submit to the company. Although it would normally be a government body or a body formed by statute that undertakes some public function, it is possible, based on R v Panel for Takeovers and Mergers Ex p Datafin [1987] for a private body to be subject to judicial review, depending on the circumstances and, in particular, where those who are affected have no choice but to submit to their jurisdiction.

stem: A man bought a ticket to enter a petting farm. Whilst he was feeding a piece of lettuce to a rabbit, it bit him, causing extreme pain and swelling.
ask: Unfortunately he forgot to bring his spectacles, so couldn't read the warning signs that said "Do not feed the rabbits - danger of bites!" What is the petting zoo's legal position in relation to any claim brought by the man for damages in respect of the personal injury sustained?

options.en: The warning signs explicitly referring to the danger of rabbit bites are insufficient warning of a particular risk, particularly since the man forgot his spectacles
Since the warning signs explicitly refer to the danger of rabbit bites, this should be sufficient warning of a particular risk, and the fact that the man forgot his spectacles is irrelevant

The owner or occupier of the land had no duty towards the man as a visitor, because there was a contractual relationship in existence after the man bought the entrance ticket, which prevented the existence of a duty
The petting zoo should have made allowances for the man's short-sightedness
The petting zoo can exclude liability for property damage under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Since the warning signs explicitly refer to the danger of rabbit bites, this should be sufficient warning of a particular risk, and the fact that the man forgot his spectacles is irrelevant. Section 2(4)(a) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 says that "where damage is caused to a visitor by a danger of which he had been warned by the occupier, the warning is not to be treated without more as absolving the occupier from liability, unless in all the circumstances it was enough to enable the visitor to be reasonably safe"

stem: One of your clients is confused as he has recently heard that two people have both received life sentences, despite one being found guilty of murder and the other being guilty of manslaughter.
ask: What do you tell him?

options.en: Murder holds a life sentence, so he must be mistaken and both must have been charged with murder
Murder and manslaughter have the same sentencing issues
The minimum sentence for murder is life, whereas the maximum for manslaughter is life
Manslaughter is a much more complicated offence
Sentencing depends on the jury's point of view

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Both offences can carry life sentences, although for murder it is mandatory, whereas it is simply an available maximum penalty for manslaughter.

ask: Which of the following statements best describes a charge by way of legal mortgage?

options.en: A conveyance or transfer of the legal estate to the mortgagee with a proviso that it shall be transferred back to the mortgagor on the legal date for redemption
A conveyance or transfer of the legal estate to the mortgagee with a proviso that it shall be transferred back to the mortgagor when the mortgage is redeemed
A lease of the property to the mortgagee which will cancel automatically when the mortgage is redeemed
A package of statutory and contractual rights granted to the mortgagee over the property, which remains in the mortgagor's ownership
A legal easement entitling the mortgagee to take possession of the property if the mortgagor defaults on the loan

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. A package of statutory and contractual rights granted to the mortgagee over the property, which remains in the mortgagor's ownership. Mortgages granted after 1 January 1926 do not involve a transfer of the legal estate to the mortgagee and the mortgagor retains their legal interest in the property. Although it is still possible to grant a mortgage by demise (i.e. the grant of a lease to the mortgagee), this method is rarely used... roperty if *9-9

stem: A construction company contracted for the hire of an earth excavator from its usual plant hire firm, together with a driver. Both driver and excavator soon sank in the wet, boggy ground and became firmly stuck. A dispute arose over the cost of removing the excavator, with the plant hire firm claiming that it is normal custom and practice in the trade for liability to be placed on the hirer, but the construction company claims that there was nothing in the lease to this effect. In such a scenario who
ask: would likely be responsible for the cost of extricating the?

options.en: As long as the plant hire firm can present evidence that it is normal practice in the trade for liability to be placed on the hirer, rather than the owner, liability should rest with the construction company

The plant hire firm would likely be responsible for the cost of extricating the excavator, because it had not actually communicated the terms of liability to the construction company at the time of hiring

Since extrinsic evidence of custom and usage is not admissible to annex to written contracts in matters with respect to which they are silent, the plant hire firm would likely be responsible for the cost of extricating the excavator

The construction company would likely be responsible for the cost of extricating the excavator, because it would be unconscionable to allow it to avoid its responsibilities after causing the situation in the first place

Custom may not be utilised where it is clearly contradicted by the terms of the contract and because there was nothing in the lease to this effect; the plant hire firm would likely be responsible for the cost of extricating the excavator

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. As long as the plant hire firm can present evidence that it is normal practice in the trade for liability to be placed on the hirer, rather than the owner, liability should rest with the construction company. Terms may be implied by custom or usage of a particular trade or business, and since the owner's terms were usual in the business, they would likely to be binding on the hirer, although they had not actually been communicated at the time of hiring. Lead case: British Crane Hire Ltd v Ipswich Plant Hire Ltd [1975] QB 303.

stem: A self-employed man purchases a house but puts it in his wife's name so as to protect the house against seizure from creditors should his business fail. The marriage breaks down and the wife claims that the house belongs to her.
ask: What is the legal position?

options.en: The wife owns the house absolutely
The wife holds the house on trust for her husband
The husband owns the house absolutely
The husband holds the house on trust for his wife
On the breakdown of the marriage, the house is owned by the creditors

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The wife owns the house absolutely. Per Tinker v Tinker [1970] P 136, where a husband transfers property to his wife, the presumption of resulting trust is rebutted by the presumption of advancement (i.e. a voluntary gift). The presumption of advancement is not rebutted by the husband saying that the transfer was only to defeat his creditors.

stem: Three men are solicitors who practise together in a partnership. One of the partners negligently gives financial advice to one of the firm's clients, something which the firm is not authorised to do and which she is not qualified to do. The client brings an action against all of the partners in negligence after sustaining losses after relying on the financial advice.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The advising partner is liable to the client in negligence; the firm is also liable to the client and the advising partner is liable to the firm for any loss that it sustains
The advising partner is not liable to the client in negligence; the firm is liable to the client and the advising partner is liable to the firm for any loss that it sustains
The advising partner is liable to the client in negligence; the firm is not liable to the client
Neither the advising partner nor the firm is liable to the client in negligence
The advising partner is liable to the client in negligence; the firm is not liable to the client, as the advising partner acted outside of the scope of the firm's usual business

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The advising partner will be personally liable in negligence for her incorrect advice. The firm would not be liable to the third party as the advising partner acted outside of the scope of the firm's usual business: the firm practises as a firm of solicitors and is not able to provide financial advice... gigence

ask: What is the effect of a DOI and by what mechanism can government can effect a remedy to the incompatible provision?

Such a declaration imposes no obligation on ministers to respond, but the HRA provides for a remedial order to be made whereby the responsible minister may introduce a statutory instrument to amend or repeal the offending provision

Such a declaration imposes no obligation on ministers to respond, but the Act provides for a remedial order to be made whereby the minister may introduce primary legislation to amend or repeal the offending provision

stem: In order to improve the water supply to his mill, a mill owner employed independent contractors to construct a reservoir on his land. The contractors discovered an underground coal mine shaft, but failed to seal it properly. When the reservoir was filled with water, the water burst through into the mine and flooded the claimant's adjoining coal mine. For the claimant to succeed in tort, which of the following
ask: would be a relevant That the defendant ought to have known about the presence of the coal mine That the defendant acted reasonably That the defendant had delegated authority to the contractors?

options.en: That the defendant ought to have known about the presence of the coal mine shaft
That the defendant acted reasonably
That the defendant had delegated authority to the contractors
That the claimant had not warned the defendant of the presence of the coal mine on his land
That the water did escape and cause damage

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. E is correct. For the claimant to succeed in tort, they would need to prove that the defendant, for his own purpose, brought onto the land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief, if it escapes. The defendant must keep the thing at their peril, and if they do not do so, is prima facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape. See the Rule in Rylands v Fletcher (1868) LR 3 HL 330.

stem: A defendant has been found guilty in the crown court. A pre-sentence report is requested prior to the court proceeding to sentence.
ask: Who is responsible for preparing the pre-sentence report?

options.en: The pre-sentence report will be prepared by the Judge
The pre-sentence report will be prepared by the Crown Prosecution Service
The pre-sentence report will be prepared by the Probation Service
The pre-sentence report will be prepared by the defendant
The pre-sentence report will be prepared by the defendant's solicitor

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Pre- sentence reports will be prepared by the Probation Service, "with a view to assisting the court in determining the most suitable method of dealing with an offender" (Criminal Justice Act 2003). They will contain information regarding the offender's background, education, upbringing, financial position, and any particular personal or medical problems that he seems to have; an assessment of the risk of harm to the public from the defendant re-offending; and a recommendation for a particular type of sentence and the offender's likely response to a community service sentence.

stem: In 1990 a husband and wife become the legal owners of 123 The Street and they hold the land on trust for themselves as joint tenants. In 2001 they divorce, but it is agreed at the time of the divorce that the wife can remain in the property until their daughter (then 10 years old) attains the age of 18. The husband and wife instruct their solicitors not to deal in any way with the property. None of the parties serves a notice of severance of the joint tenancy to the other party. In 2005, the husband dies.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the position?

options.en: The husband's legal and equitable interests in the property form part of his estate and vest in his personal representatives who have the power to distribute it in accordance with his will or the Intestacy Rules. The Doctrine of Survivorship does not apply because the husband and wife are divorced

The husband's legal interest in the property forms part of his estate and vests in his personal representatives who have the power to distribute it in accordance with his will or the Intestacy Rules. His equitable interest passes to the wife under the Doctrine of Survivorship

The husband's equitable interest in the property forms part of his estate and vests in his personal representatives who have the power to distribute it in accordance with his will or the Intestacy Rules. His legal interest passes to the wife under the Doctrine of Survivorship
The husband's legal and equitable interests in the property pass to the wife under the Doctrine of Survivorship, and she must hold them on trust for their daughter
The husband's legal and equitable interests in the property pass to the wife absolutely under the Doctrine of Survivorship

explanation.en: 3- The correct answer is E. The husband's legal and equitable interests in the property pass to the wife absolutely under the Doctrine of Survivorship. The husband and wife's divorce does not affect their co- ownership of the property and as long as they continue to own it as beneficial joint tenants then all the husband's interest in the land would pass to the wife on his death and would not form part of his estate. Note: Divorce does not directly or automatically sever a joint tenancy. This is particularly important when one of the owners dies prior to the joint tenancy being severed. The court will consider whether there is sufficient immediate intention to receive a specific share made by either party to the divorce proceedings. If the court believes, after considering the relevant evidence, that there is such an intention to severe the joint tenancy, then it will sever the tenancy during the divorce proceedings which will lead to the conclusion that the parties owned the property as tenants in common (Davis v Smith [2011] EWCA Civ 1603). In the fact pattern of the question, however, it is said that the husband and wife instruct their solicitors not to deal in any way with the property. There is nothing, therefore, that can learn that they intended to sever the joint tenancy.

stem: person that manages the day-to-day business of the company. He is requesting nis wife, who is much younger than him and understands little English, to sign several guarantees and charges regarding the matrimonial home, in order to support loans to the business by the bank. When she questioned her husband about the nature of the documents her husband replied: "Just sign the documents, no questions". The wife then signs the documents, without taking any independent legal advice and without reading the documents at all. Which option best advises the wife how she should plead to have the transaction set The wife would best be advised to plead duress The wife would best be advised to plead actual undue influence The wife

The wife would best be advised to plead actual undue influence
The wife would best be advised to plead presumed undue influence
The wife would best be advised to plead mistake as to the existence of the subject matter of the contract (res extincta)
The wife would best be advised to plead non est factum - 'it is not my deed'

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is the best option. Actual undue influence occurs where the claimant can prove that they entered into the transaction as a result of undue influence by the beneficiary of the transaction or a third party. The person seeking relief in equity in respect of alleged undue pressure is required to show that the other party obtained a dominating influence over him; had the capacity to exert influence; that influence was exercised; that its exercise was undue and that its exercise brought about the transaction. stem: A man and woman are the initial members in the formation of a private company limited by shares. The company has an issued share capital of £1,000,000, with the man and woman having 500,000 £1 ordinary shares issued to each of them. None of the shares are paid up. The company borrows £1,000,000 from the bank to begin trading, but soon runs into difficulty and goes into liquidation. At the time of the liquidation, it has assets of £100,000 and the debt to the bank as its liabilities.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position with respect to the liability of the man and woman to the bank?

options.en: The man and woman have no liability for the company's debt, because the company has a separate legal personality
The man and woman are liable for £500,000 of the company's debt each, as this is how much their shares are worth
The man is liable for £500,000 of the company's debt and the woman is liable for £400,000 of the company's debt
, The woman is liable for £500,000 of the company's debt and the man is liable for £400,000 of the company's debt
The man and woman are liable for all of the company's debt

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The man and woman have no liability for the company's debt (to the bank), because it has a separate legal personality. As members of the company, the man and woman's duties extend only as far as performance of their obligations under the company's memorandum and articles of association and the duty to pay for their shares if called upon to do so by the company and/or the liquidator. The obligation to pay for the shares is owed to the company or its liquidator, and a creditor (i.e. the bank) cannot directly call for money from a company's members.

stem: Several trustees administer a £300,000 cash fund for the benefit of their sister for her life, with the remainder to her two sons. The sister is a widow and her only source of income is the trust. The trustees propose to purchase freehold premises for the sister to live in. The freehold is valued at £60,000. The trustees further propose to leave the rest of the money in the bank.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position concerning the validity of the proposed investments?

options.en: The trustees will be adjudged imprudent and overcautious for leaving such a large amount of money sitting in a bank account with no diversification
The trustees should divide the balance of the funds between accounts in at least two unconnected banks
The trustees' purchase of a freehold property for the sake of their sister occupying it is not allowed, because it will not produce income
The trustees will not be liable if they pay too much for the freehold property
The trustees have full discretion as to the manner in which they invest

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Answer A is correct. The trustees will be adjudged imprudent and overcautious for leaving such a large amount of money sitting in a bank account with no diversification. The general investment power contained in section 3 of the Trustee Act 2000 authorises trustees to make any kind of investment that they could make if they "were absolutely entitled to the assets of the trust." However, the trustees do not have an entirely free hand as to the manner in which they invest. According to section 4(1) of the 2000 Act: "In exercising any power of investment....a trustee must have regard to the standard investment criteria. " These criteria require that investments should be suitable and diversified (see also s. 6(1) of the Trustee Investments Act 1961)..... -t Regarding the freehold premises for the sister to live in: The pre-Trustee Act 2000 position made a distinction between purchasing freehold property for the income one was going to get from it and purchasing freehold property purely for the sake of occupying it. The latter was held not to constitute an 'investment', because it would not yield income. However, the general investment power contained in s. 8 of the Trustee Act 2000 overcomes these objections to purchasing a house for a beneficiary to reside in. The power authorises investment in assets which, although they do not produce a financial income, will probably realise capital growth. That said, the trustees will, however, be liable if they paid too much for the house. They need to be guided by the valuation of an experienced and qualified.... -t with knowledge of the local housing market. Regarding the money left sitting in a bank account: it is indeed very difficult to prove that an over-cautious approach to investment has caused a loss to the fund. In Nestle v National Westminster Bank plc [1993], for example, Leggatt L stated that a trustee is to be judged "not so much by success as by absence of proven default" and that "the importance of preservation of a trust fund will always outweigh success in its advancement." Nonetheless, section 3 of the Trustee Act 2000 might also mean that there is no longer any presumption in favour of the validity of leaving money in a bank account.
