stem: An asylum seeker wishes to claims for non-pecuniary damages for distress and anxiety banned from marrying in the UK under immigration legislation, because she is an illegal immigrant. She claims that her right to marry under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) has been breached.
ask: She seeks advice regarding quantum of damages if her claim is successful under the Human Rights Act 1998 Which of the following statements best describes the most likely outcome if your client's claim is successful?

options.en: If successful, the finding of a violation will most likely be sufficient
If successful, the claimant is most likely to be awarded exemplary damages
If successful, the claimant is most likely to be awarded punitive damages
If successful, the court is likely to award damages under the HRA for tortious breach of a statutory duty
If successful, the court is most likely to make a mandatory order and award damages

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. If successful, the finding of a violation will most likely be sufficient. Courts are reluctant to award damages for violations of the Convention save in the clearest cases. It would be very unusual for a claimant to recover damages for non-pecuniary loss, unless the distress is of exceptional gravity. The finding of a violation will be sufficient unless it is necessary further to compensate the claimant for losses they have actually sustained. This would leave no room for exemplary or punitive damages. Further, a claim for damages under the HRA is not a claim in tort for breach of a statutory duty; the HRA is not a tort statute.

stem: A woman and man were in a contract of employment. Apart from the salary of the man, it was agreed that he should recover from the woman the amount of income tax payable on his salary as travelling expenses, which both parties acknowledged was not a lawful method of remuneration.
ask: The man wishes to claim arrears of salary plus arrears of expenses, most of which represented the amount payable by him as Will the man be able to enforce the contract?

options.en: The agreement is one which HM Revenue & Customs must support, and is therefore enforceable
Even though HM Revenue & Customs has been defrauded, the contract will be enforceable in equity

The contract will be enforceable, because the illegality will not invalidate the contract, unless it was the purpose of the parties that a breach committed in the course of the performance of a contract should invalidate the contract
Since the agreement was contrary to public policy, it is unenforceable
Since the agreement was prejudicial to public safety, it is unenforceable

explanation.en: D is correct. Since the agreement was contrary to public policy, it is unenforceable. A contract designed to defraud HM Revenue & Customs will be illegal, because it is illegal at common law on the grounds of public policy. Lead case: Miller v. Karlinski Times Law Reports (945).

stem: A freehold owner of an unregistered office building grants a 99 year lease of the ground floor to a woman by deed. ILITT- immediate reeaback
ask: You have been instructed by the woman to act in Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: You must apply for first registration of the freehold estate; register a notice of the woman's leasehold interest in the charges register of the freehold title; and register the woman's leasehold interest at Her Majesty's Land Registry (HMLR) with absolute leasehold title
You do not need to apply for first registration of the freehold estate, but you should register the woman's leasehold interest as a Land Charge and register it at HMLR with absolute leasehold title
You do not need to apply for first registration of the freehold estate, but you should register the woman's leasehold interest at HMLR with absolute leasehold title
You do not need to apply for first registration of the freehold estate, but you should register the woman's leasehold interest at HMLR with good leasehold title
You do not need to apply for first registration of the freehold estate, but you should register the woman's leasehold interest as a Land Charge and register it at HMLR with good leasehold title

explanation.en: BOCCECEI You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. You do not need to apply for first registration of the freehold estate, but you should register the woman's leasehold interest at HMLR with good leasehold title. As the lease is for more than seven years, it must be registered at HMLR with its own title number. It is not possible to register a legal lease as a Land Charge, nor is it necessary to apply for first registration of the freehold estate. However HMLR will only register the lease with good leasehold title until such time as the freehold estate has been registered.

stem: Your client is being investigated for alleged tax fraud for claiming at least £180,000 in expenses by designating an empty flat, and previously an allegedly non-existent property as her main residence. She is unsure as to the nature and role of the investigation. She's also concerned as to which body, if any, is responsible for the expected prosecution.
ask: Who investigates and prosecutes tax fraud?

options.en: Her Majesty's Revenue & Customs (HMRC) is responsible for investigating suspected tax fraud, but any decision whether to bring a criminal prosecution is made by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)
Her Majesty's Revenue & Customs (HMRC) is responsible for investigating and prosecuting suspected tax fraud
The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) is responsible for investigating and prosecuting suspected tax fraud
The police are responsible for investigating suspected tax fraud, but any decision whether to bring a criminal prosecution is made by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)
The police are responsible for investigating suspected tax fraud, but any decision whether to bring a criminal prosecution is made by Her Majesty's Revenue & Customs (HMRC)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. HMRC is responsible for investigating suspected crime involving all of the taxes and other regimes it is responsible for. It does not, however, decide whether a criminal prosecution is to be commenced. The decision whether to bring a criminal prosecution is made by an independent prosecuting authority. In England and Wales this was, until recently, the Revenue and Customs Prosecutions Office (RCPO). However, in January 2010, the RCPO merged with the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and tax prosecutions are now carried out by the Central Fraud Group of the CPS.

stem: A Catholic mother claimed the Police Service of Northern Ireland breached its positive obligation to prevent the infliction of inhuman and degrading treatment upon its citizens under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, after she and her daughter were subjected to daily verbal abuse and threats of physical violence from Protestant protesters, while they walked to school in Belfast. The mother initially applied for judicial review at the High Court in Belfast, arguing that the chief of police had failed to secure the effective implementation of the criminal law, but this application was dismissed. She was then granted leave to appeal that decision to the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland for reasons of 'public interest'; however, that appeal was also dismissed.
ask: Has the mother a further avenue of appeal within the United Kingdom?

options.en: The mother has no further avenue of appeal, because the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal is the highest court within the jurisdiction of Northern Ireland
The Northern Ireland Court of Appeal may grant the mother leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
The mother has no further avenue of appeal, because the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom interprets and applies the laws of England and Wales only
The mother has no further avenue of appeal within the UK, and should apply directly to the ultimate court of appeal in the European context, i.e. the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg
The Northern Ireland Court of Appeal may grant the mother leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) in London

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The Supreme Court serves as the highest court of appeal in England and Wales and in Northern Ireland. Lead case: In Re E (A Child) [2008] 3 WLR 1208. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 3 ECHR.

stem: The family court accepted your pleadings on behalf of an at-risk child, acting by their guardian ad litem (GAL), that the child should be placed in the care of the local authority. An adoption agency subsequently finds suitable adopters for the child.
ask: The adopters wish to instruct you to act for them during the application process for an Which of the following statements best describes what you should do?

options.en: You can act for the adopters, because the information you have from the original case will now be used in the best interests of the child
You can act for the adopters, because the adopters have the right to choose their solicitor
You cannot act for the adopters, because even if adoption would be in the child's best interests, these particular adopters may not be the most suitable
You cannot act for the adopters, because the children have not been asked their opinion
You cannot act for the adopters, even though there is no breach of confidentiality in this case

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. A solicitor who acted on instructions from a GAL on behalf of a child in a care case is in possession of confidential information about the child. There is a risk, therefore, that in acting for potential adopters, the child's confidentiality could be breached. Even though the solicitor and GAL agreed that it was in the child's best interests to be placed in care, it certainly does not follow that it is right for the child to be adopted now, or that it is right for these particular adopters to be the persons who take the child on - that is for the court to decide.

stem: A solicitor conducts a conveyancing transaction on behalf of a client. Prior to exchange of contracts, the solicitor has no knowledge or suspicion that the house was purchased with the proceeds of crime. Following exchange of contracts, the solicitor correctly begins to suspect that the house was purchased with the proceeds of crime.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The solicitor must disclose his suspicions to the firm's nominated officer
The solicitor may disclose his suspicions to the firm's nominated officer
The solicitor should have disclosed his suspicions to the firm's nominated officer prior to the exchange of contracts
The solicitor may not make an authorised disclosure because the prohibited act is on-going
The solicitor may not make an authorised disclosure because the prohibited act has been completed

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Section 328 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (the Act) makes it a criminal offence for a person (or corporate body) to be involved in an arrangement that a person knows or suspects facilitates the acquisition, retention, use or control of criminal property. However, a person does not commit an offence under section 328 if he makes an authorised disclosure to the relevant authorities under section 338 of the Act and obtains the appropriate consent. A solicitor, therefore, will not commit an offence under s. 328 provided he makes an authorised disclosure to the firm's nominated officer as soon as is practically possible. the transaction taking place, while the prohibited act is on-going and even after the prohibited act is completed. Following the exchange of contracts, the solicitor will be concerned in an arrangement which facilitates the acquisition of criminal property, and will be in breach of s. 328 unless he discloses his suspicions to his nominated officer on his own initiative and as soon as is practicable after his first suspicions arise.

stem: A specialist flooring sub-contractor, on behalf of the main contractor, was negligent in installing flooring in the claimant's factory. Cracks in the floor subsequently appeared and it started to break up. The floor required replacing, causing the factory owner to suffer lost profits and damages whilst the floor was being re-laid.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the legal position?

options.en: The factory owner has no claim, because it would mean superimposing a tortious obligation on existing voluntary obligations arising out of a multi-party contractual relationship
The factory owner has no grounds to claim damages in tort, because there was insufficient proximity between the factory owner and the sub-contractor
Since there was a sufficiently close relationship between the parties to give rise to a duty of care between them, the factory owner would be entitled to recover financial losses
Such a defect in property which manifests itself prior to causing any physical injury is pure economic loss, so no damages are recoverable
Only the floor was damaged; the floor was simply equivalent to a faulty product, rather than property, especially since it did not cause damage to other property

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Because the specialist sub-contractor knew what purpose the floors would be put to, and that the factory owner was relying on the expertise and skill of the sub-contractor, the relationship between the claimant and the sub-contractor was analogous to a contract (i.e. a special relationship of proximity existed). In the case of Junior Books v Veitchi (1983), the House of Lords decided that, despite there being no privity of contract between the claimant and the defendant, because the claimant was in sufficiently close proximity to the defendant, it could recover foreseeable economic loss, even though there was neither physical damage to person nor property. economic loss doctrine set out in Spartan Steel and Alloys Ltd. v Martin & Co (Contractors) Ltd. [1973].

stem: A man considers himself to be an expert when it comes to a particular type of china and regularly trawls the market stalls to buy antiques and other items for his house. He sees some pieces on display at a particular stall, clearly below market value. When he questions the owner, the man is told that he just wants the 'stuff gone'. He later discovers that the pieces he purchased were stolen.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the man's criminal liability, if any?

options.en: As he purchased the pieces for value, with no knowledge or belief that they were stolen, he has not appropriated them
As the pieces were purchased at an undervalue price, the man should have been suspicious, and will be considered to have appropriated the pieces
If the man were an expert, then he is likely to be guilty of theft, but as he is an amateur collector, criminal liability cannot attach
Stolen goods remain stolen goods, regardless of whether they have passed to another individual, innocently, or otherwise
As he purchased the pieces for value, either suspecting or knowing they were stolen, he is guilty of handling stolen property

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. According to the provisions of section 22 Theft Act 1968, an individual can be found guilty of handling stolen goods if they handle them knowing or believing them to be stolen, or assist in their retention, in a dishonest manner. Dishonesty is central for this offence. Merely suspecting they might be 'dodgy' is not sufficient. The offence of handling stolen goods is one of the most difficult to prove as there is no onus on the suspect to give an explanation as to where he got it from.

stem: Two people purchase 123 Slow Street with the aid of a mortgage advance from BankCo. They grant BankCo a charge by way of legal mortgage over 123 Slow Street as security for the loan.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the nature of the respective interests of the two people and BankCo in the property?

options.en: The two people remain the legal owners of the property, whilst BankCo becomes the equitable owner until the loan is repaid
The two people remain the legal and equitable owners of the property, whilst BankCo has an equitable interest in the property until the loan is repaid
The two people remain the legal and equitable owners of the property, whilst BankCo has a legal interest in the property until the loan is repaid
BankCo becomes the legal owner of the property, whilst the two people become the equitable owners until the loan is repaid
BankCo becomes the legal and equitable owner of the property, with the two people having no interest in it until the loan is repaid

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The two people are the legal and equitable owners of the property. BankCo has a legal interest in the property until the loan is repaid. The grant of a legal mortgage does not transfer legal or equitable ownership in the land to the mortgagee, but merely creates an interest in the land in the mortgagee's favour. If this interest is made by deed and all relevant procedural requirements are complied with, then this interest will exist in law.

stem: A caravan rental company sent your client a contract form to purchase his rented caravan outright. The company promised that once your client had completed the form, it would counter-sign the same and complete the sale. Your client completed the form as per the instructions, but the company failed to sign and return the application as promised. Your client claims a breach of contract because the caravan rental company has refused to proceed with the sale.
ask: Was there was a binding contract, and can your client therefore enforce the sale?

options.en: There was a binding contract, and your client can enforce the sale, because the letter from the caravan rental company was a firm intention to proceed with the sale when your client returned the application form

There was a binding contract, and your client can enforce the sale, because analysing the transaction in terms of offer and acceptance is superfluous when the conduct of the parties shows that there was a material agreement
There was a binding contract, and your client can enforce the sale, because your client's state of mind indicated a willingness to enter into the transaction

There was no binding contract, and your client cannot enforce the sale, because the language of the caravan rental company's letter to your client was not sufficiently definite to amount to an offer; it was simply an invitation to treat
There was no binding contract, and your client cannot enforce the sale, because the letter should be regarded as a mere advertising slogan, which meant nothing in contractual terms

explanation.en: cause the You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The letter from the caravan rental company was a firm intention to proceed with the sale when your client returned the contract form. The caravan rental company was bound to proceed with the sale because it would appear that a contract has been formed. Lead case: Storer v Manchester City Council.

stem: A man and woman are not married. They are a cohabiting couple who own a shared home. They would like to protect the basis on which their shared property is held.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains how they should protect their respective claims?

options.en: Register the legal estate in their joint names
Live together for over 10 years
Enter into a written declaration of trust
Make equal financial contributions
The couple would be unable to protect their respective claims

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. A written declaration of trust would enable an unmarried, cohabiting couple to specify the shares in which their shared property is held. The option in (A) might work, following the House of Lords' decision in Stack v Dowden [2007], which set down the presumption that if there is more than one person registered on the legal title of the house then those legal owners should be presumed to be the owners of the equitable interest in that home equally. However, these are merely presumptions, and can therefore be rebutted by any evidence which suggests that the parties' common intention was something different - as indeed occurred in the case of Stack v

stem: A woman has recently been made a director of a company and is asked to consider a proposal which will entail the company entering into a long term commitment with a third party supplier, operated by the director's friend. In deciding whether to agree to the proposal, the director considers that the proposal will result in a short term reduction in the company's outgoings and will also benefit the friend's business through an increase in work.
ask: Which of the following options best state the legal position?

options.en: The director has acted in breach of her duty to promote the best interests of the company; she would be liable to the other directors for any loss that this caused
The director has acted in breach of her duty to promote the best interests of the company; she would be liable to the company itself for any loss that this caused
The director has not acted in breach of her duty to promote the best interests of the company
The director has acted in breach of her duty to promote the best interests of the company, but as this has caused no immediate loss, she will not be liable to anyone for this
The director has not acted in breach of her duty to promote the best interests of the company unless the members pass a resolution to this effect

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. A director has an overriding duty to act in the best interests of promoting a long term increase in value of the company. They must have regard to certain factors which are contained in section 172 of the Companies Act 2006 when carrying out their functions and these do not extend to the short term aims of the company and the business interests of third parties. In the event that the company were to suffer a loss as a result of the director's decision to agree to the proposal, she would be liable to the company for a breach of her statutory duty for any loss occasioned.

stem: In order to obtain the reopening of his case, a serving prisoner wished to have oral interviews with a journalist who had taken an interest in his case. Relying on the policy of the Home Secretary, the governor of the prison was only prepared to allow the oral interviews to take place if the journalist signed written undertakings not to publish any part of the interviews.
ask: Which option best states the courts' approach under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR)?

options.en: A prisoner protesting his innocence has the right to conduct face to face visits with journalists
A prisoner protesting his innocence has the right to conduct confidential correspondence with a journalist, but not face to face visits with journalists
A prisoner has no right to an oral interview with a journalist who is willing to investigate his case

A prisoner has no right to an oral interview with a journalist who is willing to investigate his case, because of the serious risk of distress to victims and their families and general public outrage at the sight of prisoners and representatives of the media collaborating to publish details of any aspect of a prisoner's case

A prisoner has no right to an oral interview with a journalist who wants to investigate his case, or to take up his case through the media; to allow such interviews would undermine proper control and discipline in prisons

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option A is correct. In R v Secretary of State Home Dept ex p Simms [2000], it was held that a convicted prisoner has a fundamental and basic right to communicate orally with the media through a journalist, in order to challenge the safety of his conviction, and the policy of the Home Secretary made under paragraph 37 and paragraph 37A of Section A of Prison Service Standing Order 5 was unlawful to the event that it interfered with that right. The House of Lords considered whether the Home Secretary's evidence showed a pressing need for a measure which restricted prisoners' attempts to gain access to justice, and found none. The more substantial the interference with fundamental rights, the more the court would require by way of justification before it could be satisfied that the and casts light on possible miscarriages of justice carries particular importance. This particular type of "good Samaritan" freedom of speech has to be protected under Article 10 (Freedom of Expression). See R v SoS Home Dept ex p Simms [2000] 2 AC 115 (HL).

stem: Your client has issued proceedings against a company for sex discrimination and unfair dismissal. The company's legal department is acting.
ask: The company has 50 employees and your client has asked you to conduct interviews with three of its Which option represents the best advice to give to your client?

options.en: The witnesses may be interviewed, as there is no property in a witness, even if the firm's legal department is acting
The witnesses may be interviewed, provided written statements are not obtained from them without the consent of the firm's legal department
The witnesses may not be interviewed, as to do so would be to tamper with evidence
The witnesses may not be interviewed, as the firm's legal department is acting
The witnesses may not be interviewed in any circumstances

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. There is no property in a witness and nothing, therefore, to stop a solicitor from interviewing and taking a statement from a witness belonging to the other side, whether or not that witness has been interviewed or called as a witness by another party. Of course, there must be no hint of intimidation or of trying to persuade the witness to change his evidence, and, indeed, to avoid such allegations, it is wise (though not essential, as a matter of law), when seeking to interview a witness for the other side, to offer to interview them in the presence of the other side's representative. The correct answer is therefore (A), albeit that the best advice would possible worries it might cause for their employment. The solicitor can then interview the witnesses in order to obtain signed witness statements.

stem: A town council refused your client's planning application. Your client is aggrieved, because the decision was taken by a junior member of the town planning department. The prestigious nature of the planning application, however, meant it should have been looked at by a senior committee.
ask: What, if any grounds for judicial review, does your client have?

options.en: If the decision was taken by the wrong person, the most appropriate grounds for judicial review would be a breach of natural justice
If the decision was taken by the wrong person, the most appropriate grounds for judicial review would be illegality
If the decision was taken by the wrong person, the most appropriate grounds for judicial review would be irrationality
If the decision was taken by the wrong person, the most appropriate grounds for judicial review would be Wednesbury unreasonableness
If the decision was taken by the wrong person the most appropriate grounds for judicial review would be procedural impropriety

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. If the law empowers a particular authority, e.g. a minister, to take certain decisions, the minister cannot delegate this power to another authority, e.g. an executive officer or a committee. This differs from a routine job not involving much discretion being done by civil servants in the minister's name, which is not considered delegation. Unlawful delegation is a species of illegality. Therefore, a claim for judicial review could be made on the grounds of illegality, if the decision was taken by the wrong person and the power was not delegated to that individual but, rather, to the committee. There is a lesser argument for judicial review on the grounds of procedural impropriety;

stem: An employee of a company injured a customer whilst showing off his "wheelie" skills on the fork lift truck he was driving. Later that day, despite having been forbidden to give lifts to unauthorised persons and there being a notice to this effect on the dashboard, the employee picked up a hitch-hiker, who was subsequently injured in an accident, due to the employee's negligence. The company would be vicariously liable for the injury caused by the employee's "wheelie" and for the passenger's injury, but not in respect of the injury to the hitchhiker

The company would be vicariously liable for the injury caused by the employee's "wheelie" and for the passenger's injury, but not in respect of the injury to the hitchhiker. An intentional act, which is in the course of employment, renders the employer vicariously liable, even if the employee is not acting strictly the performance of his duty, (Harrison v Michelin Tyre Co Ltd [1985] 1 All ER 918). The law permits an employer to limit acts, such as giving lifts to hitchhikers, which his employee may do within the course of his employment, (Twine v Bean's Express Ltd. (1946)). stem: An Irish citizen made a false representation from the United States to a woman in Canada. This resulted in the woman's London bank account being debited. The man has been charged with an offence under the Fraud Act 2006.
ask: Which options best states where jurisdiction would lie under the Fraud Act?

options.en: Courts in England or Wales have jurisdiction, because the Fraud Act is part of the Hague Convention of International Fraud - an internationally recognised treaty
Courts in England or Wales have jurisdiction, because the property was fraudulently lost in London
Courts in Canada have jurisdiction, because the false representation to the woman was made while she was there
Courts in the United States have jurisdiction, because the false representation to the woman was made there
Courts in the Republic of Ireland have jurisdiction, because the man is an Irish citizen

explanation.en: ted. The man You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The property was lost, not gained, in London. The Criminal Justice Act (CJA) 1993 provides that if any act or omission, proof of which is required for conviction of a relevant event (crime), occurred in England or Wales, it will be capable of prosecution in England and Wales. Schedule 1 to the 2006 Act amends the 1993 Act to extend the meaning of 'relevant event' to include: if the fraud involved an intention to make a gain and (a) the gain occurred, that occurrence; and (b) if the fraud involved an intention to cause a loss or to expose another to a risk of loss and the loss occurred, that occurrence.

stem: A man let a family house in a respectable area to a woman on a 10-year lease, with the lease containing a requirement that the woman will keep the property in a good state of repair. The man discovers that part of the rear wall of the house started to collapse six-months ago and the woman has failed to take any action in respect of this. The man last received rent, payable monthly, from the woman two months ago.
ask: How would you advise the man?

options.en: The woman has not breached the terms of her lease
Even though the breach is not continuing, the man may forfeit the lease
Even though the breach is continuing, the man cannot forfeit the lease, because he accepted rent
The breach is continuing and the man may forfeit the lease despite accepting rent
The breach is not continuing so the man cannot forfeit the lease, because he has accepted rent

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The woman has breached the terms of her lease. This is a continuing breach and the man has the ability to commence action to forfeit the lease despite having accepted rent. The responsibility for repairing the premises will depend on the length and the terms of the lease, subject to statutory provisions. In a long lease, the tenant will normally be responsible for all repairs. A failure to keep the property in good repair constitutes a breach of the repairing covenant in the lease. A repairing covenant is a positive covenant, meaning that a new breach is treated as occurring every day that the covenant is not performed. Therefore, even if the landlord accepts rent (which would act as a waiver of the breach) a fresh the next day and entitle the landlord to bring forfeiture proceedings. Note: the question whether the damage is structural or not does not affect the correct answer. The fact pattern does not suggest that the obligation to repair structural elements of the property is of the man. Also, while the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 imposes repairing covenants on the landlord for structural damages, it does not apply where a dwelling is let for less than seven years (in this case the term of the lease is for 10 years).

stem: A man's will includes the following bequests to his grandson (23) and granddaughter (17): "To my grandson, 1,500 shares in my company to be held on trust until he turns 25.
ask: To my granddaughter, £75,000 to be held on trust until she turns 25" Which of the following options best explains the legal position?

options.en: The granddaughter cannot apply for any maintenance, but the grandson is entitled to an advancement
The granddaughter cannot apply for maintenance, but the grandson is entitled to the dividends on the shares in the company
The grandson can apply for maintenance and the granddaughter can claim the interest generated by the £75,000

The grandson can ask for one-third of the capital to be advanced to him and the granddaughter can claim the interest generated by the £75,000

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The grandson is entitled to the dividends on the shares, but the granddaughter cannot apply for maintenance. This is because when the grandson reaches 25 years, he will be entitled to the shares under the trust. He holds a contingent interest in the trust and under s. 31(1)(ii) of the Trustee Act 1925, adults with a contingent trust interest are automatically entitled to the income from that interest as soon as they reach 18 years. By contrast, the granddaughter's interest is derived from a contingent pecuniary testamentary disposition. The granddaughter cannot therefore apply for maintenance, since such a disposition does not carry an entitlement to the terrore apply for maintenance, since such d disposition does not carry an entitlement to the intermediate income (s. 31(3) Trustee Act 1925), unless made by a parent or person in loco parentis. The grandson also cannot apply for maintenance, as he is over the age of 18, and maintenance is only available to minor beneficiaries (hence (C) is incorrect). While it is true that the grandson could apply for one-third of the capital to be advanced to him (options (D) and (E)), the maximum advancement is one-half for trusts and trust interests created or arising before 1st October 2014, and thereafter there is no maximum, under s. 32 (1)(a) of the Act. stem: Two solicitors wish to set up a practice together with a minimum of formality. Due to the nature of their business, they are not overly concerned about personal liability.
ask: How would you advise the solicitors as to which business structure would be the most appropriate for them to use?

options.en: The solicitors should set up a limited company
The solicitors should form an LLP
The solicitors should form a partnership
The solicitors should form a co-operative
The solicitors should establish themselves as two sole traders

explanation.en: Due to the You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The solicitors should form a partnership. They wish to keep the affairs of their business private and do not want to have to file accounts etc. at Companies House. They are also not concerned about personal liability. stem: The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) held that a prisoner's rights afforded under the European Convention on Human Rights (Convention) had been violated, because he had been denied the right to vote.
ask: He subsequently pleaded before a domestic court for a mandatory injunction forcing the prison service to allow him the Which option best describes the considerations before the domestic court deciding the prisoner's plea?

options.en: The domestic court is bound by the ECtHR judgment, since the UK had signed and ratified the Convention
The domestic court would not be bound by the ECtHR judgment, because the Human Rights Act 1998 is part of domestic law
The domestic court is only bound by the ECtHR judgment if the ECtHR has rejected an appeal by the UK government on the issue
The domestic court is not bound by the ECtHR judgment if Parliament has not implemented the ECtHR judgment after six months
The domestic court is not bound by the ECtHR judgment; only the UK government is bound by international treaty to act on it

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option E is correct. All other options are incorrect. Where the ECtHR has passed a judgment, the Contracting State is required to act on it and eltect changes in domestic laws that would allow domestic courts to give harmonious judgments. Domestic courts, meanwhile, must consider ECtHR judgments and, where possible, give leave to appeal, so that all domestic avenues are exhausted. The complainant may have some remedy at the ECtHR.

stem: Two miners were instructed to bring down the insecure roof of a coal mine. They tried to collapse the roof, but when their efforts failed, and contrary to their foreman's instructions, they decided to continue working as usual. The roof suddenly collapsed on top of them, killing them in the process.
ask: Were the miners contributorily negligent for their injuries under such circumstances?

options.en: The miners were not contributorily negligent, because their employer should not have permitted or encouraged them to work in the area in which the accident occurred
The miners were not contributorily negligent, because they both should bear responsibility for their own misfortune

The miners were not contributorily negligent, because it was one of those unfortunate events or a freakish accident in what is recognised to be a risky pastime, so the defence of volenti non fit injuria applies
The miners were contributorily negligent, because each party appears to have been similarly blameworthy

The miners were not contributorily negligent; it is too speculative to reach such a conclusion, since nether survived and it is unclear whether both concurred in the joint decision to continue working, or one told the other to

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Courts must deal broadly with the problem of apportionment of blame and must have regard to the culpability of each party. Claimants, however, share in the responsibility for the damage and blame cannot be measured without considering the relative importance of their acts in causing the damage. Comment: In Stapley v Gypsum Mines Ltd [1953] AC 663, under similar circumstances the House of Lords held that a claimant was 80% responsible for his own loss.

stem: Your client is present during a fight at a football match. Bottles and other missiles had been thrown at the police. Police allege that your client was seen waving his arms and shouting 'kill the United fans'. Your client is charged with violent disorder.
ask: Which of the following options best describes the criminal standard for violent?

options.en: The standard for violent disorder is that 12 or more people who are present together use or threaten unlawful violence such that a person of reasonable firmness would fear for his personal safety
The standard for violent disorder is that threats or violence must be directed towards another person such that a person of reasonable firmness would fear for his personal safety

The standard for violent disorder is where three people or more people who are present together use or threaten unlawful violence such that a person of reasonable firmness would fear for his personal safety
The standard for violent disorder is using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour, towards another person such that a person of reasonable firmness would fear for his personal safety
The standard for violent disorder is the causing of harassment, alarm or distress to another person such that a person of reasonable firmness would fear for his personal safety

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The offence of violent disorder is committed 'where three or more people who are present together use or threaten unlawful violence and the conduct of them (taken together) is such as would cause a person of reasonable firmness present at the scene to fear for his personal safety' (section 3 of the Public Order Act 1986). The offence of violent disorder is often witnessed at football matches or in animal rights cases where missiles have been thrown at people or property. In this case, since it is not said that there are 3 or more people involved in the scene, your client cannot be charged with the offence of violent disorder.

stem: A man, aged 19, had too much to drink after a night on the town, and was arrested and charged with being drunk and disorderly in a public place. His solicitor has told him that this is a summary offence.
ask: In which court must the man stand trial?

options.en: The Crown court
The county court
The magistrates' court
The magistrates' - youth court
The divisional court

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Offences triable only summarily are tried in the magistrates' court, and as the man is aged over 18, he would be tried as an adult.

stem: A woman suffered psychiatric damage following the death of her husband from a heart attack after months of negligent medical treatment. She arrived at the hospital within an hour of being told that he had died, and identified his body twenty What would be your advice to the woman, who
ask: would like to sue the hospital for?

options.en: The woman is unlikely to succeed in a psychiatric injury claim, because the elements of proximity of relationship, time, and place were not satisfied, since she didn't witness the actual negligent act
The woman is likely to succeed, since she was spatially and temporally close enough to the scene of the event or its immediate aftermath to reasonably fear for her own safety

The woman is unlikely to succeed in a psychiatric injury claim, because identification is not capable of being part of the immediate aftermath of the event if it goes to the fact of the death as distinct from the circumstances
The woman is unlikely to succeed in a psychiatric injury claim, because she did not experience any direct impact or fear of immediate personal injury, there could be no compensation
The woman is likely to succeed, since, by hearing of his death within the hour and seeing her husband's body in the mortuary, she can be classed as a secondary victim

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the correct answer. Psychiatric injury caused by confirming identity shortly after death would not be sufficient. In Taylor v. Somerset Health Authority [1993] it was held that the primary purpose of the claimant visiting the mortuary was to assure herself that her husband was dead. This went to the fact of death, not the circumstances in which death occurred. In the circumstances of the case, it did not come within the immediate aftermath. Lead case: Taylor v Somerset Health Authority [1993] PIQR P262..

stem: A man was originally jailed in 2008 for causing grievous bodily harm (GBH) to a woman, who died in 2012 from the injuries she sustained in 2008. The man has now been charged with murder.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: A prosecution may be brought where the victim's death occurred more than three years after the original injury, pending the Attorney-General's consent to the prosecution if the defendant has already been convicted of a non-fatal offence against the victim

A prosecution may be brought where the victim's death occurred more than a year and a day before the victim's death, as long as the defendant is provisionally charged with the offence of murder within a year and a day of being arrested and the provisional charge is left on file
Provided the defendant can show that his actions happened more than a year and a day before the victim's death, the defendant cannot be prosecuted

A prosecution cannot be brought if the defendant has already been convicted of a non-fatal offence against the victim because this would offend against the rule of double jeopardy (the procedural defence that forbids a defendant from being tried again for the same crime)
A prosecution may be brought where the victim's death occurred more than one-year after the original injury as long as the prosecution receives the Sovereign's consent under the royal prerogative

explanation.en: - -2 J -- presumed not to have caused a person's death if more than a year and a day elapsed before death. This rule used to argue that for any offence involving death, an action or omission would be presumed not to have caused the death, if the act or omission took place more than a year and a day ago. Although this has now been repealed, there are still occasions where the rule may be used. For example, in accordance with section 2 of the 1996 Act, it is possible for the presumption of no link between the act and the death to be used, with the consent of the Attorney-General. Now, if a defendant is charged with the offence of murder after a year and a day, and it is shown that he directly caused the death of a person, it is murder.

stem: A man bought land from a woman promising 'to keep the land uncovered with buildings for himself, his heirs and assigns'. The man later sold the land to his friend, giving his friend notice of his promise to the woman, as well as retaining ownership of adjacent land.
ask: The friend now wants to build on his land and claims he is not restricted from doing so, because there was no privity of contract between him and Which option best advises the parties?

options.en: The friend is not restricted from building on the land, because he has acquired the property in good faith and cannot be restrained from doing acts just because his predecessor disagrees with them
The friend is not restricted from building on the land, because consideration must move from the promise, and in this situation, no consideration has been provided by the friend
The friend is restricted from building on the land, because restrictive covenants are automatically enforceable against subsequent purchasers of land who were not party to the original contract

The friend is restricted from building on the land, since he had notice of the promise when purchasing the land. The man retains adjacent land, and a negative covenant may be enforced against him to fulfil the woman's wishes

The friend is restricted from building on the land, since he had notice of the promise when purchasing the land. The man retains adjacent land, and a positive covenant may be enforced against him to fulfil the woman's wishes

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Even where someone buys from the original purchaser, that person can be made subject to restriction in relation to land, provided that certain conditions were satisfied; in particular, that the original vendor still has an interest to protect - for example, continued ownership of the adjacent land. The covenant must be substantially negative. An undertaking which seems prima facie positive, may imply a negative undertaking and then be enforceable. Lead case: Tulk v Moxhay (1848) 2 Ph 774; 41 ER 1143.

stem: A man and woman purchase a house in 1960. While the conveyance is into the sole name of the man, it contains a declaration of trust to the effect that the woman is entitled to a 50% equitable share. In 1978, the man executes a conveyance transferring the legal and beneficial title to the land to the woman and his friend to hold the land on trust for themselves as joint tenants. In 1983, the man serves a notice of severance of the joint tenancy on his friend.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position after the notice of severance has been served?

options.en: The woman and the man's friend hold the property on trust for themselves as joint tenants in equal shares
The woman and the man's friend hold the property on trust for themselves as joint tenants in unequal shares with a 75% share to the woman and a 25% share to the man's friend
The woman and the man's friend hold the property on trust for themselves as tenants in common in equal shares
The woman and the man's friend hold the property on trust for themselves as tenants in common in unequal shares with a 75% share to the woman and a 25% share to the man's friend
The woman and the man's friend hold the property on trust for themselves as tenants in common in unequal shares with a 25% share to the woman and a 75% share to the man's friend

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The woman and the man's friend hold the property on trust for themselves as tenants in common in equal shares. The express declaration of trust contained in the 1978 conveyance is exhaustive and conclusive of the position. The doctrines of implied or constructive trust cannot, therefore, be used to take account of the share that B already held in the property and the equitable maxim that "equity assumes equality" will apply, meaning that the parties will hold the property as tenants in common in equal shares.

stem: A private company limited by shares has model articles of association. A man owns 80% of the issued shares and a woman owns the remaining 20%. It is not possible to restrict the articles without a special resolution of the board of directors

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. There are no restrictions on the members entering into a shareholders' agreement and such an agreement is enforceable against the members. These agreements are often used to protect the rights of minority shareholders without a change to the articles themselves being necessary.

stem: A 12 year old boy of mixed race who has been in the foster care system for the last 8 years seeks to challenge social workers' refusal to place him with a suitable family of a different ethnicity. The Convention rights that have been violated are: the right to fair trial and the right to freedom of expression

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option D is correct. All other options are incorrect. As the European Court of Human Rights found in Airey v Ireland 2 EHRR 305, both the Article 6(1) and Article 8 rights of the Applicant, had been violated because of the absence of legal aid enabling her to access the courts and institute appropriate proceedings. In that case, it was the combination of the applicant's circumstances, the nature of the case, a complex procedure and the absence of any legal aid that led to the breach of Article 6.

stem: A person dies on the 10th of January 2012. His estate includes 5,000 shares in a private limited company purchased in April 2006 for £3,000. At the date of death, the market value of the shares was £8,000. The personal representatives (PRs) sell the shares in August 2012 for £9,000.
ask: What is the chargeable gain (assume the annual exemption is zero)?

options.en: fO

explanation.en: The best answer is D. £1,000. Because death is not a disposal, there is no charge to Capital Gains Tax (CGT) when the deceased dies. The PRs are deemed to have acquired the shares for £8,000 and have, therefore, made a gain of £1,000 on their subsequent sale. A is not correct as CT is based on the gain on sale, not the purchase price alone. B is not correct as the PRs sold the shares rather than transferring them to a beneficiary. C is not correct as chargeable gain is the difference between the probate value and the gain on sale. stem: A solicitor receives a cheque for his client in settlement of a litigation matter. The cheque is made payable to the client.

stem: The UK Parliament has devolved powers to the Scottish Parliament, Welsh Assembly and Northern Ireland Assembly. Each national legislature may debate and pass legislation within its own competence.

stem: A woman threw a lit firework into a crowded market. It was caught by a boy, and then quickly tossed away to his friend and another, until eventually it exploded in a man's face. The man wishes to issue proceedings against the woman for trespass and assault, but the woman asserts in her defence that the actions of the bystanders rendered the man's loss too remote.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the settled legal position?

options.en: The woman is not answerable in an action of trespass and assault by the man, because, while the original act against the boy was a trespass, it was neither against the boy's friend nor the man
Trespass and assault would lie because the natural and probable consequence of the act done by the woman was injury to somebody, and, therefore, the act was illegal at common law
Trespass and assault would not lie because the injury which the man suffered was not immediate, or consequential of the woman's action
Trespass and assault would not lie because the intervention of the boy and his friend was a novus actus interveniens

explanation.en: **ion? You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Intended consequences are not too remote. When the act of a third-party intervenes between the original act or omission and the damage, the original act or omission will still be the direct cause of the damage if the act of the third-party would be expected in all the circumstances. stem: A woman's mother has been diagnosed with terminal illness. The woman decides to take her mother's life in order to prevent her from suffering. At trial the judge fully accepted that this was a case of a genuine mercy killing, motivated by the woman's desire to end her mother's suffering.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position regarding so- called mercy killings?

options.en: Mercy killings are a specific offence, attracting a maximum penalty of two years imprisonment
While mercy killings are still classed as murder, judges have discretion in the sentencing process and are not bound by the mandatory sentencing regime
Mercy killings are not a criminal offence, provided the permission of the individual has been obtained in writing
Mercy killings are considered as manslaughter under English law
A mercy killing is considered murder, in the same was as any other form of murder

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. A mercy killing is treated in exactly the same way as any other murder would be, subject to the same tests as any other murder case.

stem: A woman is the freehold owner of grassy land, which is bordered on three sides by three houses, also owned by the women. She transfers the grassy land to a man but retains the three houses. The transfer contains a covenant which provides that the man will maintain the grassy land as an area of open parkland. Three years later, the man sells the grassy land to a developer who obtains planning permission to build an additional house on the land.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The covenant is of a positive nature and the burden of it has not passed to the developer
The covenant is of a negative nature and the burden of it has not passed to the developer
The covenant is of a positive nature and the burden of it has passed to the developer
The covenant is of a negative nature and the burden of it has passed to the developer
The covenant does not touch and concern the man's land

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The covenant is of a negative nature and the burden of it has passed to the developer. The covenant is similar to that in Tulk v Moxhay in that it effectively imposes an obligation not to construct any buildings on the grassy land. It benefits the properties retained by the woman (the three houses), it touches and concerns her land and is, by virtue of s.79 LPA 1925, intended to bind subsequent owners of the grassy land.

stem: An auctioneer falsely stated that all the apartments in a block of flats were let, when in fact the auctioneer knew that that these tenants had already served notice to quit. On the back of this statement, a man bought the block of flats as an investment, with a view to earning a profit from the rent paid by the existing tenants.
ask: Which statement is the most accurate regarding whether the auctioneer's statement amounted to an actionable misrepresentation?

options.en: The auctioneer's statement was no more than an expression of opinion, and not a statement of fact
The auctioneer's statement that that block was fully let, when he actually knew that the tenants had given notice to quit, was a misrepresentation
The auctioneer had no duty to the man because there was no pre-existing confidential or fiduciary relationship giving rise to a duty of full disclosure
The parties were contracting with one another, so the auctioneer was entitled to observe silence, even in regard to facts which he believed would influence the man

Due to the influence of the principle of caveat emptor, it is the duty of each party to look after his own interests and exercise his own judgment in deciding whether or not to enter into a particular contract

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The man would be led to suppose that he was purchasing with continuing tenancies at fixed rents, whereas he would, in fact, have to find new tenants after the completion of his purchase. A half-truth, therefore, may indeed be a misrepresentation. Lead case: Dimmock v Hallett (1866) LR 2 Ch App 21.

stem: A settlor wishes to settle £50,000 on trust for his five grandchildren in equal shares. The settlor does not identify which £50,000 out of his total fortune of £3.5 million is to form the trust fund. The settlor's property includes fine art worth £800,000, jewellery worth £600,000, £1.5 million in a bank account, and £600,000 in cash.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trust will be valid, because it is possible to identify precisely which property is to be held on trust
The trust will be valid, because the trust money is assumed to derive from the settlor's bank account
The trust will be valid, because the beneficiaries will hold the money as joint tenants under a single trust
The trust will be void, because it is not possible to identify precisely which property is held on trust
The trust will be void, because the trust money is not divided into five separate parcels, one for each grandchild

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The gift will fail for lack of subject matter. The property comprising the trust fund must be segregated from all other property so that its identity can be sufficiently certain. Otherwise, there will be no certainty of subject matter and the trust will fail. The settlor has not identified which £50,000 out of his total fortune of £3.5 million is to form the trust fund. The trust will therefore be void. Had there been certainty of subject matter, it would not be necessary for the £50,000 itself to be divided into five separate parcels of £10,000 for each grandchild, because the trustees would hold the £50,000 for the five beneficiaries as joint tenants under a single trust. Where the property is intangible property made up of shares of the same class), it remains a contentious issue whether the same rule applies as to tangible property. Note: The rules in Hunter v Moss and Re Harvard Securities do not create a strict distinction between tangible and intangible property. In those cases, the reason that the court was prepared to relax the rule on certainty of subject matter was because the settlor's assets were identical (i.e., all shares in the same readily identifiable company which court found that although the assets (gold bullion) had the same value, because they were not identical then the rule on certainty could not be relaxed. It wasn't necessarily because they were intangible and there is some doubt across the case law in this area. This is highlighted by reading the decision in Re Harvard Securities.

stem: While holidaying on a friend's private beach, your client was photographed in compromising poses via a telescopic lens by a freelance photographer. She wished to have these photographs banned from publication. However, there was no relationship between your client and the freelancer.
ask: What would you advise your client?

options.en: Individuals have a common law right to privacy
Individuals have an equitable right to privacy
Individuals have a right to personal privacy grounded in the doctrine of confidence
Individuals have a right to personal privacy grounded in the doctrine of breach of trust
Individuals have a right to personal privacy grounded in the absolute right to privacy afforded by the Human Rights Act (HRA) 1998

explanation.en: All other options are incorrect. In the common law, where there is no pre-existing relationship of confidence between the parties, traditional equitable breach of confidence can still arise where information is knowingly acquired, illegally, and then used against the will of the subject. Regarding option E, the right to privacy must be balance with the right to freedom of expression under the terms of the HRA. See further Douglas v Hello & Campbell v MGN.

stem: A case comes before the Supreme Court. There are two previous conflicting precedents, one from the Supreme Court (previously called the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords) in 1935 and the other from the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (Privy Council) decided in 1936.

The Supreme Court is bound by its previous decisions, but only from the time it replaced the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords as the court of final resort in the UK
The Supreme Court may depart from its own past decision, may choose to follow the persuasive authority of the Privy Council or it may follow its own previous decision
The Supreme Court is bound by the decision of the Privy Council, because that is the most recent one

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. All options are open to the Supreme Court in this context, and it may choose its own course. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is the court of final appeal for the UK overseas territories and Crown dependencies. Its decisions have persuasive value......my une.. its own

stem: You are entertaining clients from overseas. They are very interested in the workings of government and have a particular interest in the responsibility of the government. They ask you how the doctrine of individual ministerial responsibility operates.
ask: What are the mechanisms by which individual ministerial responsibility operates?

options.en: Each individual minister may speak out against government policy but is expected to bear the consequences of doing so
The minister is responsible to Parliament for their decisions and the conduct of their departments. They are expected to resign in the event of a policy disaster
Each and every minister may be blamed for the wider failings of government or other departments
A minister may be subject to and bound by a confidence motion
Each minister is expected to support government policy in Parliament and in public

They are expected to resign in the event of a policy disaster. Ministers are responsible to Parliament for their decisions and for the conduct of their departments. They are required to make announcements and to answer questions in Parliament. This is an essential principle to ensure accountability to the electorate of the actions of government. stem: A man receives a letter from his solicitor regarding a litigation matter. The letter states that the solicitor is not able, at this early stage of the proceedings, to provide him with an estimate as to the likely overall costs for the litigation. Instead, the solicitor suggests that matters should be reviewed in six weeks' time, after the defendant has filed his response to Mr the man's claim. Which of the following statements best describes the effect of the SRA Code of Conduct in this situation?
ask: nich ot the tollowing statements best describes the entect of the SkA Code ot Conduct in this situation?

options.en: The Code requires solicitors to advise clients of a precise figure regarding the likely overall costs of the matter
The Code requires solicitors to advise clients of a precise figure regarding the likely overall costs of the matter in all circumstances, including the legal charges and disbursements
The Code requires solicitors to advise clients of a precise figure regarding the likely overall costs of the matter in all circumstances, not including the legal charges and disbursements
The Code requires solicitors to explain to clients why a precise figure cannot be given at the outset and to agree a ceiling figure and a review date

The Code requires solicitors to provide clients with as much information regarding costs as possible at the start and as their matter progresses, but if a precise figure cannot be given at the outset, you should agree a ceiling figure or a review date

explanation.en: E is correct. 01.13 requires the solicitor to advise clients of the basis of their fees and charges. They must be kept informed of any rate increases (IB1.14) as well as being told about any payments that will need to be made to others, for example, expert witnesses (IB1.15). The solicitor must give his client the best information possible about the likely overall costs of the matter (including the legal charges and disbursements). Provided it is genuinely impossible for the solicitor to give a realistic costs estimate (which could be the case at the start of a litigation matter), and the solicitor gives the client an estimate of the likely overall cost of the matter as soon as he is able, the advice given to Mr Finicky would comply with the Code of Conduct.

stem: You are advising a client regarding his options about setting up as a freelance contractor. He is considering either setting up a limited company and becoming an employee, or becoming self-employed.
ask: From a tax point of view, which of the following is the best advice to give your client?

options.en: If your client is self-employed, he will have to inform Her Majesty's Revenue & Customs (HMRC) of his liability for income tax, within six months of the end of the tax year
If your client is self-employed, he will have to inform HMRC of his liability for income tax, within three months of the end of the tax year
If your client is self-employed, he won't have to inform HMRC of his liability for income tax, until the end of the tax year
If your client is self-employed, he won't have to inform HMRC of his liability for income tax, until up to six months after the end of the tax year
If your client is self-employed, he won't have to inform HMRC of his liability for income tax, until up to 12 months after the end of the tax year

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D.
