stem: Your client insisted that she would only purchase organic bananas which had not been cultivated using pesticides, adding that if they were pesticide -free, she would not even bother to ask the price. She was given an oral assurance that the greengrocer's bananas had not been treated with pesticides. When she got home, however, she discovered that the bananas were not organic and had been treated with pesticides.
ask: Was your client entitled to claim for breach of contract against the greengrocer?

options.en: No, because there was no actual contractual promise that the bananas were pesticide free, just a mere representation
No, because a person is not liable in damages for an innocent misrepresentation
No, because your client had already brought the bananas home with her, meaning any representation as to the nature of the bananas was in the past and could not amount to a warranty
Yes, because the intention of the greengrocer was clearly intended to misrepresent the nature of the bananas to your client
Yes, given the obvious importance of the greengrocer's assertion, such an assertion would become a term of the contract

explanation.en: E is correct. If the statement is such that a claimant would not have made the contract without it, then the statement is a term of the contract and not a mere inducement. The greengrocer's assurance constituted a condition of the contract - it was of such importance that, without it, your client would not have contracted. Lead case: Bannerman v White (1861) 142 ER 685.

stem: A property company is the freehold owner of a large mixed use residential and commercial block in the centre of Oldcastle. It leases a commercial unit at street level to an estates company for use only as an estate agent's office. The lease includes a right to display a billboard on the side of the building, provided that the advertising shall not in any way relate to property services.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The property company has granted the estate company an easement to display a billboard
The property company has not granted the estates company an easement because there is no dominant tenement
The property company has not granted the estates company an easement because there is no servient tenement which the easement can burden
The property company has not granted the estates company an easement because the display of a billboard is not capable of forming the subject matter of an easement
The property company has not granted the estates company an easement because the right does not accommodate the dominant tenement

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The property company has not granted the estates company an easement because the right does not accommodate the dominant tenement. The right must either directly benefit the land itself or else benefit some trade or business which is being carried on there. The right granted by the property company does neither, as the advertising of the estates company's business is specifically prohibited.

stem: The Chamber of seven judges in Strasbourg adjudicated the merits of an applicant's complaint against the UK. After hearing submissions on behalf of both the applicant and the UK, the Chamber found in favour of the UK.
ask: The applicant wishes to appeal Which of the following assertions best states to where, if at all, an applicant must lodge an appeal against the Chamber's verdict?

options.en: Appeals from the Chamber are lodged to the Upper Chamber
Appeals from the Chamber are lodged to the Lower Chamber
Appeals from the Chamber are lodged to the Great Chamber
Appeals from the Chamber are lodged to the Grand Chamber
The judgment of the Chamber is final; there is no further avenue of appeal

explanation.en: D is correct. Appeals from the Chamber are lodged to the Grand Chamber. If the Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights finds a violation, it may grant "just satisfaction" to the applicant by way of monetary compensation for certain forms of damages. The Court may also require the State concerned to refund the applicant's expenses. If no violation is found, the applicant does not have to pay any additional costs (e.g. those incurred by the respondent State). The judgment of a Chamber of the Court is not immediately final, but becomes so. The possibility of appeal to the Grand Chamber exists if there is a referral within three months of the Chamber judgment. The judgment of the Grand Chamber is final and binding.

stem: A parent wants to challenge a decision by the local education authority (LEA) concerning the allocation of secondary school places. Two of the five committee members have children who were allocated better schools; parents had no opportunity to appeal the decision; and the LEA gave no reasons for its decision.
ask: Which of the following options sets out the position regarding a possible application for judicial review of the LEA's decision?

options.en: The LEA has no obligation not to offend the rule against bias, but has a duty to provide the right to a fair hearing and a general duty to give reasons for its decision
The LEA has an obligation not to offend the rule against bias and the right to a fair hearing, but has no general duty to give reasons for its decision
The LEA has an obligation not to offend the rule against bias and the right to a fair hearing, and has a duty to give reasons for its decision
The LEA has neither an obligation not to offend the rule against bias, nor a duty to provide the right to a fair hearing but does have a general duty to give reasons for its decision
The LEA has no obligation not to offend the rule against bias, nor a duty to provide the right to a fair hearing and no general duty to give reasons for its decision

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The duty to give reasons is not generally recognised in English administrative law, unless it is expressly required by statute. A duty to give reasons may arise, however, where it is expressly required in legislation; where it is called for in fairness, under the duty of candour owed by a body under challenge; and, where a response which is unreasoned may be seen as unreasonable.

stem: A supermarket chain is put up for sale as a result of continuing financial difficulties. Three competitors enter the negotiations to buy the company as a going concern.
ask: Two of the competitors ask a firm of solicitors to represent them in the bidding Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The firm can represent the interests of both parties because there is no conflict of interests between them
The firm can represent the interests of both parties because they are competing for the same asset
The firm can represent the interests of both parties because the confidential information obtained from each party is not material to the other party
The firm cannot represent the interests of both parties because it is not accepted business practice
The firm cannot represent the interests of both parties because of the significant risk of conflict between their interests

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. There is a clear conflict of interests between the two firms - both wish to buy the chain in question, and any step taken by the firm to try to make this happen would be detrimental to the interests of the other client. Nonetheless, one firm can act for the two bidders in the bidding war, according O3.7, because they are both competing for the same asset which, if attained by one of them, will make that asset unavailable to others; there is no other conflict or significant risk of conflict between the interests of the clients in relation to that matter; the parties are sophisticated clients and are thus capable of giving their informed consent to the firm acting for both information obtained from either client is protected by the use of information barriers, because both parties have an adverse interest to one another by virtue of competing for the same asset (IB3.6).

stem: A man and woman, who honestly thought they had married one another, drew up a separation agreement. They subsequently discovered that their supposed marriage was invalid, because the man's previous wife was still alive.
ask: What effect would the existence of the man's previous wife have on the couple's separation agreement?

options.en: The man would be liable under the separation agreement for breach of contract
The woman could rescind the separation agreement due to fraudulent misrepresentation
The separation agreement would be void due to common mistake, and the man would have no liability under it
This is a category of mistake, non est factum, or "it is not my deed", which renders the contract void
The woman could rescind the premarital agreement due to the man's negligent failure to disclose to her that there was already a wife

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Common mistake occurs when both parties mistakenly contract about the same set of facts. This type of mistake is a mistake as to the existence of the subject matter of the contract or res extincta. An operative mistake at law renders the contract void. Lead case: Galloway v Galloway (1914) 30 TLR 531.

stem: A convicted sex offender seeks to challenge his inclusion on the UK's Sex Offender's Register. He argues that the lifelong duty to keep the police notified of where he is living and of travel abroad ('the notification requirements') breaches his right to privacy under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention). He was included on the register indefinitely because of the severity of his offences.
ask: Which option best states the domestic courts' approach to such notification?

options.en: There are no circumstances under which the risk of an individual carrying out a further sexual offence can be discounted to the extent that continuance of the notification requirements is unjustified
Indefinite inclusion on the register is justified because a right of review would compromise the utility of the notification requirements as a tool for the prevention and detection of sexual offences
Indefinite inclusion on the register is justified because resource implications would bar granting a right of review making it impossible to operate a review process
Lifelong registration on the sex offenders register without any right of review breaches the Convention right to privacy

While indefinite inclusion on the register interferes with an offender's right to privacy rights, this interference is justified since it is directed at the legitimate aims of preventing a crime and the protection of the rights and freedoms of others

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option D is correct. The notification requirements would constitute a disproportionate interference with the sex offenders Article 8 Convention rights because they made no provision for individual review of the requirements. In these circumstances, the Supreme Court recently declared that s 82(1) Sexual Offences Act 2003 was incompatible with Article 8 because it made no provision for individual review of the notification requirements. Lead case: R (on the application of F (by his litigation friend F)) and another (Respondents) v Secretary of State for the Home Department (Appellant) [2010]

stem: A man owns the entire share capital in a company. He approaches a solicitor and tells him he is interested in selling 75% of his shares in the company to his son.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes what the solicitor may do?

options.en: The solicitor must rely on an exclusion or exemption to avoid committing a criminal offence because: he is in business; the shares are a specified investment; and he will be carrying out specified investment activities

The solicitor need not rely on an exclusion or exemption to avoid committing a criminal offence because: he is in business; the shares are a specified investment; but the solicitor will not be carrying out any specified investment activities

The solicitor need not rely on an exclusion or exemption to avoid committing a criminal offence because: he is in business; the shares are a specified investment; but the solicitor will only be advising

The solicitor need not rely on an exclusion or exemption to avoid committing a criminal offence because: he is in business; the shares are a specified investment; but the solicitor will only be arranging

The solicitor would be guilty of a civil offence if he advises or arranges because: he is in business; the shares are a specified investment; and he will be carrying out specified investment activities

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is (A). The client is seeking the solicitor's advice and assistance in his capacity as such, so that the solicitor is in business. Shares are indeed a specified investment, and the solicitor will be carrying out specified investment activities, such as advising and/or arranging, which would involve him in a criminal offence, unless he can rely on an exclusion or exemption under the Regulated Activities Order 2001. In this case it is worth noting that, because the man is transferring over 75% of his shares in the company to his son, he can rely on the takeover exclusion for activities performed in connection with the sale of a body corporate.

stem: A man made a joke on Twitter in frustration at the closing of an airport he was due to fly out of because of snow. The message stated: "The airport is closed. You've got three days to get your act together otherwise I'm blowing the airport sky high!!" An off-duty member of airport staff read the 'joke' and reported it to police.
ask: Which option best states the man's criminal liability, if any?

options.en: On these facts, the man has not broken any law because English criminal law does not advocate using the power of arrest for simple speech acts
On these facts, the man has not broken any law because social media is used for everyday communication, and it would be totally inappropriate to prosecute routine free expression
On these facts, the man has broken the law and a court may well find he has specifically intended to be menacing in making the post
On these facts, the man has not broken any law and a court would not find that he did not specifically intend to be menacing in making the post

On these facts, the man has broken the law because all internet-based messages of grossly offensive or of an indecent, obscene, or menacing character, or sent for the purpose of causing annoyance, inconvenience or needless anxiety to others, are criminal

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The man is likely to be charged with sending, by a public communications network, a message that was grossly offensive or of an indecent, obscene or menacing character, contrary to section 127 of the Communications Act (the Act) 2003. This is a public order offence other than those related to sporting events or industrial disputes. The offence was originally intended to prosecute people making abusive telephone calls but is applicable to message board posters, bloggers, commenters, twitterati, e-mailers and presumably website hosts and other internet data. While the man could also be charged for making a bomb hoax under section 51 of the Criminal Law Act 1977, it is more difficult to prove than s 127 of the Act.

stem: A company manufactures silicone breast implants in full compliance with regulatory and statutory requirements. A woman had the company's silicone breast implants inserted, but one of them ruptured soon after insertion. The company asserts that it complied with its UK and EU obligations.
ask: Which option best states the company's legal position under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 (CPA)?

options.en: It is a defence to a breach of the CPA if the manufacturer can show that the defect is due to compliance with UK or EU laws
The company would not have a defence, even if the manufacturer can show that the defect is due to compliance with UK or EU laws, because liability is strict
The company would have a general defence under negligence, or in contract

There is no general defence in negligence, or in contract, in circumstances where the manufacturer is able to demonstrate compliance with regulatory and statutory requirements relating to the development, manufacture, licensing, marketing and supply of the product
The company would have a defence, because any defect in the breast implant was not discoverable, so the development risks defence is applicable

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. It is a defence to proceedings under Section 4(1)(a) of the Consumer Protection Act 1987 (CPA) if the manufacturer can show that the defect is due to compliance with UK or EU laws. stem: A man and woman remortgage their house with the assistance of a mortgage advance from BankCo. Unfortunately, the solicitors employed by BankCo to register its mortgage over the man and woman's house at HM Land Registry fail to do so and therefore BankCo's mortgage does not take effect in law and only operates as an equitable charge. The man and woman sell their house to a new owner for £100,000, but after the sale, BankCo realises what has happened and tries to rely upon its equitable charge to take possession of the house from the new owner.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: BankCo's mortgage binds the new owner, because it was created prior to the owner acquiring an interest in the property
BankCo's mortgage automatically does not bind the new owner, because it is not registered
BankCo's mortgage will only bind the new owner if they were aware of it
BankCo's mortgage does not bind the new owner, because they paid the purchase monies to two people
BankCo's mortgage does not bind the new owner, because they paid over £50,000 for the property

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. BankCo's mortgage will only bind the new owner if the owner was aware of it. Because the mortgage has not been registered at HM Land Registry, it operates as an equitable charge only and does not take effect in law. The Doctrine of Notice therefore applies which states that "equitable interests bind everyone except a bona fide purchaser for value without notice." The new owner would be a bona fide purchaser for value without notice, as they were not aware of the charge and had given valuable consideration in exchange for the transfer. The new owner would therefore not be bound by BankCo's charge.

stem: The following provision was included in a trust instrument: "I settle £10,000 on trust for all retired coal miners who worked for British Coal in Country Durham, still alive at 1 November 2009. " Two trustees, ordinary members of the public, are appointed.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trust would be likely to fail on the grounds of administrative workability
The trust would be likely to fail on the grounds of evidential uncertainty
The trust would be likely to fail on the grounds of conceptual uncertainty
The trust would be likely to fail on the grounds of ascertainability
The trust would be valid because the objects of the trust are certain

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The objects of the trust are certain in this case; however, the trust would be likely to fail on the grounds of administrative workability. The trustees are ordinary members of the public for whom it would be difficult if not impossible to access the records held for retired miners in County Durham and to distribute the funds accordingly. Were the trustees also the trustees of the pension fund for miners in County Durham, it would be a far more straightforward task to administer the trust.

stem: You are advising the directors of a private company limited by shares. Their company is in financial difficulty and they are mulling the options as to how best to proceed.
ask: One option is administration, but they do not know much about what administration is or its ultimate purpose, compared to liquidation or corporate voluntary What is the purpose of the modern administration procedure?

options.en: To wind down a solvent company, pay creditors and distribute the company's assets
To bind creditors and the company in an agreement in respect of payment of the company's debts
To wind down an insolvent company, pay creditors and distribute the company's assets
To salvage the company as a going concern, as far as possible
To realise the best possible return for the creditor that appointed the administrator, at any cost

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. To salvage the company as a going concern, as far as possible. The main purpose of the new administration procedure is the survival of the company as a going concern. Where it is not reasonably practicable to rescue the company (e.g. where the support of the company's bankers is not forthcoming and there are no other means of financing the company), the objective then becomes to realise some or all of the company's assets, in order to distribute them among the company's secured and preferential creditors. Administration also protects a company against claims by creditors.

stem: Your client has been charged with murder. You suspect she might be suffering from a mental disorder. You are considering submitting a defence of diminished responsibility on her behalf.
ask: Which option best states an essential component of proving the defence of diminished responsibility?

options.en: An essential component of proving the defence of diminished responsibility is that the defendant was suffering from an abnormality of awareness
An essential component of proving the defence of diminished responsibility is that the defendant was suffering from an abnormality of concentration
An essential component of proving the defence of diminished responsibility is that the defendant was suffering from an abnormality of mind
An essential component of proving the defence of diminished responsibility is that the defendant was suffering from an abnormality of mental functioning
The defence has nothing to prove; the prosecution, rather than the defence, has the burden of disproving diminished responsibility

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Section 52 CJA 2009 has replaced the definition of diminished responsibility found in the Homicide Act 1957. It applies to defendants charged with murder where the acts or omissions resulted in the death of the victim took place after October 2010. The term 'abnormality of mind' in the 1957 Act has been replaced by the term 'abnormality of mental functioning'. The reference to an abnormality of mental functioning is a major updating of the law, allowing both for a wider range of mental illnesses than the old law and for developments in medical science.

stem: A VAT registered company sold £500,000 in domestic fuel and power and was paid £100,000 for installing energy-saving materials. They also purchased items to the total value of £600,000, all at the 20% VAT rate.
ask: How much VAT would need to be paid to Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC), if any?

options.en: £0 is payable by the company to HMRC
£30,000 is payable by the company to HMRC
£30,000 is owed to the company from HMRC
£90,000 is payable by the company to HMRC
£90,000 is owed to the company from HMRC

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. £90,000 owed to the company from HMRC. Domestic fuel and power, as well as installing energy-saving materials, are subject to the reduced rate of VAT, 5%. The output tax is (600,000 X 0.05) = £30,000. Their input tax is (600,000 X 0.2) = £120,000. They are entitled to a refund of £90,000 from HMRC. A is not correct as domestic fuel and power, as well as installing energy-saving materials, are subject to the reduced rate of VAT, 5% and so the output tax is not equal to the input tax. B is the output tax, and input tax exceeds output tax. C is not correct although input tax does exceed the output tax, as this amount is the output tax.

stem: After finishing the family laundry, a resident went in to her garden, where she hung the washing out to dry. Despite barely sleeping because of the incessant noise from lorries on the highway, which were continually entering and exiting the neighbouring oil depot, she awoke early the next morning. She went to collect the laundry, only to notice that it had been ruined by acid smuts emitted from the oil depot's chimneys.
ask: What would your advice be to the resident regarding the noise and the acid smuts?

options.en: The resident could bring a claim against the oil depot in private nuisance for the noise caused by lorries on the highway and in public nuisance for damage to the laundry caused by the acid smuts from the chimneys
The resident could bring a claim against the oil depot in private nuisance for the noise caused by lorries on the highway and for damage to the laundry caused by the acid smuts from the chimneys
The resident could bring a claim against the oil depot in public nuisance for the noise caused by lorries on the highway and for damage to the laundry caused by the acid smuts from the chimneys

The resident could bring a claim against the oil depot in public for the noise caused by lorries on the highway, in private nuisance for the noise caused by lorries in the depot, and in private nuisance for damage to the laundry caused by the acid smuts from the chimneys

By choosing to live opposite such a large industrial depot, the resident has chosen to forgo her right to bring a claim, particularly as the depot is fulfilling an important function by supplying goods and services and employing a large number of people

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The resident could successfully bring a claim against the oil company in public nuisance for noise caused by road tankers, and in private nuisance for damage to clothes on the washing line. The concentrations of road tanker movements on the highway outside the resident's house at night and in the early hours of the morning would be unreasonable and as a result the oil depot would be liable for a public nuisance because the resultant noise affected the resident more than the ordinary member of the public. By the same token the noise from the lorries on the highway at night could be a private nuisance if it was found to be directly related to the operation of the depot and the noise materially her own garden. Therefore the damage to the clothes was a material injury to her property, which would give rise to a right of action in private nuisance.

stem: Four trustees are being sued for breach of trust after one of the trustees decided to sell valuable jewelry constituting trust property to a third party to pay his debts. The other trustees neither knew of this nor would have consented if they did.
ask: Which of the following correctly states the trustees' liability, if any?

options.en: Trustees are under a duty to act jointly, and liability attaches jointly and severally. The unilateral nature of the action by the wrongdoing trustee is irrelevant

Trustees are under a duty to act jointly, and liability attaches jointly and severally. However, the unilateral nature of the action by the wrongdoing trustee will mean that trustee alone is liable for breach of trust
Trustees are under a duty to act jointly, and liability attaches jointly only. The unilateral nature of the action by the wrongdoing trustee is irrelevant
Trustees are under no duty to act jointly, so liability is individual only. Therefore, only the wrongdoing trustee is liable
Trustees are under no duty to act jointly, but will be held jointly and severally liable in any event of breach of trust by any one or more of the trustees

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. Trustees are under a duty to act jointly, and liability attaches jointly and severally. However, the unilateral nature of the action by the wrongdoing trustee will mean that that trustee alone is liable for breach of trust. See Townley v Sherborne (1633) Bridg. 35.

stem: The articles of association of a private company limited by shares states that the company's business is the production of footwear in the UK. Due to the economic downturn, the company contracts with China for more cost-efficient production of one of the company's products. The majority shareholders propose to ratify the transaction in two weeks' time. A minority shareholder is aggrieved and wants to know what action, if any, can be taken.
ask: Which of the following best describes the available actions that can be taken by the minority shareholder, if any?

options.en: No action is available to the minority shareholder
The shareholder may apply for a prohibitory injunction
The shareholder must sue the directors personally in negligence to recover any loss to the value of his shares caused by the company's decision
The shareholder must sue the company directly in negligence to recover any loss to the value of his shares caused by the company's decision
The minority shareholder may bring a derivative claim

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The minority shareholder may bring a derivative claim. Section 260 of the Companies Act 2006 (the Act) provides that a member can bring a derivative claim on behalf of the company against a director for breach of duty (in this case the duty under Section 171 of the Act to act in accordance with the company's constitution), but such a claim requires the shareholder to establish a prima facie case (s 261) and to obtain the permission of the court to continue with the claim (s 263). Under Section 263 of the Act, the court must refuse to give permission where the court is satisfied that a person acting in accordance with s 172 of the Act (duty to promote the success of the company) would not MEIVE MELY DEMARVIMMING MEDIA DEVI THIN TILL IMULY to promote the success of the company) would not seek to continue with the claim, or where the act has been authorised or ratified by the company (s 263(2) CA 2006). Where this is not the case, factors the court can take into account in deciding whether to allow the claim to proceed include whether the shareholder is acting in good faith, the importance that a person acting in accordance with s 172 of the Act would attach to continuing the claim, whether the act in the circumstances would be likely to be authorised or ratified by the company, whether the company has decided not to pursue the claim, whether the member could pursue an action in his own riaht, and whether ratification of the act is imminent.

stem: A woman bought a mobile phone from a mobile phone company, signing a sales agreement with one of the company's representatives. The woman is dissatisfied with the phone, but when she called the company and told them that she wished to cancel the contract, she was told by a company representative that the sales agreement contained a clause expressly providing for the exclusion of all implied warranties. The woman argues that, whilst not disputing the presence of the clause, she knew nothing of its content as she had not read the agreement.
ask: Can the woman reject the sales agreement?

options.en: The woman cannot reject the sales agreement if it contained a clause expressly providing for the exclusion of all implied warranties
The woman can reject the sales agreement because to enforce the contract would fly in the face of the general legal requirement that a person needs to consent to a disputed term to be bound by it
The woman can reject the sales agreement; if the person receiving the agreement does not know that there are any conditions and clauses contained within it, that person is not bound by them
The woman can reject the sales agreement, because the courts refuse to countenance any result which limits parties' freedom to contract, however unjust
The woman can reject the sales agreement, because she should have been given reasonable notice of the exclusion clause at the time of signing the contract in order for it to be effective

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. It is wholly immaterial whether she has read the document or not. Where a document containing contractual terms is signed, then in the absence of fraud or misrepresentation, the person signing it is bound and it is wholly immaterial whether they had read the document or not. Lead case: L'Estrange v Graucob [1934] 2 KB 394.

stem: A Trustee of an estate decides to use some Trust property, honestly believing that the slowdown in the UK property market meant that if he bought property now he would make a large profit in the years to come and be able to repay the Trust. Sympathising with his personal problems, his good friend and banker invested the money and lost heavily. The beneficiaries under the Trust sue the Trustee and the banker to make good the loss.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The banker will not be liable for dishonest assistance, because he was not a Trustee
The banker will be liable for dishonest assistance, provided he knew that the Trustee needed the money for a purpose which is not the purpose of the Trust
The banker will be liable for dishonest assistance, provided he did not do what an honest person would have done in the circumstances
The banker will be liable for dishonest assistance, provided he realised that an honest person would have considered his actions to have been dishonest
The banker will be liable for dishonest assistance, because he received the money in the knowledge that the property was passed to him in breach of Trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The issues here clearly involve the banker's liability as a third party. The banker is not a Trustee and has not received any part of the money that the Trustee misappropriated. However, it is still possible for the banker to be liable for dishonest assistance, if he did not believe that the Trustee needed the money for the purpose he told him (although this is not still the Trust purpose), but needed the money for other purposes altogether. Lord Nicholls in Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan [1995] held that a breach of Trust by a Trustee need not have been a dishonest act on the part of the Trustee. It is sufficient that some accessory acted dishonestly for that accessory to be fixed with liability -.-ach of Trust - 9- an honest person would have done in the circumstances. Did the banker do what an honest person would have done? However, in the later decision of the House of Lords in Twinsectra v Yardley [2002], it was suggested that the defendant must also have realised, subjectively speaking, that an honest person would have considered the defendant's actions to have been dishonest. -3-

stem: A person owns a valuable set of six antique chairs and he gives one of them to his wife. Valued individually and independently, the five chairs that remain are each worth £5,000; as a set of six, however, they were worth £20,000 each.
ask: What is the potentially taxable reduction in value of the estate for Inheritance Tax purposes?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The best answer is E. £95,000. The value of the set before was 6 x £20,000 = £120,000. The value now is 5 x £5,000 = £25,000. The potentially taxable diminution is £95,000. The related property rules require valuation on the related basis, where it would have the effect of producing a higher value than if valued, independently. Each chair would, therefore, have to be valued as one of a set. A is not correct as the chairs were more valuable as part of a complete set of six. B is not correct as the five chairs are still worth £25,000. C is not correct as this is simply the current value of the chairs, not the diminution of the estate.

stem: A Welsh writer sent her publisher a manuscript containing defamatory material in Welsh about the publisher, knowing that the publisher cannot understand it as he can only read English. The publisher subsequently forwarded the manuscript to an English translator, and published the translated manuscript after receiving it back from the translator. The publisher now seeks to commence libel proceedings against the Welsh writer.
ask: Which option best advises the publisher as to the writer's potential liability, if at all?

options.en: The writer is not liable for the publication from the time the manuscript was sent to the publisher; she is liable from the time it was forwarded to the translator
The writer is neither liable for the publication from the time the manuscript was sent to the publisher nor from the time it was forwarded to the translator

The writer is liable for the publication from the time the manuscript was sent to the publisher; she should have expected that the publisher may forward the manuscript to a translator as the publisher could not read Welsh
The writer is liable for the publication from the time the manuscript was sent to the publisher; not from the time it was forwarded to the translator

The writer is not liable for the publication from the time the manuscript was sent to the publisher; she is liable from the time it was forwarded to the translator, providing the publisher can show any statement was made with malicious intent

explanation.en: ANEN You did not select the correct answer. A is the best option. The writer is not liable for the publication from the time the manuscript was sent to the publisher; she is liable from the time it was forwarded to the translator. For a defamatory statement to be actionable, it must have been published to someone other than the claimant. If it is published to a third party, however, the third party must be aware of its meaning. This is because defamation serves to protect reputation in the eyes of others, and not merely the claimant's dignity. Accordingly, the sending of a manuscript or the stating of defamatory matter to the individual concerned (the publisher) will not of itself constitute publication, unless the individual passes it to

stem: Your client is alleged to have pushed a police officer after he claims he was jostled in a football crowd. He has been charged with assault and battery. He is confused, as he thought they both constituted the same offence.
ask: How do you explain the difference, if any, to your client?

options.en: The mens rea of battery is the infliction of any form of unlawful force by one person against another person, while the mens rea of assault is an act which will cause the victim to apprehend an immediate infliction of violence
Battery deals with the situation where the offender causes an individual to fear an assault, whereas an assault is the actual contact
Assault deals with the situation where the offender causes an individual to fear an attack, whereas battery is the actual contact
Battery is a less serious form of assault, so your client should not be charged with both offences

Since assault and battery are synonymous, to be charged with both offences would contravene the rule of double jeopardy (the procedural defence that forbids a defendant from being tried again for the same crime

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Traditionally, assault and battery are separate offences. Statutory reference to 'assault," however, generally means either assault or battery. In the technical sense, however, assault is a threat to apply force immediately to the person of the victim and a battery is the actual application of that force.

stem: You are instructed on a commercial conveyancing transaction. You are preparing the deed of sale, but your client, who must sign the deed, is frustrated at what he sees as 'unnecessary legal guff' surrounding the preparation and execution of the title deed. He demands to know what these formalities are.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal formalities for a deed to be executed?

options.en: A deed must be clear on the face of it that it is intended to be a deed; be signed in private by the party and delivered to the counterparty
A deed must be clear on the face of it that it is intended to be a deed and be executed as a deed by attested signature
A deed must be clear on the face of it that it is intended to be a deed; be executed as a deed by attested signature; and delivered to the counterparty
A deed must be clear on the face of it that it is intended to be a deed, be signed by a witness; and delivered to the counterparty
A deed must be executed as a deed by attested signature and delivered to the counterparty

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. A deed must be clear on the face of it that it is intended to be a deed; be executed as a deed by attested signature; and delivered to the counterparty. The requirements for deeds for contracts of land are set out in the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, and requires that a deed be clear on the face of it that it is intended to be a deed (by the document describing itself as a deed or expressing itself to be executed as a deed); executed as a deed by being signed in the presence of a witness (or, if the person is physically unable to sign himself, by another in the presence of the party to the will and two witnesses); and delivered by being given or sent to the a witness", is incorrect, as the original parties must sign in the presence of witnesses, rather than the witnesses themselves signing as parties. That's what attested signature means - signature of the party that is attested (i.e. in the presence of a witness who attests the validity of that signature).

stem: A husband announces to his wife that he wishes to take out a mortgage to buy a house so that they can have a place of their own, but that he is £1,000 short of completing the deposit for the mortgage. The wife takes out her necklace worth £1,500 and hands it to the husband. After the purchase of the house and moving in, the husband tells the wife to leave the house. Which of the following factors
ask: would entitle the wife to a remedy under the common?

options.en: The husband was a constructive trustee for the wife's interest in the property
The wife clearly intended to have an interest in the property
The wife asked for an agreement in writing from her husband but he waived it
The wife was responsible for the upkeep of the house and its cleanliness
The wife has no remedy under the common law rules

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The wife in this question has breached the formal legal requirements under section 53 (1)(b) LPA 1925 which renders void an oral declaration of a trust of land. Her action will therefore be defeated under the common law rules. Of course, she may be able to rely on equity to argue that the husband is a constructive trustee for her interest in the property. For example, she may be able to rely on the equitable maxim that equity looks at intention and not form. The form is that the woman manifests her desire to acquire an interest in the property in writing; but she failed in this; the intention is that she clearly intended to have an interest in the property. If the wife could establish that she was misled by her husband, e.g. if she did ask for an agreement in writing but he waived it, then another has done other things, after the purchase of the house, such that enable her husband to carry on with the payment of the mortgage if the house is bought with the benefit of a loan from a bank.

stem: A company limited by guarantee has ten members, each of whom undertook to contribute £10,000 in the event that the company is wound up.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position should the company go?

options.en: Creditors of the company would be able to claim against the members directly for any debts that the company could not meet itself up to the value of £10,000 per member
Creditors of the company would be able to claim against the members directly for any debts that the company could not meet itself
The company would be able to claim against the members for any debts that the company could not meet itself
The company would be able to claim against the members for any debts that the company could not meet itself up to the value of £10,000 per member
Neither the company nor the company's creditors would be able to claim against the members for any debts that the company could not meet itself

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The company (via its liquidator) would be able to claim against the members for any debts that the company could not meet itself up to the value of £10,000 per member. As the company has a separate legal personality, its creditors have no ability to claim against the members in respect of the debts of the company. The members are only liable to contribute to the value of the guarantee that they gave when the company was incorporated, and this liability is to the company and not its creditors.

stem: A man was supposed to be a witness in a forthcoming trial but was shot dead before he could give evidence. His relatives brought a claim against the police on the basis that they had failed to prevent the murder of a witness in a criminal case.
ask: Which rights, if any, may have been violated under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)?

options.en: The Convention right that has have been violated is the right to life
The Convention right that has been violated is the right to fair trial
The Convention rights that have been violated are the right to fair trial and the right to liberty
The Convention right that has been violated is the right to a private or family life
The Convention right that has been violated is the right to freedom of expression

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The Convention right that has have been violated is the right to life. The claim in Van Colle v Chief Constable of Hertfordshire Police [2008] UKHL 50 was argued on the basis of a breach of Article 2 of the Convention. It failed in the Supreme Court, despite the claim succeeding below because, on the facts, the strict test established by the ECtHR in the case of Osman v. UK (2000) 29 EHRR 245 was not satisfied and no lesser test was justified even though the deceased had been called as a witness by the Crown. Nevertheless the Article 2 Right to Life principle still stands.

stem: A client is considering taking out a loan to provide start-up capital for a partnership that she is setting up. The loan is to be secured by means of a first legal mortgage over the client's family home and she asks her solicitor to recommend a bank to act as lender and for the solicitor to arrange the loan for her. The solicitor has already been instructed to draft the necessary partnership deeds and investment agreement between the partners.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes what the solicitor is able to do under the Financial Services and Markets Act (FSMA) 2000?

options.en: The solicitor can provide the advice and make the loan arrangements, because the loan is not a specified investment for the purposes of the FSMA
The solicitor can refer the client to an authorised third person for the advice, but cannot undertake the loan arrangements on the client's behalf
The solicitor cannot provide the advice or undertake the loan arrangements

The solicitor can undertake the loan arrangements but must refer the client to an authorised third person (ATP) for the advice, because the solicitor is only authorised to carry out non-mainstream regulated activities
The solicitor can undertake the loan arrangements but must refer the client to an ATP for the advice, because the solicitor is only authorised to carry out mainstream regulated activities

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The loan is a regulated mortgage contract and thus a specified investment for the purposes of the FSMA. The activity of recommending that a client enter into a regulated mortgage contract as a borrower constitutes a mainstream regulated activity and cannot therefore be carried out by the solicitor's firm under rule 5(7) of the Scope Rules. The client would therefore need to be referred to an ATP for this advice. However, the solicitor would be able to make the loan arrangements on the client's behalf. The arranging will be a non-mainstream regulated activity, which the firm is authorised by the SRA to carry out under s. 327 FSMA, because it is incidental to the legal

stem: You have been asked to prepare a case in which the defendant claims she was acting under duress when she stole money from the cash till in the bank where she worked. You are investigating the case and need to consider what is meant by duress.
ask: Which option best describes how the elements of duress are satisfied, if at all?

options.en: There needs to be a threat to the person themselves, since threats to third- parties would not constitute duress
There needs to be a threat of serious physical injury
There needs to be a threat of serious personal injury or psychological harm
There needs to be a threat of serious damage to property
There needs to be a threat of serious personal injury, psychological harm or damage to property

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. In order for duress to be proved, there needs to be a threat of serious physical injury. A simple threat is insufficient, but the threat could be to another person. The threat of psychological harm is insufficient, see R v. Baker and Wilkins [1997] Crim LR 497.

stem: A man hired an office space overlooking the Thames from a friend for the purpose of exhibiting his sculptures to the general public over the summer. After they signed the contract, however, and before the man had the chance to move his sculptures over to the office space, it was destroyed by fire. Although there was no evidence indicating fault on either side, and the contract made no provision for such an event, the friend insists on pursuing the man for the rent.
ask: Would the man be liable for his obligations under the contract?

options.en: The man's obligations were not discharged by the fire and should he fail to meet them as a result of such an event, he would be in breach of contract
Since an anticipatory breach entitles the innocent party to terminate performance of the contract immediately, his friend can claim damages on the date of the acceptance of the breach

Because the office space is in no fit state for an exhibition in accordance with the terms the parties contemplated in their agreement, the man would be well advised to issue proceeding against his friend for damages
Since performance would be impossible; the man would be excused from any further obligations under the contract
In unilateral contracts, such as this, the friend will be forced to perform his side of the bargain before any performance obligation falls upon the man

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Impossibility can arise due to the destruction or unavailability of something essential, leading to frustration of the contract. Lead case: Taylor v Caldwell (1863) 3 B & S 826; 122 ER 309.

stem: Two women practise together in partnership as solicitors. The firm's debts to BankCo are secured by personal guarantees extended to BankCo by both women, as well as by second mortgages on their substantial homes. One woman has a gambling addiction and has fallen behind with her mortgage payments and her home is at risk of repossession. She knows that if her home is sold then BankCo will cancel the firm's credit accounts and it will be unable to trade.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman with the gambling problem is under a fiduciary duty to the other woman to disclose her financial situation if asked to do so
The woman with the gambling problem is under a fiduciary duty to disclose her financial situation to the other woman
The woman with the gambling problem is under no duty to disclose her financial situation if asked about it by the other woman
The woman with the gambling problem is under a contractual duty to disclose her financial situation to the other woman only if the partnership agreement provides for this
The woman with the gambling problem is under a fiduciary duty to the other woman to disclose her financial situation only if the partnership agreement provides for this

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Section 28 of the Partnership Act 1890 provides that a partner is under a duty to disclose all information about all things affecting the firm to his partners. This is a positive duty of disclosure, and not merely a duty not to misrepresent when asked. This is a positive fiduciary duty imposed by the 1890 Act. As the woman with the gambling problem's financial difficulties will have a direct effect on the firm's lines of credit (and ability to trade), the duty of disclosure applies to them.

ask: authorities are seeking the citizen's extradition from custody in the United Kingdom Which option best states the legal position under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)?

options.en: Extradition to a non-European country is incompatible with the Convention
The Convention does not apply to non-European nationals such as U.S. citizens
The death penalty is inhuman and degrading punishment
Detaining an individual on 'death row' awaiting execution for several years can constitute inhuman and degrading punishment
Detaining an individual on 'death row' awaiting execution for several years does not constitute inhuman and degrading punishment where the appeals process is rigorous and fair

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option D is correct. All other options are incorrect. The question is based on Soering v UK (1989) 11 EHRR 439, a landmark ECtHR decision on the application of Article 3 (Prohibition of Torture). Although the applicant did not seek to show that the death penalty per se constituted 'inhuman and degrading treatment', the ECtHR accepted his pleadings that the "death row phenomenon" created by the delay between successful prosecution and the actual execution, was in violation of the Convention.

stem: A group of inner city residents are angry that a local community activist had died in police custody after being arrested. In order to demonstrate their grievance, they have organised a procession from the local town hall to the police station where the activist was detained after his arrest. The police have received notice of the Which one of the following statements
ask: is true concerning the provisions of the Public?

At least six clear days' written notice must be given to the police before most public processions
The police may ban the procession indefinitely by order of the Chief Constable
The police may impose any conditions they see fit on the procession
The police can ban public processions indefinitely by applying to the local authority for a banning order as long as the Home Secretary approves this

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Section 11 of the Act requires at least six clear days' written notice to be given to the police before most public processions. The police may ask for details of the intended time and route, and the name and address of at least one person intending to organise it.

stem: You have been called to the police station to represent a client. The officer disclosed to you that your client was arrested for being drunk and disorderly in a public place. When you speak to your client, she asks you if she will have to face a jury trial.
ask: Which option represents the best advice to give to your client?

options.en: The offence of being drunk and disorderly in a public place is an offence triable either way, which means that it may either be tried in the magistrates' court or the crown court

The offence of being drunk and disorderly in a public place is an offence triable either way, which means that it may either be tried before a jury in the magistrates' court or before a judge in the crown court
The offence of being drunk and disorderly in a public place is an indictable only offence, which means it must be tried in the magistrates' court
The offence of being drunk and disorderly in a public place is a summary only offence, which means that it's an offence that must be tried in the magistrates' court
The offence of being drunk and disorderly in a public place is an indictable only offence, which means it must be tried before a jury in the crown court

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The offence of being drunk and disorderly in a public place is triable only summarily, as it is considered to be one of the minor 'public order' offences. This means that it would only be dealt with by magistrates' courts, although if convicted, the defendant may appeal to the Crown Court.

stem: A man is the legal and equitable owner of a freehold property which is subject to a charge by way of legal mortgage to BankCo. The man has defaulted on his mortgage obligations and has not made any repayments of capital or interest to the mortgage account for six months. You are acting for BankCo and have been instructed to review its security to see if it would be able repossess the property and sell it. Although BankCo's mortgage deed contains an express right to possession of the land in the event of default, it does not contain an express power of sale.
ask: How would you advise BankCo?

options.en: BankCo has the power to take possession of the property and the power to sell it
BankCo has the power to take possession of the property but no power to sell it
BankCo has no power to take possession of the property but has the power to sell it
BankCo has no power to take possession of the property and has no power to sell it
BankCo has the power to take possession of the property but can only sell it if it obtains an order for sale from the court

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. BankCo has the power to take possession of the property and the power to sell it. The mortgagee has a common law right to possession which is preserved by s.95(4) of the LPA 1925, and in this case, the mortgagee also has an express right to take possession conferred by the mortgage deed. Although no express power of sale exists in the mortgage deed, the mortgagee is able to rely upon the statutory power of sale conferred by s. 101 of the LPA 1925, since the interest due on the mortgage is more than two months in arrears.

stem: A paper salesman, employed by a retailer, agreed for one year after leaving his employment not to supply paper products to persons who were, within six months before leaving his employment, customers of his employer. The two main issues an employer is concerned to protect are: (i) business integrity; and (ii) trade links

The two main issues an employer is concerned to protect are: (i) business secrets; and (ii) corporate business

The longer the duration of the covenant, the higher the burden on

stem: ACo is a private unlimited company, and its only member is BCo Limited. BCo is a private limited company, which has issued one fully paid up £1 share owned by a man who is the sole director of BCo, and both the man and BCo are directors of ACo. ACo is unable to meet its liabilities and goes into liquidation.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: ACo's creditors can claim the full value of ACo's debts from BCo and from the man
ACo's creditors can claim the full value of ACo's debts from BCo and can claim up to £1 from the man
ACo's liquidator can claim the full value of ACo's debts from BCo and the man
ACo's liquidator can claim the full value of ACo's debts from BCo and can claim up to £1 from the man
ACo's liquidator can claim the full value of ACo's debts from BCo

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. As a company has separate legal personality to its members, its creditors cannot claim directly against the members. However, where the company is in liquidation, it would be usual for the liquidator to call for a contribution from the members up to the limit of their liability. BCo's liability is unlimited because ACo is an unlimited company. Should contributing to ACo's debts force BCo into liquidation, then BCo's liquidator could, if he wished, request a contribution from the man up to the limit of his liability (£1).

stem: When a woman moved into her boyfriend's apartment, her boyfriend gave her a diamond ring, which was engraved with the words' soon we will be man and wife, and we'll buy a large house and live happily ever after.' The woman stopped actively pursuing her career as a stockbroker and devoted her time to building their dream home, which her boyfriend paid for, registering the legal estate in his name as a mere, formality. The woman organised the renovation of the house, the cost of which was paid for mainly by her boyfriend.
ask: Which option represents the best advice to give to the woman after her and her boyfriend separate?

options.en: The woman has no redress, because the legal estate of the 'dream' home was not registered in her name
The woman has no redress, because there is no hint that the couple made a written agreement to share the equitable interest in the 'dream' home
The woman has no redress, because there is no clear oral agreement on sharing the equitable interest in the 'dream' home
The woman has no redress, because she has made no direct financial contribution to the purchase price of the 'dream' home, nor is she paying off the mortgage
The woman would not be entitled to an even split of the shared assets

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The woman is not the registered legal owner and there is no hint that the couple made a written agreement to share the equitable interest. The burden is therefore on the woman to show that she has an equitable interest in the house (Stack v Dowden). First, she needs to show there was an oral agreement. Although the oral agreement in this case on sharing the equitable interest in the house seems imprecise and somewhat inconclusive, the case law has indicated that this does not matter. Secondly, she needs to prove she has acted to her detriment or made a direct financial contribution. It this seems quite likely that the client will have a share in the equitable interest. stem: Your client is a former political activist, but withdrew from protest activities in 1996. However, a recent government announcement has upset him, and he intends to join a non-violent protest march to Westminster to make his feelings known to Parliament. Your client fears that the police will crack down heavily on the protest and wants to know what his options are if that is the case.
ask: Which remedy, if any, is afforded to your client if, during the protest, the police act in a way that contravenes your client's human rights?

options.en: None; the police are immune from prosecution and are not bound by the provisions of the Human Rights Act 1998
Your client must commence a claim against the police in the European Court of Human Rights
Your client can only commence proceedings for judicial review of the police action
Your client must complain to the Independent Police Complaints Commission
Your client may challenge the actions of the police through the courts

explanation.en: The best answer is E. Your client may challenge the actions of the police through the courts. Under Section 7 of the Human Rights Act 1998, a person who is the victim of an unlawful act by a public authority (i.e. one that is incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights) may challenge the actions of the body through the courts. Under Section 8, the court has discretion to grant such relief or remedy, or make such order, within its powers as it considers just and appropriate. The remedies are, generally, judicial review; damages (but only where an award would be necessary, just and appropriate) and/or a declaration that the law (but not the decision made under the law) is in breach of human rights, also known as a

stem: A solicitor on a litigation matter instructs counsel on his client's behalf to present his client's case in court. The client now refuses to pay counsel's fees. The solicitor has no funds from the client on account.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The client is personally responsible for paying counsel's fees
The client is obligated to reimburse the solicitor for counsel's fees, and any doubt over the question of reasonableness will be resolved in the solicitor's favour
The client is obligated to reimburse the solicitor for counsel's fees, and any doubt over the question of reasonableness will be resolved in the client's favour
The client is obligated to reimburse the solicitor for counsel's fees, even where these are of an unusual nature
The client is obligated to reimburse the solicitor for counsel's fees, even where these have not been approved by the client

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. (B) is the correct answer. The solicitor will always remain personally responsible for paying counsel's or any other expert's fees, whether or not he has been put in funds by the client. On the other hand, the client will be obligated to reimburse the solicitor for all costs which have been expressly or even impliedly approved by the client, save where these are of an unusual nature or amount and the solicitor did not tell his client that he might not recover all costs from the losing party. The solicitor will thus be entitled to reimbursement on the more generous solicitor-and-client basis of detailed assessment, in which any doubt over reasonableness will be resolved in the favour of the receiving party, Ter.

stem: A city council sells a large area of land to a house builder that wishes to construct a housing estate. The house builder covenants not to build upon a small area of the land which is intended to be used as an open space for use by the residents of the estate. The city council has retained no land in the vicinity of the new estate. Sometime after the estate has been completed, the house builder transfers the open space to a development company which begins work to construct two houses on the land intended to be used for open space.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The covenant does not bind the development company because it is of a positive nature
The covenant does not bind the development company because it does not benefit land retained by the covenantee and does not touch and concern land retained by covenantee
The covenant does not bind the development company because it is personal to the house builder
The covenant does not bind the development company because it was not intended to burden the servient land
The covenant binds the development company

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The covenant does not bind the development company because it does not benefit land retained by the covenantee and does not touch and concern land retained by covenantee. The covenant is of a negative nature (being a prohibition upon building) and runs with the servient land (and is thus not personal to the building company) due to the effect of s.79 of the LPA 1925. However the city council has not retained any land in the vicinity of the estate which can be benefited by the covenant and it follows that there is nothing that the covenant can touch and concern.

stem: In April you write to a company as follows: "Our clients have instructed us to pay the £5,000 debt owing to you from the proceeds of the sale of their family home. In the circumstances, we ask that you to refrain from taking the legal proceedings which you recently threatened against our clients." The house is subsequently sold in July but after your clients purchase another property, however, there are insufficient funds left to settle the outstanding debt owing to the company.
ask: Which of the following best explains the remedies available to the company?

options.en: The company has no remedy against you, the solicitor, as no undertaking was made
The company has no remedy against your clients, only against you, the solicitor
The company can either sue your clients or submit a complaint against you, the solicitor, to the Legal Ombudsman, but not both remedies
The company can submit a complaint against you, the solicitor, to the Legal Ombudsman
The company can sue your clients in respect your (the solicitor) undertaking

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Disputes as to whether a solicitor's words constitute an undertaking are frequent. They are likely to be construed as such, as you, as a solicitor, are effectively stating that you are acting for your clients, and that on the sale of the house, the £5,000 will be paid from the proceeds of sale. The company has placed reliance on these words by not taking proceedings, which will thus be construed against the solicitor. The company can, of course, sue your clients. They can also submit a complaint to the Legal Ombudsman.
