stem: Your client is organising a march to protest against recent financial cuts by the county council to the local school system. She seeks guidance regarding any rights or prohibitions under the Public Order Act (the Act) 1986.
ask: Which option best states a general requirement under the Act?

options.en: Your client must undergo a Criminal Records Bureau (CRB) check, since the march concerns children
Your client must provide details to the police of the names and addresses of all participants
Your client must ensure that the route is properly marked out, so that the public are aware it is happening
Your client must give the police at least 48 hours' notice prior to the commencement of the march
The police may ban marches for up to three months by application to the relevant local authority for a banning order

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is E. In order to ban a planned march, the chief constable must apply to the district council, which has the power to issue the ban, subject to the approval of the Home Secretary. The Chief Constable must be satisfied that the powers to impose conditions will not be sufficient to prevent serious public disorder. If the march takes place, then the Chief Constable must apply for a banning order. The ban can cover all or part of a police area, and last for up to three months. S. 13(1) Public Order Act 1986.

stem: A solicitor acts for the executor of a deceased's estate. The assets of the estate include units in a unit trust. One of the beneficiaries under the deceased's will asks for the solicitor's advice on the sale of the units. nich ot the tollowing statements best describes what the solicitor may do!
ask: Which of the following statements best describes what the solicitor may do?

options.en: The solicitor may give advice to the beneficiary under the will, because the proposed sale arises out of the provision of the solicitor's professional services being provided to the client and is therefore exempt from the general prohibition

The solicitor may give advice to the beneficiary under the will, because the proposed sale is complementary to the provision of the solicitor's professional services being provided to the client and is therefore exempt from the general prohibition

The solicitor may give advice to the beneficiary under the will, because the proposed sale is a necessary part of the solicitor's winding up of the deceased's estate and is therefore exempt from the general prohibition

The solicitor may give advice to the beneficiary under the will, because the proposed sale is incidental or subordinate to the firm's provision of probate professional services and is therefore exempt from the general prohibition
The solicitor may not give advice to the beneficiary under the will

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. There is no indication that it is necessary for the solicitor to sell the units in the unit trust and hence the 'necessary exclusion' would not appear to apply. The sale would appear to arise out of, or be complementary to, the provision of the probate professional services (the winding up of the estate by the solicitor) being provided to the client. In this respect, there is no indication that the sale is anything other than incidental or subordinate to the firm's provision of the probate services. In order to rely on the 'incidental' exemption, however, the primary professional service and the otherwise regulated sale activity must be supplied to the same client - which is not the case here, as the executor is the solicitor's

stem: A baker had been operating a noisy business for 30 years. His neighbour for the last 23 years has just recently complained about the noise, which she claims is interfering with her right to quiet enjoyment.
ask: The baker claims the nuisance has been allowed to continue for a long enough period of time to give rise to an easement by Which option best describes the legal position?

options.en: A claimant that tolerates a nuisance for more than 3 years may lose their right to object through the defence of prescription
A claimant that tolerates a nuisance for more than 6 years may lose their right to object through the defence of prescription
A claimant that tolerates a nuisance for more than 12 years may lose their right to object through the defence of prescription
A claimant that tolerates a nuisance for more than 20 years may lose their right to object through the defence of prescription
A claimant that tolerates a nuisance for more than 25 years may lose their right to object through the defence of prescription

explanation.en: D is the best option. The defence of prescription is available where the claimant has allowed the nuisance to continue for 20, without complaining, or if the claimant consents to the nuisance. The time does not start to run until the claimant arrives, i.e., on the time they move to an area where the nuisance had been operating for years without harming anyone. In the context of the fact pattern, prescription would be a good defence for the baker (defendant) as the neighbour was silent for more than 20 years about the nuisance.

stem: The Home Secretary has banned a controversial play depicting a particular religion in a very unflattering light. Her justification for the ban is the 'protection of public morals'. The playwright claims his rights under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) have thereby been breached.
ask: Which option best describes how the European Court of Human Rights' (ECtHR) traditionally interprets measures implemented for the protection of public morals?

options.en: The ECtHR recognises a right not to be insulted in one's religious feelings by the public expression of views of other persons
The ECtHR does not recognise a right not to be insulted in one's religious feelings by the public expression of views of other persons
The ECtHR recognises that the right to freedom of expression overrides the O right not to be insulted in one's religious feelings by the public expression of views of other persons
The ECtHR recognises that the right not to be discriminated against overrides the right not to be insulted in one's religious feelings by the public expression of views of other persons
The ECtHR recognises that no contracting state may make any law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option A is correct. In the case of Otto v Austria, the ECtHR stated that one of the aims stated in paragraph 2 of Article 10 (Freedom of Expression) is 'protection of public morals' and the ECtHR interprets this to include the right 'not to be insulted in [one's] religious feelings by the public expression of views of other persons', moving on to apply a test of proportionality. The ECtHR has allowed a wide margin of discretion in this regard, and contracting states' laws protecting religious sentiments are typically validated through the application of Article 9 (Freedom of Thought, Conscience & Religion). See further Otto-Preminger-Institut v Austria (1994) Case No. 11/1993/406/485 & Wingrove v United

stem: You advise the members of a Limited Liability Partnership ("LLP") that is in serious financial difficulty. They have failed to pay a significant debt owed to a major creditor, due to difficult trading conditions and the overall financial health of the LLP. The creditor has now presented a winding-up petition against the LLP to the court, which has been granted.
ask: Your clients ask your advice on the procedure that is likely What, briefly, are the consequences of a winding-up order against an insolvent LLP?

options.en: An administrator will be appointed and the LLP's assets may be sold off to pay the petitioner; the LLP may be wound up or may trade its way out of insolvency, with all proceeds paying off the petitioner's debt

The Official Receiver will usually be appointed as liquidator; the affairs of the LLP will be investigated and the LLP will be wound up; the petition does not advance the ranking of the petitioner as a creditor

The LLP must appoint a liquidator; the liquidator will wind up the LLP's affairs by calling in the LLP's assets and distributing the proceeds of sale to creditors. The petitioner will rank as an unsecured creditor

An administrative receiver will be appointed as liquidator and the receiver will assess the situation and find the best way for the creditor to recover its money. This may or may not involve the winding up of the LLP
The LLP will be declared bankrupt and the court will manage the distribution of assets

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. The Official Receiver will usually be appointed as liquidator; the affairs of the LLP will be investigated and the LLP will be wound up; the petition does not advance the ranking of the petitioner as a creditor. The Official Receiver will become the liquidator when a winding-up order is made against an LLP - unless the Court decides against this. A copy of the winding-up order must be sent to the Registrar of Companies and placed on the LLP's public record. As the liquidator, the Official Receiver must investigate the LLP's affairs and the causes of the failure and decide whether to call a meeting of creditors, contributors and members to find a replacement liquidator in their place (notifying parties if they decide not to call a meeting). If the LLP has a number of assets, the Official Receiver may seek to appoint an insolvency practitioner as liquidator. The liquidation process proceeds - the assets of the LLP are sold and any remaining money is distributed to creditors after paying costs and expenses of the liquidation. The Official Receiver is also required to submit a report on the conduct of the members of the LLP to the Investigations and Enforcement Services within the Insolvency Service

stem: An unincorporated association dissolves. There is no agreement between the members of the association as to what should happen to property held by the association on dissolution.
ask: What is the legal position in respect of the association's property?

options.en: The property will go to the crown as bona vacantia
The property will be returned to its previous owners or donors
The property must be liquidated
The property will be distributed amongst the members in equal shares
The property will be held on trust by the members for any creditors of the association

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The property will be distributed amongst the members in equal shares. An unincorporated association has no legal identity. Per Re Bucks Constabulary Benevolent Fund [1978] 1 WLR 641, the rules of contract law apply to the distribution of property in such a case, rather than trusts law. If the contractual provisions identify how to distribute property, they will be followed; if not, the property will be distributed, in equal shares.

stem: A farmer agreed to supply grain to a buyer, but due to transport difficulties, requested to be allowed to make late delivery. The buyer agreed to the farmer's request.
ask: When the farmer delivered the grain, the buyer refused to accept delivery of the grain, since he claimed that the late delivery agreement was unsupported by Which option best advises the farmer?

options.en: The waiver of a date of delivery without consideration may be binding based on mistake
The waiver of a date of delivery without consideration may be binding based on discharge by frustration
The waiver of a date of delivery without consideration may be binding based on privity of contract
The waiver of a date of delivery without consideration may be binding based on the parol evidence rule
The waiver of a date of delivery without consideration may be binding based on promissory estoppel

explanation.en: E is the best answer. A waiver of a date of delivery without consideration may be binding based on the doctrine of promissory estoppel. The farmer may be entitled to recover damages, despite the fact that delivery was outside the terms of the contract, and that the buyer's promise to accept late delivery was unsupported by consideration. The buyer had waived the right to insist on delivery at a particular time, and could not renege on that due to the doctrine of promissory estoppel. This equitable exception to the doctrine of consideration was applied by Justice MacCardie in the case of Hartley v Hymans [1920]. Lead case: Hartley v Hymans [1920] 3 KB 475.

stem: A man finds a watch in the street near to his home, picks it up, puts it in his pocket and takes it home. A short time later, he decides to go to the shop. On his way there he sees a person in the same area he found the watch looking for something. The person asks the man if he found a watch, which matches the description of the one that the man found, but the man answers in the negative and carries on his way.
ask: Which option best describes the man's criminal liability, if any?

options.en: The man has not appropriated the watch; it had been abandoned, so he could take it legally
The man has not appropriated the watch; it has merely come into his possession
The man has appropriated the watch; even if it has come into his possession innocently, in the first instance
The man has appropriated the watch; it was an act of theft as soon as he picked it up
The man has not appropriated the watch; it was not in the possession or contro of anyone when he found it

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Where an individual finds an item in the street and later discovers that it belongs to another individual living close by, the individual is then considered to be appropriating the item, even if it has come into his possession innocently, in the first instance. If the watch had been truly abandoned, then it is ownerless and has not been appropriated. This does not appear to be the case in the scenario; there must be a genuine belief that it has been abandoned.

stem: Several youths on a school trip absented themselves from the main party, whilst the teachers who were supposed to be in charge of them were - contrary to instructions - in the pub. They boarded a bus that was parked in a nearby layby, drove off and caused considerable damage to the bus. The bus owner alleges that the school is liable for the damage because of its negligence in failing to exercise effective control and supervision over the youths.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the legal position?

options.en: Since the youths behaved in a criminal manner, the bus owner should issue and serve proceedings against them, not the school
Since the youths are classed as minors, they cannot be held responsible for mere horseplay and therefore the bus owner has no grounds for issuing proceedings

Although the school would have been vicariously liable had it been the teachers that caused the damage, it is clear that it alone cannot be liable for the unforeseen criminal behaviour of all errant youths
The school owes the bus owner a duty of care; the teachers were negligent in carrying out their obligations to control and supervise the youths and the damage to the bus was the foreseeable result
It would be inappropriate interfere with the school's functions on grounds of public policy, which requires that schools be immune from legal actions in such cases

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Since the teachers' negligence caused a foreseeable risk that the youths would damage the bus owner's property, the school (or more likely the Local Education Authority) would owe the owner of the bus a duty to take reasonable care to prevent the risk occurring. Lead case: Home Office v Dorset Yacht Co [1970].

stem: A woman was suspended from her job as director of a local authority's children's services department, following appalling failures which led to the killing of a three year old child by its step-father. 10 days later, after an urgent report into child safeguarding arrangements criticised the children's services department, the Secretary of State for Education sacked the woman at a televised press conference. The woman seeks to challenge this decision by judicial review.
ask: Which are the woman's best grounds to challenge the Secretary of State's decision?

options.en: The woman may challenge the Secretary of State's direction on the grounds of failure to give adequate reasons
The woman may challenge the Secretary of State's direction on the grounds of irrationality
The woman may challenge the Secretary of State's direction on the grounds of taking into account irrelevant considerations
The woman may challenge the Secretary of State's direction on the grounds of failure to observe the requirements of procedural fairness
The woman may challenge the Secretary of State's direction on the grounds of bias

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The Secretary of State may well have flouted proper procedures. The court would not be concerned whether the woman was blameless. The task of the court, however, would be to adjudicate upon the application and fairness of procedures adopted by a public figure such as the Secretary of State when legitimate causes for concern may arise. Whatever her shortcomings may have been, the woman is entitled to be treated lawfully and fairly and not simply and summarily scapegoated. Lead case: R (on the application of Sharon Shoesmith) v OFSTED & ors [2011] EWCA Civ 642.

stem: A Scottish prisoner's appeal to the High Court of Justiciary sitting as a Court of Criminal Appeal in Edinburgh (the highest criminal appeal court in Scotland) over his conviction for murder has been unsuccessful. He was convicted of the same offence by a Scottish jury at the High Court of first instance in Glasgow. The United Kingdom's Supreme Court has recently ruled that the conviction of an English prisoner, convicted on strikingly similar facts to the Scottish prisoner by a Crown Court jury in England, to be unsafe. The prisoner has written to you asking about his options to further appeal his case in the UK. No compatibility issues arise in this case regarding the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention).
ask: Which option offers the best advice to the prisoner?

options.en: The prisoner has no further avenue of appeal, because Scottish courts are not bound by decisions of the Supreme Court on matters of criminal liability
The prisoner has no further avenue of appeal, because the High Court in Glasgow is the highest court within that particular jurisdiction
The prisoner has a further avenue of appeal, but must first apply to the High Court of Justiciary in Edinburgh, for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court
The prisoner has no further avenue of appeal, because Scotland has its own unique legal system, which is entirely separate from England and Wales
The prisoner has a further avenue of appeal, but must first apply to the Criminal Division of the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best option. The High Court of Justiciary remains the court of last resort in Scotland for criminal cases. The Supreme Court is the final appellate court for all civil cases and criminal cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. It hears appeals from different courts in the different jurisdictions as follows: England and Wales: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) and to some degree, cases from the High Court; Scotland: Court of Session; Northern Ireland: the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland and to some degree, the High Court in Belfast. It does not have jurisdiction to hear criminal appeals from Scotland. The Supreme Court, therefore, would not Г Г a convicted person's Convention rights.

stem: A Conservative Member of Parliament was tragically killed when he accidentally shot himself when out on a New Year's Day hunt. The Prime Minister is concerned that he might lose his wafer thin majority in the House of Commons. He would like, therefore, to appoint his trusted friend as the next local MP for the constituency as quickly as possible.
ask: Which option offers the best advice to give to the Prime Minister?

options.en: The Prime Minister can appoint his friend as long as his nomination is approved by a majority of MPs
The Prime Minister can appoint his friend as long as his nomination is approved by a majority of Conservative MPs
The Prime Minister cannot appoint his friend, because the seat must remain vacant until the next general election is held
The Prime Minister cannot appoint his friend, because a by-election takes place when a seat in the House of Commons becomes vacant between general elections
The Prime Minister cannot appoint his friend, because it is the exclusive role of the House of Commons to decide on the nomination of MPs between general elections

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. Once elected, Members of Parliament normally continue to serve until the next dissolution of Parliament. If a Member, however, dies or ceases to be qualified, his or her seat falls vacant. When there is a vacant seat, the usual procedure is for the party who held the seat to put down a motion in the House to move a writ, triggering a by-election in that constituency.

stem: You represent a client who is purchasing a company. During the course of your due diligence, you discover that a number of the company's lucrative contracts were obtained by paying bribes.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The solicitor may complete the transaction for his client

stem: Two people run a business together in partnership. The partnership has substantial debts of £4,000,000 and its assets only amount to £3,000,000. nich of the tollowing statements is correct!
ask: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.en: The partnership's creditors can apply to the court for an administrator to be appointed to liquidate the assets of the partnership and can present bankruptcy petitions in relation to each partner if the partnership is insolvent
The partnership's creditors can only present bankruptcy petitions in relation to each partner, who must then sell partnership assets to raise money to pay into their bankruptcy estates

The partnership's creditors can only present bankruptcy petitions in relation to each partner, and the partners must then collectively appoint an administrator to liquidate the assets of the partnership

The partnership's creditors can only apply to the court for an administrator to be appointed to liquidate the assets of the partnership, and partners are protected from personal liability if the partnership is insolvent

stem: A Manchester company faxed an offer to a company in Prague, offering to sell a quantity of upholstery for the Czech Republic company's new car. This offer was accepted through fax, which was received by the Manchester company.

stem: During the course of his employment, a plumber was exposed to asbestos. This exposure caused him to develop lung cancer which eventually led to his premature death. Despite warnings from his doctor, the plumber continued to smoke heavily both prior to and after his exposure to asbestos.

stem: Your client was arrested by the police for breach of the peace. explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is (C). For trusts over homes, a distinct set of rules have arisen that do not apply to other land. For example, while contributing to the mortgage will create an equitable interest, as in Lloyds Bank v Rosset [1990], housekeeping and contributing to domestic expenses will not, as in Burns v Burns [1984]. Where a wife contributes to her husband's business activities, it may be found that she has suffered detriment which will ground a right in property (Heseltine v Heseltine [1971]). Where either partner carries out extensive building work on the marital home, or moves to another country, thus giving up secure accommodation, detrimental reliance will generally be entitled to rely on their contributions to the acquisition or maintenance of property where there have been assurances made to them that they would be able to occupy that property as their home. Indeed, in one case, the family maid, who had formed an emotional understanding with one of the family and become his partner, was held to have suffered detriment in looking after the family and not getting a job in reliance on the representation made to her (Greasley v Cooker [1980]).

stem: Your client is planning to purchase a house from a man for its market value. The man informs your client that the house forms part of a trust for a beneficiary. Your client likes the house and decides to purchase it anyway.

explanation.en: answer is C. No, because your client had actual notice of the beneficiary's interest, and he is therefore not protected by the doctrine of notice. stem: A person was due to be interviewed by police, but on the advice of the duty solicitor who advised the person that the evidence against him was strong, he opted to remain silent during the interview. While the right to silence is protected by Article 6(1) of the Convention, there is no express entitlement to do so. Although the right has been held to be part of the generally recognised international standard of justice and is part of the system established by the Convention, the right is not absolute. Further it follows from case law from the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) that Article 6 (which guarantees the right to a fair trial) requires the prosecution at least to establish prima facie that the accused has committed an offence, and that it is permissible for a court to draw an inference of guilt from the accused's failure to provide an explanation only where this is the common sense conclusion to be drawn. In the case of Murray (John) v UK (1996) 22 E.H.R.R. 29, the ECtHR stated that the right to remain silent is not absolute: "Whether the drawing of adverse inferences from an accused's silence infringes Article 6 is a matter to be determined in the light of all the circumstances of the case, having particular regard to the situations where inferences may be drawn, the weight to be attached to them by national courts in their assessment of the evidence and the degree of compulsion inherent in the situation." stem: A woman gives a letter of authority to a solicitor which she says is from her mother. The letter authorises the solicitor to transfer the mother's house into the woman's name. stem: The following provision was included in a trust instrument:
ask: "I settle £1,000 to be held by the trustee on trust so that the trustee shall distribute all of the £1,000 equally to any of my grandchildren who have enrolled for a full-time university degree course before 1 October 2010, with the power to retain the whole of that £1,000 for the remainder beneficiary." Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trustee has power to distribute the property according to their discretion about the amount of property to be held for each beneficiary
The trustee has power to distribute the property according to their discretion and the beneficiaries have no proprietary rights in the equitable interest of the trust fund
The trustee has power to distribute the property according to their discretion, because the trust is for a fixed number of beneficiaries
The trustee has power to distribute the property, but is not subject to any trust obligation
The trustee is required to distribute the property equally and has no discretion about the amount of property to be held for each beneficiary

explanation.en: .. rA 200 for the The correct answer is E. The trust is a fixed trust, because the property is being held 'equally' for a fixed number of identified beneficiaries. Before the trust can be administered, it is necessary to ascertain how many grandchildren of this class there are, and their identity. The trustee only has an obligation to act in the limited manner identified in the trust instrument, but no discretion of any sort. The beneficiaries thus have proprietary rights in the equitable interest of the trust fund in accordance with the terms of the trust instrument.

stem: A man and woman operate a hairdressing salon together as partners. They have no written partnership agreement. The man also decides to offer his services as an independent mobile hairdresser, cutting people's hair in their own homes when the salon that he runs with the woman is closed, but does not tell the woman about this.
ask: Which of the following statements most accurately describes the position?

options.en: The man's new venture is in competition with the business that he runs with the woman; he must account to the firm for any profits and the woman could obtain an injunction preventing him from continuing to trade

The man's new venture is in competition with the business that he runs with the woman; he must account to the firm for any profits that he makes, but the woman could not prevent him from continuing to trade

The man's new venture is in competition with the business that he runs with the woman; she could prevent him from continuing to trade, but he is under no duty to account to the firm for any profits that he makes

The man's new venture is in competition with the business that he runs with the woman; however, he does not need to account to the firm for any profits that he makes and there is no way for the woman to prevent him from continuing to trade, as there is no express partnership agreement in place

The man's new venture is not in competition with the business that he runs with the woman; he does not need to account to the partnership for any profits and the woman could not prevent him from continuing to trade

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Section 30 of the 1890 Act provides that a partner must not compete with the firm. They are liable to account to the firm for any profits and the other partner (s) can obtain injunctive relief to restrain continued trading. It is possible for a partner to obtain the consent of the other partners to trading in competition with the firm, and it is also possible for the partners to contract out of this provision by including a standing consent in the partnership agreement.

stem: A Bill of lading with regard to chartered goods had not been delivered in to the hands of the recipient by the time the goods arrived at their destination. The ship was therefore arrested at port. The recipient had agreed by letter of indemnity to indemnify the charterer and its 'servants and agents in case of any liability, loss, damage or expense' resulting from such an event.
ask: The ship owners now claim that the letter of indemnity conferred the benefit of indemnity to them, since it had not been rebutted by the charterer that the ship owners were acting as its 'servants and In regard to the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 ("the Act"'), are the ship owners, as third parties to the recipient's letter of indemnity, entitled to enforce the recipient's promise of indemnity?

options.en: The recipient's indemnity would not confer a benefit upon the ship owners to enforce the promise, since they were only the charterer's agents in delivering the cargo

The recipient's indemnity would confer a benefit upon the ship owners to enforce the promise, but there would have to be evidence of an intention to include the ship owners' right to enforce the terms for it to take effect

The recipient's indemnity would not confer a benefit upon the ship owners to enforce the promise, because there was no positive indication that the recipient had agreed that the ship owners should be entitled to claim the benefit as if the ship owners were parties to the contract
The recipient's indemnity would confer a benefit upon the ship owners to enforce the promise, as they were acting as the charterer's agents in delivering the cargo

The recipient's indemnity would confer a benefit upon the ship owners to enforce the promise, but only if there was a positive indication in the letter of indemnity that the ship owners had agreed that the recipient should be entitled to claim against the ship owners as if they were parties to the contract

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best answer. The recipient's indemnity would confer a benefit upon the ship owners under section 1(1)(b) of the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999. The ship owners were acting as the charterer's agents in delivering the cargo and, on a proper construction; the recipient's indemnity was intended to be enforceable by the ship owners. According to the Act, because the indemnity was expressed to be for the benefit of the charterer and its 'servants and agents", this shows that the recipient intended the indemnity to confer benefits on third parties, including the ship owners. The Act prescribes that a person not a party to a contract may enforce a term of that contract if: (a) the contract so....ct r- the contract purports to benefit that person provided the contract identifies that person by name or as a member of a class. In this case the indemnity, on its true construction, purported to confer the benefit of indemnity to the ship owner under s 1(1)(b) of the Act because the ship owner had acted as one of the charterer's agents. Note: section 1 (2) of the Act allows exclusion of section 1(1)(b) if the contract specifies that a third party should not be able to enforce the term. Since the presumption under s 1 (2) was not rebutted, however, the ship owner could enforce the recipient's promise of indemnity. In nastica mart cammarcial cAntractarr an - - (4) was not rebutted, nowever, the snip owner could enforce the recipient's promise of indemnity. In practice, most commercial contractors appear to be amending their standard contracts to ensure they do not give rights to third parties and take advantage of section 1(2) of the Act. The extent to which the contract will be enforceable will depend on judicial interpretation but the case of The Laemthong Glory shows that the rights of third parties under the Act entitles the ship owners to the same remedies as if they were party to the contract. stem: A victim of assault was placed on a life-support machine after being attacked by the defendant.
ask: Over a year later, having diagnosed brain death, doctors switched off the Which option best states the established legal position?

options.en: The original injuries are not the operating cause of death; switching off the life- support machine broke the causation between the original jury and death
The original injuries are the operating cause of death; switching off the life- support machine, however, broke the causation between the original jury and death
The original injuries are the operating cause of death; switching off the life- support machine did not break the causation between the original jury and death

The original injuries are not the operating cause of death; switching off the life- support machine broke the causation between the original jury and death, because doctors have an absolute duty to their patients

The original injuries are not the operating cause of death; although switching off the life-support machine did not break the causation between the original jury and death, the victim did not die within a year and a day of the infliction of injury by the defendant

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. In the case of R v Malcherek [1981], the defendant had attacked the victim causing injuries that were sufficient to mean that the victim was placed on life support. The doctors then chose to turn off the life support machine as the victim was brain dead. Despite the argument put forward by the defendant, that the action which caused the death of the victim was the switching off the life support machine, the Court of Appeal held that there had been no break in causation Lead case: R v Malcherek [1981] 73 Cr App R 173. ru your unu u uuy vi une infliction of MIU HIUL MIN

stem: A fur company carries on the business of breeding foxes on its land. During the breeding season, the vixens are very nervous and any disturbance interferes with the breeding process. A neighbouring farmer maliciously fired guns on his own land adjacent to the breeding pens, for the purpose of injuring the fur company by interfering with the breeding of the foxes. What is your advice to the fur company
ask: which now seeks an injunction to restrain the?

options.en: In such a case an injunction is likely to be granted to restrain the farmer, since his malicious actions clearly constitute a nuisance
In such a case an injunction is unlikely to be granted to restrain the farmer, since the firing took place on his own land, over which he was entitled to shoot

In such a case an injunction is unlikely to be granted to restrain the farmer, since the fur company is using the land for an unusually sensitive purpose and a man who carries on an exceptionally delicate trade cannot complain if it is spoiled by his neighbour doing something lawful in his property if it wouldn't harm an ordinary trade
In such a case an injunction is unlikely to be granted, since the motive of the farmer is immaterial as he has not committed any actionable wrong
In such a case an injunction is likely to be granted to restrain the farmer, since by discharging his firearm near or over the fur company's property, he has actually trespassed on its land

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The malicious firing of the gun by the farmer on his land to scare foxes during their breeding time on the adjoining fur company's land constitutes a nuisance. The farmer's unreasonableness made his conduct a nuisance, and he would be liable for the full extent of the damage even given the particular nervousness of the vixens. His actions were entirely malicious. Had his primary motive been to shoot rabbits or even to improve his aim, the position might have been different. Lead case: Hollywood Silver Fox Farm v Emmett [1936] 2 KB 468.

stem: A new dental practice provides just £70,000 of dental treatment in the VAT year. The practice spends £20,000 on dental equipment (subject to VAT at 20%), £1,000 on newspapers, and £500 on food (not including any restaurant meals or hot takeaway food) and £500 on professional membership subscriptions. The practice is not registered for VAT.
ask: How much VAT would need to be paid to Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs, if any?

options.en: £10,000 is owed by the practice to HMRC
£4,300 is owed to the practice from HMRC
£4,100 is owed to the practice from HMRC
£9,600 is owed by the practice to HMRC
£0 is owed by the practice to HMRC

explanation.en: HMRC. Businesses that are below the VAT threshold do not need to charge VAT. However, they cannot recover input tax either. A is not correct as the practice is not VAT registered. In any event, most dental treatment is VAT exempt. B is not correct as the practice is not VAT registered. In any event, newspapers and food are zero rated. C is not correct as the practice is not VAT registered and membership subscriptions are VAT exempt if certain conditions are met. D is not correct as the practice is not VAT registered, most dental treatment is VAT exempt, newspapers and food are zero rated and membership subscriptions are VAT exempt if certain conditions are met.

stem: An employment solicitor is asked to negotiate a dismissal package for a client who has been unfairly dismissed by his employer.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the legal position?

options.en: The solicitor may not negotiate the dismissal package, because litigation services may be required
The solicitor may not negotiate the dismissal package, because no exclusion or exemption applies
The solicitor may negotiate the dismissal package, because employment services are immune from involvement in investment activities
The solicitor may negotiate the dismissal package, because no pension top-ups and transfers are involved in the negotiations
The solicitor may negotiate the dismissal package, because only conveyancing, corporate, probate, trust and matrimonial services involve regulated investment activities

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. Employment solicitors may also be involved in carrying on regulated investment activities, such as where a client, who has been unfairly or wrongfully dismissed by his employer, instructs a solicitor to negotiate his dismissal package. Pension top-ups and transfers may also be involved when negotiating the terms of the settlement, which pose specific problems under the Scope Rules. Nor will any exclusion or exemption apply to the solicitor's activities. Therefore, B is the correct answer.

stem: The Royal Angling Alliance (RAA) was established by statute to determine whether fishing is permissible or prohibited in all lakes and watercourses and to regulate such use when it is permitted. The RAA has a committee of seven members, all of whom are selected by the Secretary of State for the Environment. Four RAA members are paid consultants to the Royal Farming Alliance (RA), and the RAA has just voted to allow the RFA to abstract water from a lake to supply irrigation water to local farmers, to the potential detriment of the local anglers that also use it. Identify which principle of judicial review
ask: is raised by the RAA's decision?

options.en: The RAA's decision raises an issue of illegality, because it has fettered its discretion
The RAA's decision raises an issue of procedural illegality, because its actions were ultra vires
The RAA's decision raises an issue of procedural impropriety, because it failed to give adequate reasons
The RAA's decision raises an issue of procedural irrationality, because it failed to act reasonably
The RAA's decision raises an issue of procedural impropriety, because it acted in a biased manner

explanation.en: E is correct. The RAA's decision raises an issue of procedural impropriety, because it acted in a biased manner. The question is whether the fair minded observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility that the RAA's members' decision was biased, due to their connection with the RFA. Lead case: Magill v Porter [2001] UKHL 67.

stem: A man asked a car dealer to help find him a well-tuned car. The car dealer duly supplied him with a car and told him that the car had only done 10,000 miles. The man subsequently learned that the car dealer's statement as to its mileage was untrue, because it actually had 40,000 miles on the clock.
ask: Does the man have grounds for claiming damages for breach of warranty because the car dealer made a false statement about the car's mileage?

options.en: The man has no grounds for claiming damages for breach of warranty, because there is no proof that the car dealer knew that the car had actually done 40,000 miles and an innocent misrepresentation is not a warranty

The man has no grounds for claiming damages for breach of warranty, because there is no evidence that the car dealer intended for the man to rely on her statement that the car had only done 10,000 miles, and since an innocent misrepresentation is not a warranty, it does not give rise to damages

The man has grounds for claiming damages for breach of warranty; the statement as to the mileage was a term of the contract, because the car dealer should be taken to have better knowledge of such matters than the man
The man has grounds for claiming damages for breach of warranty, because every representation made in the course of such dealing is to be treated as a warranty
The man does not have grounds for claiming damages for breach of warranty because what the car dealer said was not intended and understood as a legally binding promise

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The statement was of a promissory nature, even if innocently made as the seller was a motor car dealer and in a much better position to know the state of the car. Lead case: Dick Bentley Productions Ltd v Harold Smith (Motors) Ltd [1965] 1 WLR 623.

stem: A trustee, who describes herself as an 'amateur' and 'rather ignorant of business ', orally appoints her friend, a bookmaker, as her agent to invest trust funds. The bookmaker invests the funds and also chooses the investment policy. The investment turns out to have been an unwise choice in the circumstances, depleting the funds considerably.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trustee breached her trust, because she appointed an agent to invest the trust funds on her behalf
The trustee breached her trust, because she did not provide her agent with an investment policy statement
The trustee did not breach her trust, because she appointed the agent in good faith
The trustee did not breach her trust, because the losses to the trust fund were not caused through her own wilful default
The trustee did not breach her trust, because the bookmaker's recklessness caused the depletion of the trust funds

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. A trustee is permitted to appoint an agent to invest trust funds, provided that the trustee delegates the asset management functions to the agent in the form of an agreement evidenced in writing, in which the agent agrees to comply with the 'policy statement' provided by the trustee. The policy statement is intended to guide the agent as to how to exercise delegated asset management functions in the best interests of the trust (s. 15(1) Trustee Act 2000). Here, the trustee has provided no policy statement and has therefore breached her trust. The delegation is thus invalid. Moreover, by appointing her bookmaker as her agent, she has breached her general duty of (s. 23(a)). The trustee's lack of experience and expertise and the fact that there is no suggestion of dishonesty or bad faith on her part, will be unlikely to 'let her off the hook', because even if she was not negligent, she was surely reckless, and unable therefore to rely upon the immunity afforded by s.30(1). She has not lived up to the standard of care expected of trustees generally (s. 1(1)).

stem: The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) receives applications for relief from the following parties: (1) a contracting State; (2) a non-contracting State; (3) a Non- governmental Organisation (NGO); and (4) a private company.
ask: Which option best states the respective parties' standing?

options.en: The contracting State, the NGO, and the non-contracting State have standing; the private company does not
The contracting State, the private company, and the non-contracting State have standing; the NGO does not
The NGO, the private company, and the non-contracting State have standing; the contracting State does not
The NGO, the private company, and the non-contracting State and the contracting State all have standing
The contracting State, the NGO, and the private company have standing; the non-contracting State does not

explanation.en: E is the best option. The contracting State, the NGO, and the private company have standing; the non- contracting State does not. The person complaining may be a natural person, or a legal person, such as a company (The Sunday Times v UK (1979) 2 EHRR 245). Cases can only be brought against one or more States that have ratified the Convention. Both NGOs and contracting States can lodge applications. They may also be authorised by the President of the Court to intervene in proceedings as third parties.

stem: A public company limited by shares has three directors: (1) a woman who acts as managing director; (2) a primary holding company, which is represented on the board by its own managing director; and (3) a secondary holding company, which is also represented on the board by its own managing director.
ask: Which statement would best describe the position if the woman were to die?

options.en: No further action would be required, as the public company would meet the minimum requirements for the number of directors that it must have
An additional director would need to be appointed, which could either be an individual or a company
An additional director would need to be appointed, which must be an individual and must be appointed as managing director
Either director of either holding company must be appointed as managing director
An additional director would need to be appointed, which must be an individual

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. All companies must have at least one director who is a natural person. Although the directors of the two holding companies are natural persons, they sit on the board of the public company as representatives of their respective holding companies. It is those two companies that are actually the directors of the public company. It is not necessary for a company to have a managing director, although it is usual practice for such an appointment to be made to a natural person.

stem: A man owns the fee simple estate in a 4,000 acre farm. He is a 30 year old bachelor in excellent health and has no close relatives whatsoever. He is killed in a farming accident without making a will.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The man's estate in the farm will pass under the Intestacy Rules to his closest friends
The man's estate in the farm will pass under the Intestacy Rules to his favourite charity
The man's estate in the farm will pass under the Intestacy Rules to its previous
The man's estate in the farm will pass to the Crown as bona vacantia
The man's estate in the farm will pass to his landlord

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The man's estate in the farm will pass to the Crown as bona vacantia. The fee simple absolute in possession is notionally only a right to use land indefinitely and therefore should the estate owner die without leaving any heirs, the fee simple estate will be extinguished and the land will revert back to the Crown to be held in demesne.

stem: Your client has been arrested for inflicting grievous bodily harm (GBH). Following medical reports, it appears your client might be charged with the lesser offence of causing actual bodily harm (ABH) instead.
ask: Which option best states what must be shown by the prosecution for your client to be charged with inflicting GBH?

options.en: To prove infliction of GBH, the prosecution must show that the individual was sufficiently injured to require hospital treatment
To prove infliction of GBH, the prosecution must show that there were visible injuries
To prove infliction of GBH, the prosecution must show that the wound was serious
To prove infliction of GBH, the prosecution must show that the whole skin had been broken
To prove infliction of GBH, the prosecution must show that the individual was visibly bruised

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. To show that a suspect unlawfully and maliciously wounded or inflicted GBH under Section 20 of the of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861, there needs to be a breaking of the skin; visible injury is irrelevant. While the wound need not be serious, the whole skin must be broken. Statute: Section 20 of the of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861.

stem: A woman sued a pharmaceutical company, alleging that its contraceptive pill had caused her to suffer a thrombosis.
ask: The pharmaceutical company countered with expert evidence that there was no increased relative risk of the injuries complained Given these circumstances, who has the burden of proving fault and damage under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 (CPA)?

options.en: The woman must prove that the product was defective, that the defect caused her damage and that there was an increased relative risk of the injuries she complains of

The woman must prove that the product was defective and that the defect caused her damage, whilst the pharmaceutical company has the burden of proof to show there was no increased relative risk of the injuries she complains of

The pharmaceutical company must prove that the product was not defective, and that the defect had not caused her damage, whilst the woman has the burden of proof to show there was an increased relative risk of the injuries she complains of

The pharmaceutical company must prove that the product was not defective, and the woman must prove that the defect had caused her damage, and show there was an increased relative risk of the injuries she complains of

The pharmaceutical company must prove that the product was not defective, that the defect did not cause the woman damage and that there was no increased relative risk of the injuries the woman complains of

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Under the CPA, the claimant must prove that the product is defective, and that the defect caused her damage. Where the manufacturer relies on a defence under the CPA, however, the manufacturer has the burden of proving that defence. Section 2 Consumer Protection Act 1987.

stem: An import/export business and a discount store are being sued by a local store for patent infringement. The import/export business buys cosmetic products from abroad and the discount store sells them within the UK. Since the discount store lacks funds, the import/export business is paying the solicitor's fees in respect of both clients, but you - acting for both companies - receive a phone call from the import/export business' managing director, informing you that the discount store has fallen behind in paying the import/export business' invoices and he therefore plans to issue a winding up petition.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes what you can do?

options.en: You can disclose the information to the discount store and continue acting for both parties
You can disclose the information to the discount store, but would have to cease acting for either party
You cannot disclose the information to the discount store but may continue acting for both parties
You cannot disclose the information to the discount store but can continue acting for both parties provided the import/export business consents to you disclosing the information to the discount store
You can neither disclose the information to the discount store nor continue to act for both parties

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. All affairs of clients must be kept confidential except where disclosure is permitted by law or by your client (04.1). A solicitor who is acting for a client is also under a duty to disclose to a client all information which is relevant to that client's matter - regardless of the source of that information (04.2). Therefore, you owe a duty of confidentiality to the import/export business, but also owe a duty to the discount store to disclose all 'material' information relevant to its interests - which, according to the guidance notes, means any information which might reasonably be expected to affect the client's decision- making in a significant way with regard to his matter. the fact that the import/export business is funding the litigation) but cannot be disclosed to the discount store due to the duty of confidentiality you owe to the import/export business. You would therefore also have to cease acting for at least the discount store (and possibly both parties), unless the import/export business is willing to waive its confidentiality to allow you to inform the discount store of your conversation.

stem: The Ministry of Justice is garnering proposals for reform of a number of prerogative executive powers to be set out in a Green Paper to be taken forward. Comments are requested both on the contents of the report and on the scope for further reform. The Ministry would particularly like to receive comments distinguishing those powers reserved to the Sovereign's general prerogative powers and the Sovereign's personal prerogative powers.
ask: Which option best describes a personal prerogative power which still resides in the jurisdiction of the Crown?

options.en: A prerogative power which still resides in the jurisdiction of the personal prerogative of the Crown is the power to appoint Queen's Counsel (QC)
A prerogative power which still resides in the jurisdiction of the right to make war or peace or institute hostilities falling short of war

explanation.en: E is correct. The appointment of a Prime Minister is one of the two main prerogative powers recognised under the common law which are still reserved to the jurisdiction of the Crown. stem: A man contracted with a homeowner to build a swimming pool in the homeowner's garden for £700,000, and the contract stated that the pool should be 2.4 metres at the deep end. When the pool was completed, however, the homeowner found that the maximum depth of the pool was 2.2 metres, and while the pool is entirely suitable for the purpose for which the homeowner wished to use it, he is refusing to pay the man until he totally reconstructs the entire pool. Ripping out the entire pool and fulfilling the exact contract specification would cost the man £270,000. Which measure of damages
ask: do courts usually award in contractual disputes of this?

options.en: The difference in value
The reliance interest
The restitution interest
The cost of reinstatement
Specific performance

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The difference in value measure of damages is a species of expectation interest aimed at avoiding unreasonable awards where the cost of reinstatement, would be totally out of proportion to the benefit to be obtained by the claimant. Lead case: Watts v Morrow [1991] 4 AlI ER 937.

stem: A testator leaves a trust in his will, in order to provide for his family after his death, which occurred in 2013. The terms of the trust are: 'To my wife for life, remainder to my children, if they reach the age of 25 and qualify as a barrister.' The testator's 24 year-old son asks the trustees for financial assistance. He has just qualified as a solicitor and requests £100,000 from the trust to establish himself in practice.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trustees cannot advance the money, because the child may not reach age 25 and become a barrister
The trustees cannot advance the money, because starting a business does not constitute an advancement according to the law
The trustees have discretion to advance half of the child's eventual share, provided the child's mother gives her written consent
The trustees have discretion to advance half of the child's eventual share, even without receiving the written consent of the child's mother
The trustees must advance the whole of the child's eventual share, provided the child's mother gives her written consent

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The requested advance for the purpose of starting a business falls within an 'advance or benefit' pursuant to s. 32 of the Trustee Act 1925. The fact that the child's interest is subject to a double contingency and that he might not become both 25 and a barrister does not rule out an advancement under s. 32. The written consent of his mother would be needed, however, and he could only be given half of his eventual share, as the trust was created before 1st October 2014, when the restriction was removed. The trustees have discretion to make the advancement and could, technically refuse the request, although the wishes of the testator do not seem particularly

stem: The Indian Government demanded that an Indian terrorist suspect be extradited from the UK to India. The Indian Government gave assurances that all legal procedures would be followed and that the suspect would receive good treatment by the police. The suspect argued that although the police were not empowered to torture him or treat him inhumanely, they did, in India, function outside their powers, and the Indian Government was unable to control them completely.
ask: Which option best describes how the UK Government might comply with the Human Rights Act 1998, in this situation?

options.en: The UK Government would not be responsible for any activities happening within Indian Territory, after the suspect had ceased to be under UK control
The UK Government could comply by obtaining written guarantees from the Indian Government that the suspect's situation would be closely supervised by Amnesty International
The UK Government could comply by extraditing the suspect to another region within India, where he would not be threatened by the actions of the police
The UK Government could not extradite the suspect, since the suspect had established that a real risk existed that he would be tortured, while in India
The UK Government could not extradite the suspect, since the suspect had established the case against himself to be false

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. Option D is correct. All other options are incorrect. The question is based on Chahal v. UK, an important ECtHR decision on the application of Article 3 (Prohibition of Torture). Chahal avoided extradition by establishing that he was at "real risk".

stem: You are called to the police station to represent your client. He has been arrested for participating in the armed robbery of a post office.
ask: He claims that he was forced to participate in the robbery when the leader of the gang to which he belongs held a gun to his head and threatened him and his children with violence if he did not Which option best states which defence, if any, that is available to your client?

options.en: The defence available to your client is necessity, because his actions arose as a result of extreme pressure and threats against him from the gang leader
The defence available to your client is duress, because there was no voluntary actus reus
The defence of duress is not available to your client, because the threat came from a fellow member of the same gang
The defence available to your client is mistake, because he could not have anticipated that the gang leader would behave in such a manner
The defence available to your client is duress of circumstance, because a person is permitted to commit a crime to prevent a greater evil occurring to them or others

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The defence of duress is not available where, as here, your client voluntarily and with knowledge of its nature joined a gang which he knew might pressurise or threaten him to commit a criminal acts. Lead Case: R v Sharp (David) [1987] 3 WLR 1.

stem: A man has been charged with actual bodily harm (ABH) and is minded to elect summary trial. He seeks advice regarding the maximum sentencing powers of the magistrates' court.

The magistrates' court can sentence for summary offences which involve a maximum penalty of 3 months' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to £5,000
The magistrates' court can sentence for summary offences which involve a maximum penalty of 6 months' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to £5,000
The magistrates' court can sentence for summary offences which involve a maximum penalty of 12 months' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to £1,000
The magistrates' court can sentence for summary offences which involve a maximum penalty of 12 months' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to £5,000

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The magistrates' court can sentence for summary offences which involve a maximum penalty of 6 months' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to £5,000. Source: Powers of Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000....olve a

stem: A solicitor prepared a will for a long-standing client and undertook the conveyancing on the purchase of a modest family home.
ask: Five years later, the client instructs the solicitor in the purchase of an expensive holiday home, costing an unusually large amount of money Which of the following statements best explains the legal position?

options.en: A solicitor who is unaware of the fraudulent activities of his client will be exempt from criminal liability
A solicitor who is unaware of the fraudulent activities of his client may find himself nonetheless criminally liable
A solicitor can assume the best of his client if he has represented the client in an earlier transaction
A solicitor who unwittingly facilitates a dubious transaction can only be liable to a civil action
A solicitor who unwittingly facilitates a dubious transaction can only be liable to criminal prosecution

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Solicitors play a crucial and trusted role in the transfer of property in the UK. Criminals will try to exploit the professional services offered by solicitors to enable them to engage in mortgage fraud. Even where solicitors are unaware of the fraudulent activities of their clients, they may find themselves criminally liable because of the wide definition of fraud in the Fraud Act 2006 and the extensive offences under anti-money laundering regulations. Solicitors must therefore ensure that they do not, even unwittingly, facilitate a dubious transaction. The Law Society's Practice Note on Mortgage Fraud clarifies that if a solicitor is a party to an attempt to deceive a mortgage lender, then both solicitor and the buyer may be liable to criminal prosecution and/or civil action. If it turns out that your client has engaged in mortgage fraud, and you could have helped prevent it had you undertaken proper due diligence, you may find yourself on the receiving end of such a claim. Such claims are particularly likely where property values have fallen and the lender can no longer cover the loss by selling the property. In the case in question, the solicitor prepared a will for a client and undertook conveyancing on the purchase of a modest family home. Several years later, the client instructed the solicitor in the purchase of a holiday home that appeared to be beyond the client's means to earlier retainers. Such conduct warrants closer inspection of the mortgage application. According to the Law Society's Practice Note on Mortgage Fraud, you should ask questions of the client to verify this information. You should check all mortgage and contractual documentation carefully. Seek explanations from the client for any discrepancies in the document. It may be a simple misunderstanding of the documents or an inadvertent error needing correction. You should consider whether the identity you have been given is consistent with the actual presentation of the client and the transaction as a whole.

stem: While developing a housing estate, corporation workers dug a trench in the middle of a piece of open ground belonging to the corporation and an adjoining site where the building work was going on. An infant boy aged five, who was under the supervision of his mother at the time, fell into the trench while taking a short-cut across the open space and was injured.
ask: Would the corporation likely be held liable for the child's injury?

options.en: trespasser, there was in this case such a reckless disregard of ordinary humanity so as to impose liability on the corporation

The corporation is unlikely to be held liable for the infant's injury; the child was under the supervision of his mother at the time the accident occurred, and one would expect the mother to appreciate any obvious dangers

The corporation is likely to be held liable for the infant's injury; if the corporation as an occupier had resigned itself to the occasional and perhaps inevitable presence of trespassers on its property, it must take upon itself the obligations of a licensor

The corporation is unlikely to be held liable for the infant's injury; even if the corporation as an occupier had resigned itself to the occasional and perhaps inevitable presence of trespassers on its property, it does not take upon itself the obligations of a licensor

The corporation is likely to be held liable for the infant's injury; even if the child was a trespasser, the corporation breached its duty by assuming that all parents are responsible and will not permit young children to be sent into danger without protection

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The facts of the scenario broadly reflect the High Court case of Phipps v Rochester Corp [1955]. In Phipps it was established that "[a]s a general rule [the occupier] will have discharged his duty towards [the children] if the dangers which they may encounter are only those which are obvious to a guardian or of which he has given a warning comprehensible by a guardian." Although the child, in the scenario, was on the land as a licensee, there was no breach of the corporation's duty towards him. It was entitled to assume that parents or guardians would behave in a naturally prudent way, and was not obliged to take it on itself, in effect, to discharge parental duties. See tort manual or other guardians, who will look after them..." This case is still good law and has not been superseded by either Occupier Liability Acts. Lead case: Phipps v Rochester Corp [1955] 1 All ER 129.

stem: Two weeks ago, a woman persuaded a man to steal clothes from a clothes store. The man went to the store and stuffed an expensive pair of Jeans in to his bag while the woman waited for him at home. The woman has been arrested.
ask: Which option best describes the woman's potential criminal liability, if any?

options.en: The woman did not commit any criminal offence; she cannot therefore be liable for the man committing theft
The woman did not commit any criminal offence as she did not participate in the actual act
Although the woman did not commit the full criminal offence, she may be liable for encouraging or assisting the man to commit theft
Although the woman did not commit the full criminal offence, she may be liable for inciting the man to commit theft
Although the woman did not commit the full criminal offence, she may be liable for attempting to commit theft

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Sections 44 to 46 (Part 2) SCA 2007 create the inchoate offences of: (1) Intentionally encouraging or assisting an offence; (2) Encouraging or assisting an offence believing it will be committed; and (3) Encouraging or assisting offences believing one or more will be committed. Together they replace the common law offence of incitement (now abolished). Statute: ss.44-45, Serious Crime Act 2007.

stem: A man is the freehold owner of a former stately home, which is not registered at HM Land Registry. The man is in the process of converting the property into flats, and enters into a contract agreeing with the woman that he will grant her a 999 year lease of one of the flats in three months, when the works will be completed.
ask: What kind of interest, if any, does the woman have in the property?

options.en: The woman has no interest in the property until the works are completed
The woman has the benefit of an equitable lease, which is an estate contract within the meaning of the Law of Property Act 1925
The woman has the benefit of an equitable lease, which is an estate contract within the meaning of the Land Registration Act 1925
The woman has the benefit of a legal lease, which is an estate contract within the meaning of the Land Charges Act 1972
The woman has the benefit of an equitable lease, which is an estate contract within the meaning of the Land Charges Act 1972

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The woman should protect her interest by registering a Class C(iv) Land Charge. The woman has the benefit of an equitable lease, which is an estate contract within the meaning of the Land Charges Act 1972. In order to protect this, it must be registered. A Class F Land Charge is used to protect Home Rights and local land charges are generally encumbrances arising from regulatory matters with the local authority.
