stem: A bank obtained a 'comfort letter' from a company, asserting that it was company policy to ensure that the business of its subsidiary was at all times in a position to meet the subsidiary's liabilities to the bank. The subsidiary having gone into liquidation, the bank claims sums owed by the subsidiary against the company.
ask: Would the 'comfort letter' amount to a legally binding promise?

options.en: The 'comfort letter' amounts to a legally binding promise, because the consequences of the company's decision to repudiate its moral responsibility are matters a court cannot turn a blind eye to
The 'comfort letter' amounts to a legally binding promise, because the bank clearly acted in reliance on the letter in making the advance

The 'comfort letter' amounts to a legally binding promise, because it was of paramount importance to the bank that the company should ensure that its subsidiary was at all times in a position to meet its liabilities, since commodity markets like oil are of their very nature speculative

The 'comfort letter' does not amount to a legally binding promise, because the letter was a statement of present fact and not a promise as to future conduct; a court will not make up for the lack of express promise by implying such a promise
The 'comfort letter' does not amount to a legally binding promise, because comfort letters are of minimal commercial importance and entirely devoid of legal effect

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. There must be something in the letter to show that, as a matter of commercial probability or common sense, the parties must have intended the letter to be a contractual promise. If the promise is not expressly stated, it is a mere representation of fact. Lead case: Kleinwort Benson Ltd v Malaysian Mining Corp. Berhad [1988] 1 WLR 799.

stem: A beneficiary is dissatisfied with the annual income that she receives from her family trust. She learns that a solicitor who undertakes the running of the trust, including investment decisions, has been banned from legal practice.
ask: She is concerned that the trustees are not fulfilling their obligations under the terms of the trust and seeks your Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trustees may delegate the entire running of the trust to the solicitor
The trustees may be liable for the actions of their agent
The trustees may be penalised for being cautious in their investment decisions
The trustees will not be liable for the actions of their agent, if he was appointed in good faith
The trustees will not be liable for any financial loss

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is (B). The solicitor's employment seems questionable, as the trustees must exercise reasonable care and skill in selecting, appointing and supervising agents. A solicitor may not be suitable for investment advice, particularly one who is not allowed to practise. They clearly cannot delegate all the running of the trust to him and should have drawn up a proper written agreement and investment policy statement. Trustees will not be excused from liability for the actions of an agent, even if the agent was appointed in good faith. Under the Trustee Act 2000, the trustees must exercise reasonable care and skill to escape liability. Although Cowan v Scargill insisted that trustees have a duty to

stem: Three people are the founders of an endeavour dedicated to alleviating the poverty of down-and-out solicitors hit hard by the global recession. They are headquartered in rented office space in the centre of Oldcastle where they plan their fundraising activities and organise their army of volunteers and paid office staff, including their accounts department who administer the endeavour's bank account. They aim to generate as much profit as possible through their work which they then pay over to the Solicitors Benevolent Fund held by the Law Society.
ask: Which option best states the endeavour's legal status?

options.en: The endeavour is a partnership
The endeavour is not a partnership, because it is not carrying on a commercial business
The endeavour is not a partnership, because the three people are not carrying on their business in common
The endeavour is not a partnership, because the three people are not carrying on their business with a view to profit
The endeavour is not a partnership, because it is not carrying on a commercial business with a view to profit

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The three people are carrying on the activities of the endeavour in common (evidenced by their shared bank account and facilities) and ultimately with a view to profit, which they will donate to the Solicitors Benevolent Fund. However they are not carrying on a commercial venture, as they are a charitable organisation. Their organisation is therefore not capable of being a partnership within the meaning of the Partnership Act 1890.

stem: The European Convention on Human Rights (the "Convention") has been ratified by 47 member states of the Council of Europe. Member States are bound to secure everyone within their jurisdiction the rights and freedoms defined in the Convention.
ask: Which one of the following statements best describes which rights the Convention primarily guarantees?

options.en: The Convention primarily guarantees civil, political and private economic rights in the UK courts
The Convention primarily guarantees social, political and private economic rights in the UK courts
The Convention primarily guarantees economic, social and political rights in the UK courts
The Convention primarily guarantees civil and political rights
The Convention primarily guarantees social, economic, civil and political rights

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The Convention guarantees civil and political rights. Economic and social rights were left aside until later. operation in Europe. Keynote addresses by Ms. Päivi Hirvelă, Judge at the European Court of Human Rights. Conference in Helsinki, 10-11 September 2008. See also the Council of Europe's website, which states, "The European Convention on Human Rights guarantees civil and political human rights".

stem: A claimant's sheep were swept overboard during a storm while being carried on the deck of the defendant's ship. The defendant admits to being in breach of the relevant statute, which requires ships to carry livestock in pens below deck. The court determines that an action for breach of statutory duty lies.
ask: Which option best states the next question the court must consider, if any?

options.en: Once it has been established that an action for breach of statutory duty lies, the court must determine that the damage suffered is recognised by the statute in question
Once it has been established that an action for breach of statutory duty lies, the court must determine the correct quantum of damages
Once it has been established that an action for breach of statutory duty lies, the court must determine whether the defendant is a public body
Once it has been established that an action for breach of statutory duty lies, the court must determine whether the defendant is a private entity
Once it has been established that an action for breach of statutory duty lies, the court must determine whether the statute provides a specific means of enforcement, such as by criminal penalty

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best option. A factor to be considered by the court is whether any action for breach of statutory duty is limited by the object of the relevant statute. In other words, an action is only available with reference to the kind of harm contemplated by that statute. If it does not do so, there is no breach of the tort regarding the particular damage. Per answer A, once it has been established that an action for breach of statutory duty lies, the court must decide whether the harm that the claimant has suffered falls within the area of the harm against which the legislature intended to guard. Lead case: Gorris v Scott (1874) LR 9 Ex 125

stem: ACo Ltd is a private limited company and has issued £500,000 (unpaid) shares to BCo. BCo is an unlimited private company with five members each holding 20% of the shares. Aco and BCo are set to go into liquidation, and BCo has no assets or liabilities.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: ACo's creditors may claim the full value of ACo's debts from the five members
ACo's creditors may claim up to £500,000 from the five members
ACo's liquidator may claim the full value of ACo's debts from BCo
BCo's liquidator may claim the full value of ACo's debts from the five members up to a limit of £500,000
ACo's liquidator may claim the full value of ACo's debts from the five members

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. ACo's liquidator would not be able to claim against the five members directly, as they are not members of ACo. However, the liquidator could call for BCo to pay the amount due on its shares (£500,000). As BCo has no assets of its own and would be in liquidation, its liquidator could in turn call for an unlimited contribution from the five members. However, this contribution would be effectively capped at £500,000, as this is the extent of BCo's liabilities.

stem: Two weeks ago, a woman persuaded her friend to steal clothes from a clothes store.
ask: The woman has been arrested and charged with encouraging or assisting a criminal Which option best describes a possible defence for the woman, if any?

options.en: It is a defence for the woman to show that it was reasonable for her to act the way she did
It is a defence for the woman to show that her friend did not actually commit the offence
It is a defence for the woman to show that her friend did not actually attempt the offence
It is a defence for the woman to show that her friend did not actually commit or attempt the offence
It is a defence for the woman to show that her friend did not know that he was committing an act of theft

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Section 50 of the Serious Crime Act 2007 provides a defence to the offences in Part 2 where the encouragement or assistance is considered to be reasonable in the circumstances the person knew to exist or he reasonably believed to exist. The seriousness of the anticipated main offence; the purpose of the act of encouragement or assistance; and the authority under which he/she was acting will be taken in to consideration when determining if the behaviour was reasonable.

stem: An installation company won a tender to install eight lifts in a commercial building, and after fair contract negotiations, ordered the lifts from a lift company. Although the installation company requested that all transactions should be in Euros, the lift company insisted on using English sterling exclusively, but by the time the lifts were ready for delivery, sterling had dropped against the Euro by 15%. The lift company subsequently threatened not to complete the construction of the lifts unless the installation company was prepared to pay 15% on top of the agreed contract price, and the installation company decided to pay the extra under protest.
ask: Would the installation company be legally entitled to demand a 15% reduction?

options.en: The installation company would not legally be entitled to demand a 15% reduction, because, at the very least, the threat should involve the commission of a tort, or a breach of contract
The installation company would not legally be entitled to demand a 15% reduction, because a mere threat to break a contract does not amount to duress
The installation company would legally be entitled to demand a 15% reduction, because the installation company had no practical alternative course but to submit to the lift company's demands
The installation company would legally be entitled to demand a 15% reduction, because any illegality in the form of a crime or tort against the person would be considered as duress

The installation company would not legally be entitled to demand a 15% reduction, because not every threat of non-performance will amount to duress, since there is a distinction between duress and hard bargaining

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. There was duress, because the lift company's threat to break its contract had no legal justification, and the installation company had no realistic alternative but to submit. Lead case: North Ocean Shipping Company v Hyundai Construction, The Atlantic Baron [1979] QB 705; [1978] 3 All ER 1170.

stem: The owner of a property grants a 25 year lease of the whole to a tenant in 1979. In 1984, the tenant assigns the unexpired term of his lease to his friend. The owner transfers the freehold to his sister in 1989.
ask: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.en: Privity of contract and privity of estate exist between the owner's sister and the tenant's friend; they can enforce all covenants contained in the lease against each other
Privity of contract exists between the owner's sister and the tenant's friend, but no privity of estate exists between them; they can enforce all covenants contained in the lease against each other

Privity of contract exists between the owner's sister and the tenant's friend, but no privity of estate exists between them; they can only enforce against each other those covenants which touch and concern the land
Privity of estate exists between the owner's sister and the tenant's friend, but no privity of contract exists between them; they can enforce all covenants contained in the lease against each other

Privity of estate exists between the owner's sister and the tenant's friend, but no privity of contract exists between them; they can only enforce against each other those covenants which touch and concern the land

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Privity of estate exists between the owner's sister and the tenant's friend, but no privity of contract exists between them. They can only enforce against each other those covenants which touch and concern the land. As they are not the original parties to the lease, there is no privity of contract. However since they are in a direct landlord and tenant relationship, privity of estate exists between them. They can therefore enforce against each other all those covenants in the lease which touch and concern the land.

stem: A trust fund is invested in a number of different business assets, which include the majority of the shares in a private limited company, being one of the original investments of the trust. The trustees seek your advice about how they should act in general in relation to the shareholding and any steps in particular that they are required to take in order to safeguard the investment. The trust document does not contain any express powers of investment.
ask: Which option best describes the trustees' obligations in these circumstances?

options.en: The trustees must obtain the fullest information on the conduct of the business
The trustees must ensure that regular dividends are received from the shares
The trustees must insist that one of the trustees is appointed as a director of the company
The trustees must retain the shares, because they were one of the original investments of the trust
The trustees must receive all documentation available to shareholders

explanation.en: You did not select the best answer. The best answer is A. The trustees must obtain the fullest information on the conduct of the business. Section 4 of the Trustee Act 2000 requires trustees to look at the "standard investment criteria" when investing. These criteria are defined in s. 4(3) as the need to check carefully the suitability of investments for the trust, and the importance of diversification, i.e. spreading the trust fund over different types of investment. In Bartlett v Barclays Bank [1980]), it was held that the standard of observation and control in relation to the the "same care as the ordinary prudent man of business would extend towards his own affairs." Essentially, this means that the trustees are permitted to take risks, but not to expose the beneficiaries to hazard within the scope of the investment policy. In that case, the trustees were investing in a private company. Their obligation was therefore "to ensure an adequate flow of information in time to make use of a controlling interest." This means that in some situations the trustees will be required to intervene and ensure that they are able to amass sufficient information to manage the TL - + amass sufficient information to manage the investment. The trustees needed to procure some control in return for the significant investment in the private company. In Re Lucking's WT [1968], it was said that a trustee should even ensure that he is represented on the company board. However, this principle was interpreted more liberally in the Bartlett case, in which it was stated that a trustee need not be on the board if the circumstances did not require this, provided that the trustee retained a sufficient flow of information from the company in accordance with the size of the shareholding. Other methods of control over the company's affairs may be sufficient.

stem: HILUUSE CLUNUE A man and woman formed a private company limited by shares three years ago, with the aim of running a business together. The man and woman each own 50% of the issued share capital in the company. Although they remain very strong personal friends, they have very differing views on how best to resolve a fundamental issue relating to the company's management and they are unable to resolve the deadlock.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man is likely to be able to obtain an order requiring the woman to purchase his shares
The woman is likely to be able to obtain an order requiring the man to purchase her shares
The woman may commence a derivative action against the man
The man may commence a derivative action against the woman
Either party could petition the court for an order to wind the company up

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is E. Neither party would be likely to obtain an order requiring the other to purchase their shares, because they have an equal shareholding in the company and are both being prejudiced equally by the deadlock. A derivative claim would only be appropriate where a director has breached their duties to the company, and in this case both directors consider that they are acting in the best interests of the company. In cases of extreme deadlock, the court can make an order winding the company up under s.122 Insolvency Act 1986, even though the company may be solvent.

stem: A book was published by a former close friend of the claimant, a television personality. The book revealed deep and personal information about the claimant. The claimant believes that the information was private in the sense it is protected by the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention). If the court determines that an individual had a reasonable expectation of privacy, it then asks: how the balance should be struck between the individual's rights to publish on the one hand and the publisher's right to privacy on the
ask: If the court determines that the information was private and protected by the Convention, which question, if any, does it ask?

options.en: If the court determines that an individual had a reasonable expectation of privacy, it then asks: how the balance should be struck between the individual's rights to publish on the one hand and the publisher's right to privacy on the other?

If the court determines that an individual had a reasonable likelihood of privacy, it then asks: how the balance should be struck between the individual's rights to privacy on the one hand and the publisher's right to publish on the other?

If the court determines that an individual had a reasonable expectation of privacy, it then asks: how the balance should be struck between the individual's rights to privacy on the one hand and the publisher's right to publish on the other?

If the court determines that an individual had a realistic prospect of privacy, it then asks: how the balance should be struck between the individual's rights to privacy on the one hand and the publisher's right to publish on the other?

If the court determines that an individual had a good possibility of privacy, it then asks: how the balance should be struck between the individual's rights to privacy on the one hand and the publisher's right to publish on the other?

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. If the answer to the first question as to whether the individual has a reasonable expectation of privacy is "yes", the second question is how the balance should be struck between as between the individual's right to privacy on the one hand and the publisher's right to publish on the other. The court must balance the competing Convention rights under Articles 8 and 10, applying the test of proportionality to each. In performing this parallel analysis neither Article 8 nor Article 10 has precedence over the other. Lead case: McKennitt v Ash [2008] QB 73, [40].

stem: A French European Commissioner is involved in a heated debate with his English colleague over further European integration. The English Commissioner tries to explain to the French Commissioner the principle of parliamentary sovereignty, which makes it the supreme law-making body when compared to all other government institutions. The French commissioner asks the English commissioner on which legal authority this supremacy is based?
ask: Which option best informs the French Commissioner in respect of the basis of parliamentary sovereignty in the UK?

options.en: The principle of parliamentary sovereignty is established by the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949
The principle of parliamentary sovereignty is established by the separation of powers
The principle of parliamentary sovereignty is established by the Royal prerogative
The principle of parliamentary sovereignty is established by The Statute of Westminster 1931
The principle of parliamentary sovereignty is established by a basic and inherent common law rule of the UK Constitution

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. There is no Act that establishes the principle of parliamentary sovereignty, nor is there case law that can be cited as the origin of the principle. Parliamentary sovereignty is simply a basic and inherent common law rule of the UK Constitution that itself forms part of the UK Constitution.....ute of

stem: MortgageCo is in the process of selling a property as mortgagee in possession to a woman. You are acting for the woman and, on checking the title to the property, you see that MortgageCo's charge ranks after a first charge to BankCo and before a third charge to SubPrime Finance. You have been instructed by your client that she wishes to purchase the property free from any charges.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: You will be required to obtain an undertaking from MortgageCo's solicitor that he will redeem all of the charges
You will be required to obtain an undertaking from MortgageCo's solicitor that he will redeem the charge to BankCo
You will be required to obtain an undertaking from MortgageCo's solicitor that he will redeem the charges to BankCo and SubPrime Finance
You will be required to obtain an undertaking from MortgageCo's solicitor that he will redeem the charge to SubPrime Finance
You will not be required to obtain any undertakings from MortgageCo's solicitor in relation to the redemption of any charges

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. You will be required to obtain an undertaking from MortgageCo's solicitor that he will redeem the charge to BankCo. Section 104 of the Law of Property Act 1925 provides that a transfer by MortgageCo will overreach the charge to SubPrime Finance, because it ranks in priority to the charge to MortgageCo. However, MortgageCo cannot overreach the charge to BankCo, because that charge ranks in priority to the one to BankCo and will therefore have to be redeemed.

stem: A cricket ball was hit over a 17 foot high fence, travelled 100 yards, and hit a woman who was standing on the footpath outside her house. The cricket club claims that this had happened only six times in the past thirty years and this was the first time anybody had actually been struck.
ask: What is the woman's likelihood of success if she claims compensation?

options.en: The woman's likelihood of success is good, because an accident of this sort calls for an explanation, and the cricket club has a duty to take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which would be likely to injure its neighbour
The woman's likelihood of success is good, because the cricket club was aware of the potential risk so the accident was foreseeable
The woman's likelihood of success is good, because applying the legal maxim of res ipsa loquitur, the cricket club was clearly negligent
The woman's likelihood of success is slim, because there was no evidence of any injury in the previous 30 years, so there was no negligence now

The woman's likelihood of success is slim, because the risk was so remote and the cost of reducing it so high, that it would not be reasonable for the cricket club to provide any further safeguards than it did already.

explanation.en: E is correct. In Bolton v Stone [1951] the House of Lords held, on similar facts that the risk was too remote for the reasonable person to contemplate. Further on grounds of public policy, the court was loath to place further restriction on normal every day activities such as playing cricket. Lead case: Bolton v Stone [1951]1 All ER 1078.

stem: A man needs some groceries, but it is raining and he therefore decides to take his brother's car. Since his brother is not at home, and he has previously given the man permission to borrow the car, he takes the keys and drives the car to the supermarket. The man returns a couple of hours later to find that his brother has called the police, reporting the car stolen.
ask: Which option best describes the man's criminal liability, if any?

options.en: Since the man only briefly borrowed the car there can be no intention to permanently deprive
Since the car belonged to the man's brother and he has borrowed it in the past, his action cannot be seen as theft
Since the man did not damage the car in any way, and returned it as he found it, he is not criminally liable
Now that it has been reported to the police, he must be charged with theft, and it is for the jury to decide if the man is criminally liable
The man is unlikely to be charged with theft, but may be charged with taking the vehicle without the owner's consent

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Criminal liability for theft is unlikely in this example, because the man appears to honestly believe that his brother would have consented to his taking the car, and there does not appear to be any intention to permanently deprive. It is possible, however, that the man could be charged with taking a vehicle without the owner's consent (TWOC). If he has not stolen the vehicle with the intention to permanently deprive the owner his act falls outside of the scope of Section 1 of the Theft Act 1968. The fundamental element of the TWOC offence is taking without consent, as this does not require the intention to permanently deprive and could refer to the man who has taken the vehicle with the intention

stem: A British soldier was killed while serving in Germany. The German coroner recorded death by misadventure. The soldier's family in the UK are dissatisfied with the verdict and wish to challenge it in Strasbourg.
ask: Which option best advises the family?

options.en: Complaints are always lodged against a contracting state, but there is a provision for contracting states to complain against other contracting states
Complaints are always lodged against a contracting state, and there is no provision for contracting states to complain against other contracting states
Complaints are always lodged against a contracting state, but there is a provision for contracting states to complain against other individuals
Complaints are never lodged against a contracting state, because there is a provision for contracting states to complain against its own institutions, in this case the British Army
Complaints by individuals are never lodged against a contracting state, but there is a provision for contracting States to complain against other contracting states

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Complaints are always lodged against a contracting state. However, there is a provision for contracting states to complain against other contracting states. Typically, however, complaints are lodged by natural or legal persons against a contracting state.

stem: The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of a company is approached by the Financial Director, who informs the CEO that the company is near insolvency and recommends that the company goes into voluntary liquidation. The CEO, who owns the majority shareholding in the company, is concerned that her investment will be lost if it goes into liquidation and arranges for all the company's real estate holdings to be transferred to her husband. The husband is aware that her intention to transfer the real estate holdings is to put those assets out of the reach of the company's creditors in the event of its liquidation.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The CEO, Financial Director and CEO's husband could be ordered by the court to make such contributions to the company's assets as the court thinks fit
The CEO and Financial Director could be ordered by the court to make such contributions to the company's assets as the court thinks fit
The CEO and her husband could be ordered by the court to make such contributions to the company's assets as the court thinks fit
The husband of the CEO and the Financial Director could be ordered by the court to make such contributions to the company's assets as the court thinks fit

Neither the CEO, her husband nor the Financial Director could be ordered by the court to make such contributions to the company's assets as the court thinks fit; the company has separate legal personality

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Although the company has a legal personality separate to the CEO and Financial Director as its directors and members, there are some circumstances where the so-called "veil of incorporation" can be lifted by the courts. Section 213 of the Insolvency Act 1986 provides that the court may order any person, who is knowingly a party to the carrying on of business with the intention of defrauding the company's creditors, to make a contribution to the company's assets in a liquidation. As the CEO and her husband were parties to the fraud, they would be liable to be ordered to make a contribution by the court.

stem: A trustee is responsible for a family trust, which includes as trust property a dilapidated cottage that the trustee wishes to purchase and renovate as a family holiday home. The trust already provides the beneficiaries with an excellent income, and it would be wasteful for the trust to spend the money necessary to repair the cottage which has fallen into such a state of disrepair. None of the beneficiaries have expressed any interest in the cottage.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trustee can purchase the cottage, because it would not be in the best interests of the beneficiaries to spend money on repairs
The trustee can purchase the cottage in light of the fact that he has been open, fair and honest about his intentions
The trustee can purchase the cottage, because none of the beneficiaries have expressed any interest in it
The trustee can purchase the cottage provided he has disclosed his conflict of interest and the beneficiaries fully accept and freely consent to this
The trustee cannot purchase the cottage even if he discloses his conflict of interest

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The trustee can purchase the cottage provided he has disclosed his conflict of interest and the beneficiaries fully accept and freely consent to this. Generally, however, the self-dealing rule prevents a trustee from purchasing trust property. Any such transaction will thus be voidable, regardless of how open, fair and honest the trustee has been. Only if the fiduciary can show there was full disclosure of the conflict of interest or profit and that the principal beneficiary fully accepted and freely consented to the fiduciary's course of action will the trustees have a defence to being sued for breach of duty (Holder v Holder [1968]).

stem: A man decided to take advantage of London's public bicycle rental scheme, buying a ticket from the machine, which he put in his pocket after hardly glancing at it. When he was half way down a street, the front wheel fell off the bicycle he was riding, causing him to suffer injury. The Greater London Authority (GLA) argues that it is indemnified by a statement on the ticket that states: 'the local authority will not be liable for any accident or damage arising from hire of bike'.
ask: Which option best states, under common law rules, whether the GLA can rely on the clause on the ticket?

options.en: The GLA can rely on the clause on the ticket; the exclusion clause was effectively incorporated, because it was contained in the ticket, which can be regarded as a contractual document
The GLA can rely on the clause on the ticket; a contract had arisen because reasonable notice of the exclusion clause had been given when the ticket was issued
The GLA can rely on the clause on the ticket; tickets are items that a reasonable person would expect to contain contractual terms, and the exclusion clause printed on it was therefore incorporated
The GLA cannot rely on the clause on the ticket; there must have been some act on the part of the man to indicate acceptance of the exclusion clause
The GLA cannot rely on the clause on the ticket; the ticket was a mere receipt

explanation.en: E is correct. According to the case of Chapelton v Barry [1940], the purpose of the ticket was simply to provide evidence for the hirer that he had discharged his obligation to pay for the bicycle. It's true that exclusion of liability for personal injury would be prohibited under section 2(1) Unfair Contract Terms Act (UCTA) 1977. Where UCTA 1977 is engaged in any given multiple-choice question (MCQ), however, the statute is expressly identified in the question (e.g. 'Considering UCTA 1977 etc...') - otherwise common law rules apply. This question is intended to illustrate that terms only bind a party if he or she has been made aware of their existence either before or at the time that the contract is made. Placing the terms on the.... e receipt

stem: Cracking appeared in parts of the structure of a block of flats, and the owner's engineers warned that if an adjacent tree was not removed, the property would need to be underpinned. The council was asked to remove the tree, but although it declined to do so, it did carry out some root pruning.
ask: A new owner acquired the freehold of the property and was forced to carry out underpinning work at a What's your advice to the new owner, who now wishes to bring an action for damages against the council in nuisance?

options.en: Since the damage had occurred during the previous owner's occupation, and the new owner had not been able to show that any of the remedial work he had carried out had been required because of new damage to the foundations during his time as owner, any claim against the council will be dismissed
Since the only party eligible to sue for damages would be the owner of the property at the time the cracks first appeared, the new owner is not entitled to sue, because ownership had changed hands
The remedial work done by the council was sufficient both to remedy the existing damage from the roots and to safeguard against future damage from the same source

Since the nuisance by encroachment of the roots had continued after the new owner acquired the freehold of the property, he would be able to recover the cost of removing the nuisance, despite the absence of any further physical damage after the date of purchase

The previous owner had failed to maintain the tree, which led to the damage to the new owner's property; therefore, the council did not have a sufficient degree of control over the hazard causing the nuisance for liability to attach

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. If a claimant can show a continuing nuisance, protests to the defendant that the nuisance is continuing to cause physical damage to the claimant's property and the defendant refuses to prevent that nuisance causing further physical damage to the claimant's property, the claimant can recover damages for the whole cost of whatever remedial works may be necessary to prevent future damage, even if there has been a change of ownership. Lead case: Delaware Mansions Ltd v Westminster City Council [2002] 1 AC 321.

stem: A man owns a large farm with two fields, each has a house on it. The first house ("first house") is routinely accessed by a main driveway running through the field of the other house (retained by the man) to the highway. The man sells the field with the first house a poultry farmer. The deed grants an express easement over an alternative access way that the man is constructing, but in wet weather, the alternative access is impassable by the poultry farmer's wagons, and he begins to use the main driveway, crossing through the field that has been retained by the man to access the first house in the field that he purchased from the man.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The poultry farmer has the benefit of an easement implied by necessity to use the driveway
The poultry farmer has the benefit of an easement implied by common intention to use the driveway
The poultry farmer has an easement by implied grant to use the driveway
The poultry farmer has an easement conferred by the Law of Property Act 1925 to use the driveway
The poultry farmer does not have the benefit of any easement to use the driveway

explanation.en: You did not select the best answer. The best answer is C. The poultry farmer has an easement acquired by implied grant under Wheeldon v Burrows to use the driveway. The poultry farmer does not have an easement of necessity, as he has an alternative access route granted by the express easement. The fact that an alternative access route was designated by the deed precludes the poultry farmer from raising a claim that there was a common intention that he be granted an easement over the drive. However, the requirements of the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows would be satisfied, since the driveway was used for the benefit of the first house before the disposition of the field (as the other access has not been constructed), it was continuous

stem: The Prime Minister (PM) is set to reshuffle his cabinet, with a number of senior positions to be reallocated. One of those Ministers that have been shifted out is the head of the Ministry of Justice (MoJ).
ask: The PM must choose a new Minister to head the MoJ and prior to his swearing in ceremony asks what the official role of his new Which option best advises the PM?

options.en: The Ministry of Justice is a ministerial department headed by the Lord Chancellor
The Ministry of Justice is a ministerial department headed by the Secretary of State for Justice
The Ministry of Justice is a ministerial department headed by the Lord Chancellor and his deputy the Secretary of State for Justice
The Ministry of Justice is a ministerial department headed by the Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice who is one and the same person
The Ministry of Justice is a ministerial department headed jointly by separate individuals who are the Lord Chancellor and the Secretary of State for Justice respectively

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. The Ministry of Justice is a ministerial department headed by the Secretary of State for Justice and Lord Chancellor (combined roles). The full title of the position is: "Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice". The ministry was formed in 2007 when some functions of the Home Secretary were combined with the now defunct Department for Constitutional Affairs. The latter had replaced the Lord Chancellor's Department in 2003. The Ministry of Justice is responsible for courts, prisons, probation and constitutional affairs. It oversees the justice system by what it terms 'pathways to justice'. It is also vested with responsibility of protecting the public through into society. The department is also responsible for some areas of constitutional policy (those which were not transferred in 2010 to the Deputy Prime Minister).

stem: You have rendered a bill to your client for £1,000.00 plus VAT (£200.00). Three months later, you are advised that your client has fled the country. You decide to write off the debt.
ask: Which of the following represents the correct tax position and the accounting entries you should make at this immediate moment in time?

options.en: You are always eligible to claim VAT relief so should debit the bad debts and HMRC ledgers as against the client's ledger account: Debit bad debts ledger office account (£1,000.00) Credit client ledger office account (£1,000.00) Debit HMRC ledger office account (£200.00) Credit client ledger office account (£200.00)

You will never be able to reclaim the VAT so need to debit the profit costs only in the bad debts account as against the client's ledger account: Debit bad debts ledger office account (£1,000.00) Credit client's ledger office account (£1,000.00)

You are not yet able to claim VAT relief as the debt is less than six months old, so must debit the profit costs only in the bad debts account as against the client's ledger account: Debit bad debts ledger office account (£1,000.00) Credit client ledger office account (£1,000.00)

You are not yet able to claim VAT relief as the debt is less than six months old, so must debit the whole amount in the bad debts account as against the client's ledger account until you become eligible: Debit bad debts ledger office account (£1,200.00) Credit client ledger office account (£1,200.00)

You are able to claim VAT relief as the debt is less than six months old, so must debit the whole amount in the bad debts account as against the client's ledger account and credit the VAT from the bad debts account as against the HMRC account: Debit bad debts ledger office account (£1,200.00) Credit client ledger office account (£1,200.00) Debit HMRC ledger office account (£200.00) Credit bad debts office account (£200.00)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. You are not yet able to claim VAT relief as the debt is less than six months old, so must debit the whole amount in the bad debts account as against the client's ledger account until you become eligible. VAT relief can be claimed on debts that are between six months and four years and six months old. You need to comply with HMRC requirements in respect of your accounting records, so must debit the whole amount in the bad debts ledger. When the time comes, you then credit the HMRC claimable from the bad debts account.

stem: A woman took delivery of a car under a contract of hire-purchase and, mistakenly thinking that she had a right to sell it as long as she continued to pay the instalments, sold the car to A man. The man sold the car to a lawyer, who then sold it on to a farmer, who sold it in turn to an old woman. After the old woman had had the use of the car for almost a year, she received notification from the original hire-purchase dealers claiming delivery up to them of the vehicle.
ask: With reference to the Sale of Goods Act 1979 (SGA), would the old woman be entitled to recover the whole purchase price?

options.en: The old woman would be entitled to recover the whole purchase price, but the woman who originally took delivery of the car would be entitled to set off anything for the near one year use of the car which the old woman had enjoyed
The old woman would be allowed to recover the full purchase price, but the farmer would be entitled to set off anything for the near one year use of the car which the old woman had enjoyed
The old woman would be entitled to recover the whole purchase price, because she did not receive any part of that which she contracted to receive

The old woman would not be entitled to recover the whole purchase price, because the implied condition in every sale of goods contract - that the seller has this right at the time when property is to pass - does not apply to a private purchaser
The old woman would not be entitled to recover the whole purchase price, because she has since used the car in the one year intervening period so too much time has elapsed

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The old woman would be entitled to recover the full purchase price, as the defendant had been in breach of s 12(1) SGA. Lead case: Butterworth v Kingsway Motors [1954] 1 WLR 1286. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 12(1) Sale of Goods Act 1979.

stem: A man is interested in creating a discretionary trust. He has three nephews. He appoints a trustee to his trust.
ask: With which of the following formulae will the man need to follow to succeed in creating a discretionary trust?

options.en: "I give to my trustee £150,000 to hold for such of my three nephews as he, at his absolute discretion, shall select to benefit"
"I give to my trustee £150,000 to hold for my first nephew, should he obtain a 2:1 degree in his LL.B exam"
"I give to my trustee £150,000 to divide between my three nephews"
"I give to my trustee £150,000 to divide between my three nephews provided they agree to the division"
"I give to my trustee £150,000 to hold for my second nephew for life and then to my first nephew"

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. A discretionary trust is a trust under which the trustees are given discretion as to who, within a class chosen by the settlor, should receive trust property and how much each should receive. A beneficiary under a discretionary trust has no enforceable right to any part of the property or its income, although the trustees must consider the claims together with those of the other beneficiaries. Only in (A) will a discretionary trust be created, because the trustee can select who is to benefit from the property. (B) creates a contingent interest, while (E) creates an interest in remainder, but it is fixed. The interest in (C) and (D) is also fixed to be divided between the three

stem: When two women and a man set up a solicitors' practice in partnership three years ago, the two women contributed £100,000 each in cash to the partnership's funds, and the man introduced an office building worth £300,000. The two women propose that an additional office is opened to act as a conveyancing office, with the firm branching out into estate agency work and an additional conveyancing solicitor being employed to deal with the additional work, but the man opposes all of these proposals. They have no formal partnership deed in place.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: A unanimous decision of all partners would be required in order to implement all of these measures
The two women could overrule the man regarding the employment of an additional solicitor, but not regarding the new office or the decision to trade as an estate agency
The two women could overrule the man regarding the employment of an additional solicitor and the new office, but not the decision to trade as an estate agency
The two women could overrule the man regarding all of the measures
A simple majority of partners would be required to implement all of these measures according to each partner's capital contributions

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. A simple majority of partners is required to make decisions regarding "ordinary matters" ', but a unanimous decision of all partners is required to change the nature of the partnership business. In all cases, each partner has one vote and voting power is not determined with regard to each partner's capital contributions to the business. As the employment of an additional solicitor and opening of a new office would be regarded as "ordinary matters", the two women would have a simple majority to implement these changes without the man's consent. However, the change in type of partnership business from a solicitor's practice to a mixed solicitor's practice and

stem: A new Protocol is mooted to the European Convention on Human Rights ("the Convention"). The proposed Protocol will have the effect of creating a freestanding right to free school milk for children when it is signed by sufficient states. The Education Secretary is unsure whether the government will sign the Protocol once it enters into force and seeks legal advice.
ask: Which option best advises the Minister how Protocols are domestically incorporated into law, if at all?

options.en: Protocols which add rights to the Convention are binding on those Member States that have signed them
Protocols which add rights to the Convention are automatically incorporated into the Human Rights Act 1998
A Member State must sign and ratify a protocol before it will be bound by its provisions
Once a contracting Member State signs a protocol, it will be incorporated in to the Human Rights Act 1998
A Member State that signs a protocol may be bound by its provisions upon ratification

explanation.en: ~ tocol once it You did not select the correct answer. C is the best option. A Member State must sign and ratify a protocol before it will be bound by its provisions. A Protocol to the Convention is a text which adds one or more rights to the original Convention or amends certain of its provisions. Protocols which add rights to the Convention are binding only on those Member States that have signed and ratified them; a State that has merely signed a Protocol without ratifying it will not be bound by its provisions. Note that option E is incorrect, as the Member State will (not may) be bound by the Protocol's provisions when it signs and ratifies it.

stem: A woman is thinking about buying a 50-acre freehold property. When she is looking around the land, she notices a track running across one of the outer fields. The estate agent tells her that he thinks that the neighbouring property enjoys an easement over the field to gain access to the public highway.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The easement would be protected by way of a Restriction in the Charges Register
The easement would be protected by way of a Notice in the Charges Register
The easement would be protected by way of a Restriction in the Proprietorship Register
The easement would be protected by way of a Notice in the Proprietorship Register
The easement would be protected by way of a Notice in the Property Register

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The easement would be protected by way of a Notice in the Charges Register. As the easement is an encumbrance on the estate, the entry would appear in the Charges Register. Restrictions only appear in the Proprietorship Register as a means of restricting the proprietor's ability to deal with the land.

stem: A man was brought to trial in 1996 as the result of a misguided private prosecution initiated on behalf of a murder victim's family. The defendant was acquitted on the judge's direction, because of insufficient evidence. New DNA evidence subsequently came to light this year, strongly implicating the man in the murder.
ask: Which of the following is the best answer?

options.en: The Court of Appeal must order a re-trill if there is new and compelling evidence and it is in the interests of justice for such an order to be made
The Supreme Court must order a re-trial if there is new and compelling evidence and it is in the interests of justice for such an order to be made
The High Court (Queen's Bench Division) must order a re-trial if there is new and compelling evidence and it is in the interests of justice for such an order to be made
A prosecution would be barred under the common law principle known as autrefois acquit, more commonly referred to as the rule against double jeopardy
A prosecution would be barred under the common law principle known as habeas corpus, more commonly referred to as the rule against double jeopardy

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. A prosecution would have been barred under the old common law principle known as autrefois acquit, more commonly referred to as the rule against double jeopardy. The Macpherson inquiry in to the death of Stephen Lawrence in 1999 recommended that the ancient principle of double jeopardy should be reconsidered. The law was changed in the Criminal Justice Act 2003 and brought in to force in 2005. The law now states that the court of appeal must order a re-trial if there is new and compelling evidence and it is in the interests of justice for such an order to be made. Criminal Justice Act 2003.

stem: A man was informally hired as a labour only sub-contractor by a company who had responsibility for hiring and dismissing him. Although he did have to follow the company's directions regarding what to do and when to do it, he was neither on the 'books', nor were deductions made for tax and National Insurance purposes. He was seriously injured at work, and would like to claim against the company for his injuries, but this depends on whether he was an employee or an independent contractor.
ask: Which option best describes the man's status?

options.en: company
If the hirer can dismiss the worker and tell him what to do and where to do it, he is an independent contractor, and therefore entitled to claim damages against the company

If the hirer can dismiss the worker and tell him what to do and where to do it, he is independent contractor, and therefore not entitled to claim damages against the company; otherwise it would be open to anyone to decide how he was to sell his labour

If the hirer can dismiss the worker and tell him what to do and where to do it, he is an employee, and therefore entitled to claim damages against the company, because the question of liability is determined by the agreement between the hirer and the worker

If the hirer can dismiss the worker and tell him what to do and where to do it, he is an employee, but he is not entitled to claim damages against the company, because it would be contrary to public policy to allow a man to say that he was self-employed for the purposes of tax avoidance and then an employee for the purpose of claiming compensation

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. In the case of: Ferguson v John Dawson (1976) the Court of Appeal held that whatever label was put on the parties' relationship, other factors must be considered, such as whether the hirer could dismiss the workers and tell them what to do and where to do it. Even the express declaration of the parties regarding the nature of their contract, therefore, is but one factor to take in to account, despite the arrangements voluntarily entered into. Accordingly the worker was an employee of the company which was therefore liable to pay him damages. Lead case: Ferguson v John Dawson & Partners -- **г

stem: Your client asks you to make contact with a third party who you know is represented by another solicitor. The third party's solicitor has refused to pass on messages to his client that you have communicated to him. Which of the following statements best describes what the solicitor may
ask: do in such a?

options.en: The solicitor may not communicate directly with the other party, because the third party is separately represented
The solicitor may not communicate directly with the other party, because the name and address of his legal representative is known to the solicitor
The solicitor may not communicate directly with the third party, because exceptional circumstances for initiating direct contact do not exist

The solicitor may contact the third party directly only to request the name and address of the other party's legal representative

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is (D), according to rule IB11. 4. This is allowed in exceptional circumstances, such as where the other party's legal representative has refused to pass on messages to his client, provided that in such a situation, a warning letter is sent to the legal representative before contacting the represented third party, giving the

stem: The common law courts were the King's courts and only through them could the King decide questions of title to land and punish felonies. Yet the King possessed a residual power of administering justice through his Council where the courts of common law were insufficient.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes how the common law system?

options.en: The common law was developed by judges through decisions of courts and similar tribunals
The common law was developed through legislative statutes or executive branch action
The common law was developed by convention through Royal Proclamation of the King's Council
The common law was developed by constitutional conventions and the royal prerogative
The common law was developed by historical royal prerogative and international treaties

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The common law system developed by judges through decisions of courts and similar tribunals, rather than through legislative statutes or executive branch actions.

stem: A colleague is struggling to complete a VAT calculation and asks for your advice. He wants to know how much VAT needs to be paid over to Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC). The company has sold £1,000 ex VAT in the month and has purchased £300 ex VAT. VAT rate is 20%.
ask: Which option best states the amount of VAT that should be paid?

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. £140. The amount of tax collected would be £200 (20% of £1,000) and the amount paid would be £60 (20% of £300); therefore, the amount that remains to be paid for VAT is £140.

stem: A far-right group is planning a march in a neighbouring county. Emotions are running high, because the Boundary Commission is planning to merge the two counties concerned. The police foresee a real potential for disorder if the march is allowed to take place.
ask: Which option best states the legal position?

options.en: The march may be banned for a period of 28 days
An order to ban a public procession may only be made by the local authority acting independently
Two police officers of the rank of Superintendent (or above) must agree that an order to ban a public procession is appropriate
An order to ban a public procession must be confirmed by the Home Secretary
There is no power to ban a public procession under the Public Law Act 1986

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. A Chief Constable must apply to the local authority for a banning order; to prevent the march going ahead at all, if he/she is satisfied that imposition of conditions on a march will not be sufficient to prevent serious public disorder. The local authority must obtain the consent of the Home Secretary before issuing the order. While this latter step arguably offers protection for the individual, because it involves an independent look at all of the issues and less local bias, it could be argued that the Home Secretary is a political figure and therefore the decision should be made by a more impartial figure, such as a judge.

stem: The Royal Angling Alliance (RAA) was established by statute to determine whether fishing is permissible or prohibited as to all lakes and watercourses and to regulate such use when it is permitted. The RAA has a committee of seven members, all of whom are selected by the Secretary of State for the Environment. Instead of making decisions about angling use itself, the RAA has decided that it should follow the views of the Royal Countryside Trust (RCT) concerning all lakes and watercourses within its Identify which principle of judicial review
ask: is raised by the RAA's decision?

options.en: No principle of judicial review is raised, because the RCT is not a public body amenable to judicial review
The RAA's decision raises an issue of illegality, because it has fettered its discretion
The RAA's decision raises an issue of procedural impropriety, because it failed to give adequate reasons
The RAA's decision raises an issue of irrationality, because it failed to act reasonably
The RAA's decision raises an issue of procedural impropriety, because it has acted in a biased manner

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The scenario raises an issue of fettering of discretion. A public body or tribunal is not entitled to fetter the exercise of its discretion. Lead case: Port of London Authority, ex p Kynoch Ltd [1919] 1 KB 176.

stem: A woman was watching a live television broadcast of a football match when the roof of the stand behind the goal collapsed due to its shoddy construction. The woman's son was at the match, and while the TV pictures did not show the suffering of recognisable individuals, she reasonably feared that he was one of those reportedly killed or injured. Seven hours later she identified the body of her son after making her way to the mortuary, and is now suffering from nervous shock.
ask: Which option best advises the woman as to a possible psychiatric injury claim?

options.en: Her claim would be rejected, since she must have been present at the accident or its immediate aftermath

Since she viewed the possible death of her son live on television relay, suffered a sudden appreciation by sight or sound of a horrifying event, and was sufficiently close in space and time to the accident concerned, the woman would qualify as a secondary victim

Since the woman was so close in space and time to the accident concerned or its immediate aftermath when she viewed her son's body in the mortuary, there was a sufficiently direct connection for the woman to qualify as a secondary victim

By viewing the disaster on live television and seeing her son's body in the mortuary, the woman would be entitled to recover damages as a secondary victim, since, taken together, these constituted a single incident
Since it was the woman's son that was killed, she qualifies as a primary victim

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Since she viewed the events only through the "third- party" medium of television, the woman would be too far removed from the shocking events to be within the "immediate aftermath" to qualify as a secondary victim. Lead case: Alcock v. Chief Constable of South Yorkshire 1992 1AC 310.

stem: A man owns two shops which are on opposite sides of the street; he runs a fishmonger's business from one of the shops and lets the other shop.
ask: He decides to sell the other shop to a developer and includes a covenant in the transfer to "use the premises as anything other than a fishmonger." A fishmonger is considering purchasing the shop from the developer to set up a business to rival the property Would the fishmonger be bound by the covenant?

options.en: The fishmonger would be bound by the covenant
The fishmonger would not be bound by the covenant, because it is of a positive nature
The fishmonger would not be bound by the covenant, because it does not benefit land retained by the covenantee
The fishmonger would not be bound by the covenant, because it does not touch and concern the covenantee's land
The fishmonger would be bound by the covenant. because it was made with the intent to bind the servient land

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. The fishmonger would be bound by the covenant. The covenant is of a negative nature as it prevents the use of the land for a single purpose, but does not impose an obligation to use it for anything. The man (property owner) has retained land which the covenant touches and concerns (the business conducted on the land would be injured as a result of such close competition) and the covenant binds successive owners of the servient land due to the effect of s.79 Law of Property Act 1925.

stem: Two people are members and directors of a private limited company, each owning 50% each of the issued share capital. They conduct all business by informal discussion, and without formal minutes of meetings being taken. After the company's accounts have been finalised, the members/directors decide to pay themselves a generous dividend out of the company's profits. Six months later, they sell the company to a competitor, but after reviewing the company's records, the CEO of the acquiring company notices that there is no record of a resolution having been passed to approve the dividend, and requests that the members/directors repay the dividend.
ask: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.en: A resolution is required to approve a dividend; the dividend paid to the members/directors is unlawful and must be repaid
A resolution is not required to approve a dividend; but the dividend paid to the members/directors is still unlawful and must be repaid
A resolution is required to approve a dividend; but the dividend paid to the members/directors is lawful and does not need to be repaid
A resolution is not required to approve a dividend; the dividend paid to the members/directors is lawful and does not need to be repaid
All resolutions must be approved by a unanimous resolution of the members and board of directors

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. A resolution of the members is required to approve a dividend and this resolution must be proposed by the board of directors. However, the dividend paid to the members/directors would be lawful as a result of the Duomatic Principle, which stipulates that where all members entitled to attend a general meeting assent to a matter which could be approved by a resolution passed by such a meeting, then the matter will be approved, notwithstanding that no formal resolution was passed. This is the case in this scenario, since the members/directors are the only members of the company and both assented to the payment of the dividend.

stem: A family trust's solicitor and bank advise the trustees against selling trust property after being requested to do so by a beneficiary. The beneficiary is insistent, however, and her children, who are just 18 years old, give their written consent to the sale. The trustees then sell the trust property. After the beneficiary dies, the trust fund goes to the children, who now discover that the trust is worth very little.
ask: The children sue the Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trustees have acted with reasonable care and skill, because they are not professional trustees
The trustees have acted properly, because they are not required to preserve any of the trust fund for the remaindermen
The trustees have acted properly, because all of the beneficiaries have consented to the breach of trust
The trustees have acted properly, because they have acted honestly and reasonably
The trustees have not acted with reasonable care and skill and have breached the trust by selling the trust property

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The trustees have not acted with reasonable care and skill and have breached the trust by selling the trust property. Although we are given no information that they are professional trustees, they have not met the standard of the ordinary prudent man of business. The facts are similar to those in In Re Pauling's Settlement Trust [1964] Ch 303 and Head v Gould [1898] 2 CH 250, where the trustees breached the trust by giving into the persistent demands of the life interest for money. The trustees must also preserve the trust fund for the remaindermen. The beneficiaries appear to have consented to the breach, but there must be doubt about whether the remaindermen freely consented,). Moreover, s. 61 would not help the trustees reduce their liability. They have not acted honestly and reasonably as they have ignored expert advice: (Re Evans). Equitable compensation would thus demand that the trustees restore the trust fund, by reinstating the value of the houses. It is also likely that the courts would impound the estate of the beneficiary, if there is anything left to impound.

stem: The (fictitious) Immigration Act 2012 (the Act) precluded the right to silence and imposed a reverse burden of proof on truck drivers who, knowingly or not, imported illegal immigrants in to the UK, concealed within their vehicles. A driver was arrested and charged for transporting illegals under the Act. He is considering instituting separate proceedings against the UK Government for breaching his right to a fair trial under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention).
ask: Which option best states the time limits, if any, imposed by the Human Rights Act (HRA) 1998 on the driver to institute separate proceedings?

options.en: Separate proceedings must be brought within three months (or less) of the date on which the act complained of took place, or after a longer period, if the court or tribunal judges that to be fair under the circumstances

Separate proceedings must be brought within six-months (or less) of the date on which the act complained of took place, or after a longer period, if the court or tribunal judges that to be fair under the circumstances

Separate proceedings must be brought within one year (or less) of the date on which the act complained of took place, or after a longer period, if the court or tribunal judges that to be fair under the circumstances

Separate proceedings must be brought within three years (or less) of the date on which the act complained of took place, or after a longer period, if the court or tribunal judges that to be fair under the circumstances

There are no time limits, because the requirement under the Human Rights Act 1998 that statutes must be read and given effect in a way that is compatible with Convention rights applies to all legislation, whenever enacted

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Cases in which a person complains that a public authority has acted in a way that is incompatible with Convention rights must be brought within one year beginning with the date on which the act complained of took place. That period can be extended by the court if it considers it equitable to do so. That means that there would need to be good grounds for an extension of time. The court will consider all the facts that are relevant. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 7(5) HRA 1998.

stem: A woman is the fee simple owner of a seaside chalet and agrees with a man that he can purchase the chalet from her at any time within the next 10 years. They record the agreement in a document which compiles in all respects with the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989 (LPA), but which is not executed as a deed.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The man has a legal interest in the chalet and this interest binds third parties in accordance with the Doctrine of Notice
The man has an equitable interest in the chalet and this interest binds third parties in accordance with the doctrine of notice
The man has a legal interest in the chalet and this interest binds all third parties
The man has an equitable interest in the chalet and this interest binds all third parties
The man has no interest in the chalet, as this was not created by deed

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The man has an equitable interest in the chalet and this interest binds third parties in accordance with the doctrine of notice. The man has the benefit of an Option which is an equitable interest registrable as a Class C(iv) Land Charge or using a Notice in registered land. An Option is not capable of being a legal interest (see s.1(2) LPA) and can therefore only exist in equity. There is, therefore, no requirement for an interest to be created by deed for it to be validly created.

stem: Your client, a financial director for a company, is looking at improving the company's public relations as well as reducing its taxable liabilities. Gift Aid has been recommended to him as a means of achieving this. He is seeking an explanation of what Gift Aid actually is and how it might best be utilised.
ask: Which of the following best describes the use of Gift Aid?

options.en: Any form of giving which does not result in a financial benefit to the company will qualify as Gift Aid
Gift Aid donations are counted as non-trade charges on income, therefore reducing the tax liability
Gift Aid involves making donations to a registered charity only
Gift Aid needs to be approved by her Majesty's Revenue and Customs (MRC) before it can be claimed
Gift Aid is concerned with individuals' corporations claim donations

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The charitable donations are classified against income when Gift Aid is claimed, thus reducing the amount that will be chargeable to tax.

stem: A firm is authorised by the Solicitors Regulation Authority to carry out non- mainstream regulated activities. The firm sends out a monthly marketing journal to its clients.
ask: The journal editor is interested in including a section entitled "Market Selection - Buy These Shares!" Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The proposed section constitutes a real time communication and requires the approval of an authorised third person ("ATP")
The proposed section constitutes a real time communication and requires the approval of the general manager of the solicitor's firm before it can be circulated by the firm to the firm's clients
The proposed section constitutes a real time communication and can therefore be circulated to the firm's clients without prior approval of its contents
The proposed section constitutes a non-real time communication and requires the approval of an ATP
The proposed section constitutes a non-real time communication and requires the approval of the general manager of the solicitor's firm before it can be circulated by the firm to the firm's clients

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is (D). The section in the journal will constitute a non-real time (written) communication. Section 21 Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 prohibits a solicitor who is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority from making a financial promotion, unless its contents are approved by an authorised or exempt person. The exclusion for non-real time incidental financial promotions would not seem to apply. - costumen unu requires

stem: You act for a supplier that has just contracted with the sales agent of a company on a transaction. Negotiations resulted in your supplier client agreeing to supply materials to the company for £325,000 instead of the sales manager's offer of £300,000. It since transpires that the sales manager only had authority to negotiate up to £300,000, and that he made this clear at the start of negotiations, but your client thought it was a negotiation tactic and ignored it. The company argues it is not bound by the contract and your client wants to know its legal position and remedies.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: The company is not bound by the contract, because the agent exceeded his actual authority by agreeing to a figure above his negotiation limit
The company is not bound by the contract, because your client's knowledge of the agent's limit on negotiation authority means that it was acting in bad faith
The company is bound by the contract, because your client's knowledge of the agent's limit on negotiation authority is not sufficient for it to be acting in bad faith
The company is bound by the contract, because the agent's negotiation authority is just a tactic and is not considered a limitation of authority
The company is not bound by the contract, because an agent cannot enter into contracts on behalf of the company; it must be a director

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The company is bound by the contract, because your client's knowledge of the agent's limit on negotiation authority is not sufficient for it to be acting in bad faith. Under Section 40(1) of the Companies Act 2006, the power of the directors to bind a company, or authorise others to do so, is deemed to be free of any limitation under the company's constitution. The company's constitution, by way of model articles, has no specific provision limiting negotiation authority of directors or agents - instead conferring very wide powers on the directors to run the company - so this is a limit created on the agent, and in accordance with the company's constitution. Even if there was a constitutional limit, the provisions of Section 40(1) would not mean this extricates a company from a contract entered into in excess of such limitations. Turning to Section 40(2), a person dealing with a company is not to be regarded as acting in bad faith by reason only of knowing that an act is beyond the powers of the directors under the company's constitution.
