stem: A woman has a rare exotic parrot, which she feels she is neglecting due to work commitments. Her friend suggests that she would be able to take better care of the parrot, since she is at home more often. The woman gives the bird to her friend, who sold the parrot to an exotic bird breeder.
ask: How is appropriation defined under the Theft Act 1968?

options.en: An authorised assumption of the owner's rights amounts to appropriation
An authorised assumption of the owner's rights does not amount to appropriation
Only a dishonest assumption of the owner's rights amounts to appropriation
Appropriation must be made with a view to gain
Appropriation must be made for the thief's own benefit

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. As defined in Section 3 in the Theft Act 1968, appropriation is the acquiring of owner rights over property which is not the rightful property of the individual appropriating the property. Section 3 states: "Any assumption by a person of the rights of an owner amounts to an appropriation and this includes where he has come by the property (innocently or not) without stealing it, any later assumption of a right to it by keeping or dealing with it as an owner" Crucially, it should be noted that, in dealing with appropriation, no intent is necessary and the property could have been appropriated innocently. Statute: s.3 (1) Theft Act 1968

stem: Acting on intelligence that anti-capitalist demonstrators were planning to gather in Leicester Square before going on to vandalise selected targets in the capital, the police cordoned off all exits, trapping, or "kettling," within it a large number of demonstrators as well as shoppers and cinema goers. A woman, who was with the demonstrators, asked that she be allowed out of the cordon in order to collect her child from its kindergarten. The police refused and the woman now wishes to sue the police for the tort of false imprisonment.
ask: Did the police act lawfully in holding her in the square?

options.en: It is unlawful to use 'kettling' as a crowd control tactic, even if they are likely to become violent, if innocent shoppers have been caught up in the police cordon
It is unlawful to use 'kettling' as a crowd control tactic, even if they are likely to become violent, if no offence has actually been committed
It is lawful for the police to use 'kettling' as a crowd control tactic if demonstrators are likely to become violent

It is unlawful for the police to use 'kettling' as a crowd control tactic, because it breaches English common law's traditional role of protecting individual liberties over promoting collective security
It is unlawful for the police to use 'kettling' as a crowd control tactic, because it breaches demonstrators' human right of not having a representative of the State interfering with their liberty

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. Crowd control measures adopted by police in order to prevent a breach of public order, which result in several thousand people being confined within a police cordon for several hours, do not amount to a violation of the right to liberty if the measures are used in good faith, are proportionate and are enforced for no longer than is reasonably necessary. LEAD CASE: Austin (FC) (Appellant) & another v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis (Respondent), [2009] UKHL 5. moving u repromur of the

stem: An airline company is seeking an injunction restraining the cabin crews' trade union from calling strike action over pay and conditions, because it says, the action will inconvenience passengers and the airline company stands to lose millions of pounds, threatening its very existence. The strike action is due to go ahead next week, which is the start of a busy holiday period. The airline company claims that collective agreements are in place between it and the union and cite the union leadership's previous statements to the effect that it would do everything to avoid strike action.
ask: Are the collective agreements which the airline company has reached with the trade union legally binding?

options.en: The collective agreements are legally binding, because the consequences of any decision by the union to repudiate its moral responsibilities are matters a court cannot turn a blind eye to

The collective agreements are legally binding, because the collective agreements can only be rebutted by taking account of verbal statements, and the union leadership previously stated that it would do everything to avoid strike action
The collective agreements are legally binding, because collective agreements between trades unions and employers are legally binding, so the union cannot go back on the deal

The collective agreements are not legally binding, because the collective agreements can only be rebutted by looking at the context of the dispute, and although this will inconvenience passengers and threaten the company's future, courts must not stifle a union's right to free association
The collective agreements are not legally binding, because the general common law view is that collective agreements between trade unions and employers are not legally binding between the parties

explanation.en: E is correct. Aspirational agreements such as these are not contracts in the legal sense and are not enforceable at law. Lead case: Ford Motor Co. v AUEFW [1969] 2QB 303. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 179 Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992.

stem: A beneficiary is dissatisfied with the annual income that she receives from her family trust. She asks the trustees for more information upon how the trust fund is invested and why it is producing so little income for her. From the trust accounts, she learns that the whole trust fund is invested in shares in the family property company and in a house where her mother, who is not a beneficiary of the trust, lives.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trustees' investment in the shares of the company is in accordance with their duties and powers of investment, provided the trust instrument requires this
The trustees' investment in the shares of the company and in the property is in accordance with their duties and powers of investment

The trustees' investment in the property is in accordance with their duties and The trustees' investment in the property is in accordance with their duties and powers of investment, provided the trust instrument requires this
The trustees' investment in the shares of the company and in the property is not in accordance with their duties and powers of investment
The trustees' investment in the shares of the company is in accordance with their duties and powers of investment

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is (A). The trustees are generally permitted to make any kind of investment, although if they are professional trustees they will have a higher duty of care. The 'standard investment criteria' apply under the Trustee Act 2000, in particular the need for diversification. Shares in one company do not seem wise, unless the trust instrument itself requires it. The house, on the other hand, would seem to be covered by section 8, which allows investment in land and purchase of land for 'any other reason' (even if not provided for in the trust instrument).

stem: A man aged 35 has been convicted of racially aggravated murder of a woman 16 years ago. He is due to be sentenced following a pre-sentence report. Since he committed the offence, the law has changed, requiring the starting point for a minimum term for racially motivated murder to be 30 years, rather than 15 years as the law stood when the man committed the offence.
ask: With reference to the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention), which option best advises the man?

options.en: The sentence is not limited to the maximum sentence at the date when the offence was committed
It is an absolute right, under the Convention, not to be retrospectively held guilty of a crime for doing something that wasn't criminal when the offence was committed
An offender who was a juvenile when he committed murder must be sentenced to detention at Her Majesty's pleasure in a young offenders' institute
The sentence is limited to the maximum sentence at the date when the judge passes the sentence
The sentence is limited to the maximum sentence at the date when the offence was committed

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Article 7 of the Convention prohibits retrospective punishment, that is, punishment using law which was not applicable at the time of the crime: "(1) No one shall be held guilty of any criminal offence on account of any act or omission which did not constitute a criminal offence under national or international law at the time when it was committed. Nor shall a heavier penalty be imposed than the one that was applicable at the time the criminal offence was committed; and (2) This Article shall not prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognised by civilised norms." Article 7 forbids the imposition of a heavier sentence that was 'applicable' at as long as sentences do not exceed the maximum sentence which could have been imposed at the date the offence was committed. Criminal Justice Act 2003 Schedule 21.

stem: The House of Commons introduced a public bill. The bill was subsequently sent up to the House of Lords. The Lords are refusing to approve the bill by delaying its hearing.
ask: Which option best states the routes, if any, open to the House of Commons?

options.en: The House of Commons cannot pass the bill unless it receives approval from the House of Lords
The House of Commons can send the bill to the monarch after a period of 24 months has elapsed
The House of Commons can reintroduce and pass the bill at the next session without approval from the House of Lords and submitted for Royal Assent
The House of Commons can reintroduce and pass the bill after a general election without approval from the House of Lords and submitted for Royal Assent
The Prime Minister is obliged either to resign, making way for another MP who can command confidence, or request the Monarch to dissolve Parliament, thereby precipitating a general election

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 (which do not apply for bills seeking to extend Parliament's length to more than five years), the House of Lords may not delay most other public bills for more than two parliamentary sessions, or one calendar year. The bill is then submitted for Royal Assent, even though the Lords did not pass it. These provisions, however, only apply to public bills that originate in the House of Commons.

stem: A customer bought a new lawn mower for £440 from a gardening centre. A few weeks later, the lawn mower broke down while the customer was using it to mow his lawn. The gardening centre has refused to refund the lawn mower's purchase price to the customer because it says the consumer did not follow the instructions provided when he purchased the lawn mower. The customer now intends to commence proceedings against the gardening centre.
ask: In which court would you advise the customer to commence proceedings?

options.en: County court - small claims track
County court - fast track
County court - multi-track
The magistrates' court - small claims track
The Commercial Court - multi-track

explanation.en: You did not select the best answer. The best answer is A. The County court small claims track is the usual track for claims with a value of £10,000 or less. A standard consumer compensation claim with a financial value of £440 would be a typical small claim case that would be allocated by the county court to the small claims track.

stem: Three property developers wish to carry on business as a partnership. They buy and sell real estate using the partnership money, with all land that they purchase and any mortgage over each property, in the name of whichever partner is dealing with each transaction. Since the value of the firm's real estate holdings have reduced significantly, the total value of its assets is now much less than its liabilities and their creditors have applied to have the partnership wound up.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Each partner will be liable for a third of the partnership's debts
Each partner is jointly and severally liable for the partnership's debts
Each partner is liable for those debts incurred in relation to transactions that they dealt with
Each partner is liable for the partnership's debts up to the amount of their capital account
Each partner is jointly and severally liable for the partnership's debts but their own personal assets are not available to the partnership's creditors

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Although each property is in the names of different partners, the money used to purchase each is partnership money and the property would be partnership property. Each partner has unlimited joint and several liability for the partnership's debts and this liability extends to their personal assets, should their creditors petition for their bankruptcy.

stem: The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) receives an application on a matter that engages public morality. The ECtHR states that the UK authorities are in a better position than international judges to make a decision. The ECtHR is based on the social and cultural traditions in the UK.
ask: Which key judicial principle has been applied by the ECtHR in this case?

options.en: The judicial principle applied by the ECtHR is the "Margin of Appreciation"
The judicial principle applied by the ECtHR is "Judicial Deference"
The judicial principle applied by the ECtHR is "Proportionality"
The judicial principle applied by the ECtHR is "Purposive Interpretation"
The judicial principle applied by the ECtHR is the "Subsidiarity"

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. One of the key judicial principles applied in ECtHR jurisprudence is that of the "Margin of Appreciation". The ECtHR is empowered to give the final ruling on whether the margin of appreciation as exercised by the contracting State is reconcilable with Convention Rights. Contracting States are allowed a margin of appreciation; that is to say, they may restrict Convention Rights, based on the political, social and cultural traditions with which they are more closely attuned than is the ECtHR.

stem: You are called to the police station to attend a suspect has been charged with attempted murder. She is alleged to have bought a can of petrol to be used to torch her cheating boyfriend's house when he was asleep inside. She was arrested when she was overheard telling someone what she planned to do.
ask: Which option best states a key element the prosecution prove to gain a conviction for attempted murder?

options.en: The prosecution must show that the suspect was about to commit the offence imminently
The prosecution must show that the suspect's acts were more than merely preparatory
The prosecution must show that the suspect was temporally, spatially and physically about to commit the offence and that the suspect was within the general locality of the suspected target
The prosecution must show that the suspect at least intended to cause the victim grievous bodily harm
The prosecution must show that the suspect actually attempted to commit the offence

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The requirement is that the actions need to be more than merely preparatory. There are no specific definitions, in that it isn't necessary for the defendant to be within a certain period of time or distance from the crime, but simply preparing to commit a crime is insufficient. Statute: Section 1(1) Criminal Attempts Act 1981.

stem: Two people trade together as a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP).
ask: The partnership agreement provides that should the LLP go into insolvent liquidation, each will contribute a maximum of £10,000 towards any debts that cannot be discharged from Which of the following statements is correct?

options.en: The two partners are liable to the LLP to contribute up to £10,000 each to any liquidation; their creditors can also petition for their bankruptcy if any debts remain undischarged thereafter
The two partners are liable to the LLP's creditors to contribute up to £10,000 each to any liquidation; their creditors can petition for their bankruptcy if any debts remain undischarged thereafter
The two partners are liable to the LLP to contribute up to £10,000 each to any liquidation; their creditors cannot petition for their bankruptcy if any debts remain undischarged thereafter

The two partners are liable to the LLP's creditors to contribute up to £10,000 each to any liquidation; their creditors cannot petition for their bankruptcy if any debts remain undischarged thereafter
The two partners are neither liable to the LLP's creditors nor to the LLP for any of its debts as it has a separate legal personality

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Members of an LLP are directly liable to the LLP up to the limit defined in the partnership agreement. The LLP can call for contributions from them in a liquidation in the same way that a limited company can call for contributions from its members. This liability is owed to the LLP and not its creditors. However, once the members have satisfied any such liability, they have no further liability for the remaining debts of the LLP and the LLP's creditors have no ability to claim directly from the members.

stem: A non-professional trustee would like to recover remuneration and expenses for her management of a trust, including the purchase of office equipment and stationery.
ask: The trust instrument provides that the trustee is entitled to all 'professional charges.' Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The trustee can recover remuneration under the terms of the trust instrument, because of her past services to the trust
The trustee can recover remuneration under the trust instrument, because all trustees are deemed to be professionals
he trustee can recover remuneration by applying to the court for an award, provided she has carried out her duties as trustee in a proper manner
The trustee cannot recover her expenses under the terms of the trust instrument
The trustee cannot recover remuneration and expenses, because trustees are not permitted to profit from their trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The general rule in respect of remuneration of trustees, as laid down in the case of Bray v Ford, is that a trustee will not be entitled to profit from their trust in the absence of express provision to the contrary. It is true that, in this case, the trust instrument provides that the trustee is entitled to all 'professional charges'. Unfortunately, however, remuneration clauses are construed strictly against the trustee. It follows that, because the trustee is a non-professional, she will be unable to claim 'professional' remuneration under the trust instrument. She may apply to the court for an award (under its inherent jurisdiction to ensure the good remuneration for her past services to the trust (Foster v Spencer); however, such an application is likely to fail if the trustee has not carried out her duties as trustee in a proper manner. The Trustee Act 2000 introduces a presumption in favour of the remuneration of professional trustees and trust corporations, but no such presumption is raised in favour of non-professional trustees. In respect of expenses the trustee may, however, recover from the trust any reasonable expenses that she has incurred from the monies she must repay to the trust (s. 31(1) Trustee Act 2000).

stem: During money laundering checks, a client gives a married name, but when asked to provide identification, she produces a passport and two utility bills in her maiden name. The client is clearly the person shown on the passport.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: No further client identification is required, because the client has produced her passport and two utility bills
No further client identification is required, because the client is obviously the person shown in the passport
No further client identification is required, because the client is clearly not seeking to establish an account in a false name
No further client identification is required, because of the presumption of innocence
Further client identification is required, because the client's married name has not been sufficiently identified

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. There is every probability that the client has recently married and is now using her married name. However, this information must be verified, because it is possible that the client is seeking to establish an account in a false name which would not show any connection to her. She must therefore be asked to produce her marriage certificate in order to authenticate her married name. Copies of all the identification material must be retained on the file.

stem: An 18 year old claimant broke his neck when diving into shallow murky water in a council owned lake. The council has for many years, however, pursued a policy of rohibiting swimming and erected notices at the lake's entrance and elsewhere stating "Dangerous Water.
ask: No Swimming" Which option best states the council's legal position?

options.en: The council is not liable, because it has done everything reasonably possible to ensure the safety of visitors
The council is in breach of its common duty of care and is therefore liable
The council is liable, as it is in breach of its duty to him as trespasser not to cause him deliberate or reckless injury
The council is liable, because it is under a duty to take reasonable care to see that the claimant did not suffer injury by reason of the danger from diving
Although the murky water prevented the claimant from seeing the bottom of the lake, this is not due to the state of the premises, so, the council is not liable

explanation.en: 'sewhere You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Once he entered the lake to swim, he was no longer a "visitor" and became a trespasser, to whom no duty, under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, was owed. Lead case: Tomlinson v. Congleton BC [2003]. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 1(1) Occupiers' Liability Act 1984.

stem: A person dies leaving an estate, worth £337,000, to her son. Two years later, the son dies leaving his estate, worth £437,000, to a friend. Assumptions (if applicable): Nil rate threshold is £325,000 IHT rate = 40% of amount over nil rate band
ask: What is the Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability on the son's estate?

stem: A man regularly paid his share of a £600 a month repayment of a loan, but his two other partners stopped paying altogether and subsequently declared bankruptcy. The man agreed with the creditor that if he continued to pay £200 a month, he would only be liable for one third of the debt. When he had paid one third, the creditor reneged on the agreement and issued a statutory demand for the whole of the outstanding balance.
ask: Which option best states the legal position?

options.en: The principle of promissory estoppel would not provide a ground for setting aside the statutory demand, because as a rule, a party to a contract will be consciously aware of what consideration he is giving for the promise he is accepting

The principle of promissory estoppel would not provide a ground for setting aside the statutory demand; by continuing to make the monthly instalment payments that he was already making, the man did not make a sufficient alteration of his position

The principle of promissory estoppel would not provide a ground for setting aside the statutory demand, because even if the man relied on the creditor's promise in not pursuing his co-debtors, it would not have improved the man's position, given the bankruptcy status of his co-debtors

The principle of promissory estoppel would provide a ground for setting aside the statutory demand, because the man had relied on the assurance that he could repay only part of the debt, and reneging from the promise would of itself be inequitable

The principle of promissory estoppel would provide a ground for setting aside the statutory demand, because it would be inequitable on the part of the creditor to pursue the man for the full amount of the debt, since he lost the opportunity to chase his co-debtors, or at least agree to some accommodation with them

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Promissory estoppel would apply, as it would be inequitable for the creditor to go back on the promise. Lead case: Collier v P&MJ Wright (Holdings) Ltd [2007] EWCA Civ 1329, [2008] 1 WLR 643, [2007] All ER(D) 233 (Dec) (Collier).

stem: Your client has been arrested for criminal damage. He denies causing any damage. He asks you to explain how the Criminal Damage Act 1971 (CDA) defines damage.
ask: Which option best explains the definition of damage, if any, under the CDA?

options.en: The CDA defines damage as being permanent
The CDA defines damage as something that devalues property
The CDA defines damage as something that is visible
The CDA does not define damage; it depends on the particular facts
The CDA defines damage as something that is visible and permanent

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. There is no specific definition of criminal damage and it all depends on the facts; the other points raised such as damage being permanent may indicate that damage has occurred, but there is no definitive definition. In Roe v Kingerlee [1986] QBD, Lord Justice Woolf stated: "... what constitutes criminal damage is a matter of fact and degree and it is for the justices, applying their common sense, to look at what occurs and decide whether it is damage or not...". The damage need not be visible; provided it undermines the value of the product, the damage can be internal to the item.

stem: A treaty on EU trade, which is subject to ratification, is to be published and laid before Parliament. The Trade Minister seeks clarification regarding the ratification procedure. In particular the Minister is concerned about the effects, if any, of a negative resolution.
ask: Which option best advises the Minister?

options.en: If 21 days expire with no such resolution being passed by either House, the government can proceed to ratify the treaty
If the 21 sitting days expire with no such resolution being passed by either House, the government can proceed to ratify the treaty
If the 21 sitting days expire with no such resolution being passed by the House of Commons, the government can proceed to ratify the treaty
If the 21 sitting days expire with no such resolution being passed by the House of Lords, the government can proceed to ratify the treaty
If the 21 sitting days expire with no such resolution being passed by either House, the government cannot proceed to ratify the treaty

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is the best option. Section 20 Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 (CRAIG) provides that a treaty that is subject to ratification or its equivalent, is to be published and laid before Parliament. It provides for a period of 21 sitting days (days on which both Houses sit), beginning with the sitting day after a copy of the treaty is laid before Parliament, within which either House may resolve that the treaty should not be ratified. If the 21 sitting days expire with no such resolution being passed by either House, the government can proceed to ratify the treaty. CRAIG contains provisions for the period to be extended and, if either House resolves that the treaty should not be ----3, a Minister may lay a statement indicating that they are of the opinion that the treaty should nevertheless be ratified (and why). If such a statement follows a resolution of the House of Commons that the treaty should not be ratified, this triggers a further 21- day period during which the House of Commons may come to the same resolution again. S.20 CRAIG also defines the legal effect of a negative vote by either House. Note, the definition of "sitting days" is limited to days on which both Houses sit. stem: Your client has installed a new stand-alone greenhouse on his freehold property. He isn't sure whether the greenhouse constitutes real or personal property.
ask: What would you advise him?

options.en: The greenhouse constitutes real property, because it concerns an interest in land
The greenhouse constitutes personal property, because it personally belongs to your client
The greenhouse constitutes real property, because it is a building
The greenhouse constitutes real property, because it is real and it is property
The greenhouse constitutes personal property, because it does not fall within the categories that constitute real property

explanation.en: whether or not held apart from the surface, buildings or parts of buildings (whether the division is horizontal, vertical or made in any other way) and other corporeal hereditaments; also a manor, an advowson, and a rent and other incorporeal hereditaments, and an easement, right, privilege, or benefit in, over, or derived from land...", per s205(1)(ix) of the Law of Property Act 1925. The opposite of real property is personal property, which is defined negatively as anything that is not real property. A greenhouse is likely not to be considered a building, and, not falling within any of the other categories of land or relating to an interest in the same, will thus be considered personal property.

stem: A woman and her partner sought fertility treatment, but a month after starting treatment the couple were informed that the woman had pre-cancerous tumours on her ovaries which had to be removed. Before the woman underwent the operation, doctors removed embryos to be created and stored, but were informed that in accordance with UK legislation, it would be possible for either of them to withdraw his or her consent at any time before the embryos were implanted in the woman's uterus. Following the breakdown of the relationship the man successfully applied to the High Court requesting that the embryos should be destroyed. The woman seeks an injunction to restore his consent.
ask: Which option best states the rights of the parties under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)?

options.en: There is no right to have a child under the Convention. This is a domestic matter
The legal requirement to destroy the stored embryos once consent had been withdrawn would violate the embryos' right to life under the Convention
The legal requirement to destroy the stored embryos would violate the woman's right to respect for a private life

It discriminates between women who can conceive without medical assistance and women, such as the woman, who require medical assistance for conception, not to restore the original consent to use and store the embryos
There is no absolute right to have a child under the Convention

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. There is no absolute right to have a child under the Convention. In Evans v The United Kingdom (Application no. 6339/05), the Grand Chamber of the ECtHR stated that it "...does not find that the absolute nature of the law is, in itself, necessarily inconsistent with Article 8...Respect for human dignity and free will, as well as a desire to ensure a fair balance between the parties....underlay the legislature's decision to enact provisions permitting of no exception...In addition...the absolute nature of the rule served to promote legal certainty and to avoid the problems of arbitrariness and inconsistency inherent in weighing...'entirely incommensurable' interests" LUILLI

stem: A juvenile at the age of 17 booked and attended driving lessons but refuses to pay for them. The owner of the driving school is seeking to enforce payment.

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best option. A minor is considered to be any person under the age of 18 years. The Family Law Reform Act 1969, s 1 reduced the age of majority from 21 to 18. This is also referred to as the age at which a person reached 'majority'. As the juvenile is 17 years old, the driving school cannot enforce payment. Statute: Family Law Reform Act 1969, s 1.

stem: A man fatally stabbed a woman with a knife. Because he was so intoxicated, the man wrongly believed that the woman was a tailor's dummy.
ask: Which option best states the law regarding intoxication?

options.en: Intoxication is not a defence to a specific intent crime if the defendant's intoxication prevented the formation of intention
Being voluntarily intoxicated at the time of an alleged offence is a complete defence
Intoxication may act as a defence to a specific intent crime if the defendant's intoxication prevented the formation of intention
Being voluntarily intoxicated at the time of an alleged offence means permits the defendant to rely on the defence of automatism
Intoxication may act as a defence to a basic intent crime if the defendant's intoxication prevented the formation of intention

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. stem: A husband and wife are the joint legal owners of a house which they hold on trust for themselves as joint tenants. The wife is convicted of unlawfully killing her husband and commits suicide in prison six months later. Both had made wills leaving their entire estate to their respective children from previous marriages.
ask: Which option best advises the deceased wife's estate's entitlement to property?

options.en: The deceased husband's estate alone is beneficially entitled to the whole of the property
The deceased wife's estate alone is beneficially entitled to the property
The deceased husband and wife's estates are each beneficially entitled to 50% of the property
The deceased husband's estate is beneficially entitled to 50% of the property with the other 50% passing to the Crown
Nether estate is entitled to anything; the whole property passes to the Crown

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The deceased husband's estates are each beneficially entitled to 50% of the property. Had the deceased wife not been responsible for the deceased husband's death, then she would have inherited his share of the property according to the Doctrine of Survivorship. Because she is responsible for his death, however, the forfeiture rule (Cleaver v Mutual Reserve Fund Life Association [1892] 1 QB 147) prevents her from inheriting his share. Both parties' shares will pass to their estates in accordance with their respective wills.

stem: A husband contributes 50% of the purchase price for the acquisition of the matrimonial home. The wife alone is registered on the legal title of the home.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the effect of the husband's contribution to the purchase price?

options.en: The husband is entitled to 100% of the equitable interest in the matrimonial home because there is a presumption that the husband did not intend to make a gift to the wife of the money
The husband is entitled to 50% of the legal interest in the property

stem: A boy has been arrested for racially abusing a black woman. The boy wrote racially offensive Twitter messages on the woman's Twitter account. The boy has now been charged with using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour, or disorderly behaviour intending to and causing harassment, alarm or distress under the Public Order Act 1986.
ask: Which option best states a key element that the prosecution must show to convict the?

options.en: The offence requires that such 'harassment, alarm or distress' is actually caused to the person against whom the behaviour is directed, or some other person
The offence requires that such 'harassment, alarm or distress' is likely to be caused to the person against whom the behaviour is directed, or some other person
The offence requires that such 'harassment, alarm or distress' will probably be caused to the person against whom the behaviour is directed, or some other person
The offence requires that such 'harassment, alarm or distress' will possibly be caused to the person against whom the behaviour is directed, or some other person
The offence requires that such 'harassment, alarm or distress' will certainly be caused to the person against whom the behaviour is directed, or some other person

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Section 4A of the Public Order Act 1986 (POA), is the offence of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour, or disorderly behaviour intending to and causing harassment, alarm or distress. There must be an actual victim, although it does not have to be the intended victim. Section 4A carries a greater penalty than section 5 of the POA and is intended for the more directed and persistent type of behaviour required to prove the elements of intent and causation. Statute: s. 4A of the Public Order Act (POA) 1986.

stem: D sent an unsealed letter to a married couple living together, X and Y, defaming X and Y. The au pair (a living-in nanny or domestic assistant employed by X and Y) opened and read the letter. X and Y claim that this was publication to a third party.

stem: A man voluntarily drinks a bottle of vodka and, consequently, enters into a state of automatism.
ask: He walks drunkenly into a crowd of people, striking out at them and Which option best explains the man's criminal liability, if any?

options.en: The man avoids liability on the basis that he did not act voluntarily
The man is guilty of battery because his state of automatism was self-induced
The man is not guilty of battery because his state of automatism was self- induced
The man was not acting voluntarily and would not have foreseen the risk of applying unlawful force to another person
The man was acting voluntarily but would not have foreseen the risk of applying unlawful force to another person

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The defence of automatism does not allow an individual who is intoxicated to rely on this defence, nor does it allow a person who took a drug a defence when he should have been aware of the drug's effect on him. The man is therefore guilty of battery because his state of automatism was culpably self-induced. If the man had not drunk a bottle of vodka, he would have been acting voluntarily and would have foreseen the risk of applying unlawful force to another person.

stem: A property developer owns the fee simple in a large area of meadow on the outskirts of Oldcastle. The property developer wishes to develop the land eventually, but in the meantime she has agreed to let it to a man, who intends to graze his cattle there. The property developer grants the man a periodic tenancy which contains a proviso that the property developer cannot serve notice to quit on the man unless the property developer is ready to develop the land.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The tenancy is for an uncertain term but is capable of taking effect as a lease
The tenancy is for an uncertain term and is not capable of taking effect as a lease
The tenancy is not for an uncertain term and is capable of taking effect as a lease
The tenancy is not for an uncertain term and is not capable of taking effect as a lease
The tenancy is not for an uncertain term and takes effect as a license

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The tenancy is for an uncertain term and is not capable of taking effect as a lease. A periodic tenancy has a certain term, since it lasts only as long as each period. A restriction on the right to determine at the end of any period will result in uncertainty in the same manner as a grant for an uncertain term, and would fall foul of the rule in Lace v Chantler [1944] KB 368 requiring the term to be certain.

The director must seek the approval of Mortgage pic's members for this loan being made to her, because it exceeds £50,000

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Where a loan is made by a company to one of its directors as part of a credit transaction made in the ordinary course of the company's business, there is no requirement for the approval of the members to be sought in order to ratify the transaction. Sections 204-207 of the Companies Act 2006.

stem: A Northern Irish man was convicted and imprisoned in Northern Ireland for Irish Republican Army membership, but subsequently had his conviction quashed. nich option best advises the Nortnern Irish man!
ask: He wants to know if he may claim statutory compensation against the UK Government Which option best advises the Northern Irish man?

options.en: He cannot claim statutory compensation against the UK Government, because Northern Ireland courts are not bound by decisions of the UK Supreme Court on matters of criminal and civil liability
He cannot claim statutory compensation against the UK Government, because the UK Supreme Court interprets and applies the civil law of England, Wales and Scotland only
He cannot claim statutory compensation against the UK Government, because the Supreme Court panel's ruling only has force if the offences were committed on the British mainland

He may claim statutory compensation against the UK Government, but only after it has been referred back to the Northern Ireland Appeal Court for 'reinterpreting' the judgment to give proper effect under Northern Irish law
He may claim statutory compensation against the UK Government, because the Supreme Court serves as the highest court of appeal in England and Wales and includes Northern Ireland

explanation.en: E is correct. The Supreme Court acts as the final court of appeal in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In respect of appeals from the Court of Appeal in England & Wales and the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland, an appeal to The Supreme Court from any order or judgment of the Court of Appeal in England and Wales or in Northern Ireland may only be brought with the permission of the Court of Appeal or of The Supreme Court. Lead case: R (on the application of Adams) (FC) v Secretary of State for Justice Re MacDermott and another appeal [2011] UKSC 18.

stem: An English language centre claimed that the Home Secretary's decision to increase the level for English language courses under the points based system regulating entry into or stay in the UK of non-nationals was unlawful, because Parliament had not been afforded the opportunity to scrutinise the rationality for the change. The Administrative Court subsequently ruled that the changes were implemented by altering guidelines rather than making formal changes to the Immigration Rules through Parliament. The Administrative Court, therefore, declared as unlawful the changed minimum educational requirements of those applying to study English in the UK and referred the matter back to Parliament. Identify which remedy of judicial review
ask: is raised by the Administrative Court's?

options.en: A mandatory order
A prohibiting order
A quashing order
A declaration
An injunction

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The effect of the quashing order, or declaration of invalidity, would be to refer the matter to Parliament in this case, so Parliament can scrutinise the relevant provision in the Immigration Rules. Policy guidelines cannot usurp the Immigration Rules themselves. Lead case: English UK Ltd, R (on the application of) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2010] EHCC 1726 (Admin).

stem: Talking to a colleague in the Family Department, you suddenly realise that your respective divorce clients have very striking similarities in terms of childcare arrangements and the allocation of joint property. It transpires that the separated couple, who go by different surnames and live at different addresses, are both represented by your firm. The wife is a longstanding client.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you ought to respond in order to comply with the SRA Code of?

options.en: Your firm can act for both clients, but must ensure that the files are not mixed up
Your firm cannot continue to represent both clients, as there is a client conflict
Your firm cannot continue to represent both clients, as there is an own interest conflict on the part of the solicitors
Your firm can continue to represent both clients, provided that they are represented by two different solicitors within the firm
Your firm can continue to represent both clients if they provide informed consent for the firm to do so, since they have a common interest (childcare and property arrangements)

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. Your firm cannot continue to represent both clients as there is a client conflict. Your firm cannot act if there is a client conflict (03.5), unless the clients have a common interest (03.6) or are competing for the same objective (03.7), provide informed consent, and representing both parties would not be detrimental to either client's interests. That is not the case here, where childcare and property division may well be disputed. A is incorrect. Your firm most likely cannot represent both clients and must refer one to an independent firm. The files must be transferred as appropriate without mixing up information or disclosing confidential information. C is incorrect. The scenario involves a client conflict, not an own issue conflict. The fact that one solicitor represented the other party at some stage does not preclude the firm continuing to represent the remaining client, provided that the person handling the file is not privy to confidential information and protects the confidentiality of any information provided by either client. D is incorrect. You cannot generally act for two sides in a dispute (03.5). IB3.2 and IB3.3 clearly indicate that the firm should decline to act for clients whose interests are in direct conflict, particularly where the solicitors will need to negotiate on matters of substance on the clients' behalf (IB3.3). and O3.7 envisage scenarios in which a firm may represent two sides in a matter, this is only where there is informed consent and neither side would be disadvantaged. In a divorce context, this would almost never be the case, as there is a direct conflict and matters of substance must be negotiated such as the custody of children and division of property (IB3.2 and 3.3).

stem: A mother with a substantial history of anxiety and depression claims to have suffered psychiatric injury after seeing the aftermath her child suffering injury as a result of the defendant's negligence. Counsel for the defendant argues that the mother's symptoms do not amount to a recognised psychiatric injury. The judge seeks clarification as to what is a recognised psychiatric injury.
ask: Which option best advises the judge?

options.en: A recognised psychiatric illness is one which has been recognised by the legal profession
A recognised psychiatric illness is one which has been recognised by the Law Commission
A recognised psychiatric illness is one which has been recognised by the psychiatric profession
A recognised psychiatric illness is one which has been recognised by the reasonable and prudent person
A recognised psychiatric illness is one which has been recognised by the standard of the ordinary skilled man exercising and professing to have that special skill

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best option. A recognised psychiatric illness is one which has been recognised by the psychiatric profession. The Court of Appeal addressed the question of what is a recognised psychiatric injury in Hussain v Chief Constable of West Mercia [2008], in which Stanley Burnton LJ stated: "...A recognised psychiatric illness is one which has been recognised by the psychiatric profession. In general, they are illnesses that are within the ICD (International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems) classification published by the World Health Organisation..." Lead case: Hussain v Chief Constable of West Mercia

stem: A man who has learning difficulties pretends to break in to a woman's apartment at night, knowing that she is asleep inside. His intention is to give the woman a severe fright. The woman is killed trying to escape.
ask: Which option best states a key element of criminal liability in this situation?

options.en: The man must have acted unlawfully
The man's conduct must be such that a reasonable and sober person would have been in fear for their safety
The man's conduct must be such that a person with the woman's characteristics would have been in fear for her safety
The man must have acted unreasonably
The man as a reasonable person must have realised that it was likely that there would be physical harm experienced by another individual

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. In the case of DPP v Daley [1980] AC 237, the defendant was chasing the victim and throwing stones at him. The victim fell over and was later found dead. The judge laid out several criteria that had to be met in order for a defendant to be found guilty in these types of cases: the victim feared being hurt, immediately prior to sustaining injuries; the fear was the reason that he tried to escape the situation; he met his death whilst trying to escape; the fear of being hurt was reasonable, in all the circumstances; the fear was as a result of the defendant's action; and the conduct of the defendant was such that a reasonable and sober person would also have been in fear for his safety.

stem: The (fictitious) Infringement Green Belt Bill 2012 (the Bill) is introduced into the House of Commons for a second reading. The purpose of the Bill is to allow travellers to remain on greenbelt land.
ask: The government minister responsible for the Bill has been asked to make a Statement of Compatibility in regard to the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) in order to comply with the provisions of the Human Rights Act 1998 (the HRA) Which option, if any, is open to the minister?

options.en: incompatible, but the government wishes to proceed with the Bill regardless

The minister responsible for the Bill must make a written statement to Parliament that the proposed new legislation is compatible with Convention rights and that if it is incompatible, the government will not proceed with the Bill

The minister responsible for the Bill must make a written statement that the proposed new legislation is compatible with the Convention rights, or that it is incompatible, but that the government wishes to proceed with the Bill regardless

The minister responsible for that Bill need not make a statement to Parliament that the proposed new legislation is compatible with the Convention rights; if it is incompatible, however, a statement must be made that the government will proceed with the Bill regardless

The minister responsible for that Bill must make a written statement to the House of Commons that the proposed new legislation is compatible with Convention rights and that, if it is compatible, a statement must be made to the House of Lords

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Section 19(1) of the HRA mandates that, prior to the second reading of a Bill in Parliament, the minister responsible must make a written statement that he considers the Bill is compatible with the Convention rights, or that he is unable to make such a statement but wishes Parliament to proceed with the Bill anyway. This is an executive statement giving the personal opinion of the minister introducing the Bill - it is not binding on Parliament or the courts. It is intended to encourage ministers and the civil service to consider the human rights implications of proposed legislation before it is introduced. - othe

stem: An oil company agreed to sell 50,000 barrels of Kuwaiti crude oil to a petrol company for shipment to Hull in England. Due to a terrorist attack, the Suez Canal was closed; meaning access to the Mediterranean Sea was blocked. Since the only alternative route available to the oil company was to ship the oil round the Southern coast of Africa, tripling delivery time and cost of carriage, the oil company has refused to ship the oil arguing that the contract was frustrated.
ask: Which option best states the courts' approach in such a situation?

options.en: The contract is not frustrated; the fact that the re-routing would triple the time and cost is irrelevant

The contract is frustrated because a supervening event has prevented the oil company supplying, and the petrol company from obtaining, what the oil company had contracted to provide and the petrol company was to acquire under the contract
The contract is frustrated by the closure of the pipeline, because its continued availability was a fundamental assumption at the time when the contract was made

To impose upon the oil company the obligation to ship by an emergency route would be to impose upon it a fundamentally different obligation, which neither contracting party could have dreamed of, so the contract is frustrated

Because the main means of delivery is frustrated, namely that the oil was expected to be carried via a particular route and by a particular method, performance is impossible, and the whole contract is rescinded

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. The mere fact that the means or method of performance had become impossible would be insufficient to frustrate the contract. A contract will remain binding even if it turns out to be more expensive or difficult to perform than envisaged. Thus the contract would not be frustrated by the closure of the pipeline, so that the oil would need to be sent via a different route, even if it was more costly. Lead case: Tsakiroglou & Co v Noblee and Thorl [1962] AC 93; [1961] 2 AlI ER 179.

stem: A discount store contracted to buy 250,000 dolls at £1 each from a manufacturer in China in order to meet the pre-Christmas sales rush in the UK. The manufacturer threatened to terminate the contract unless the discount store promised to pay £1.50 for each doll because of a sudden devaluation of the Yuan (Chinese currency) at the time of delivery. The discount store agreed to pay the extra money without protest, because it wanted to fill its Christmas order book, but several months later, it seeks to recover the extra payment on grounds of economic duress.
ask: Which option best advises the discount store?

options.en: There was no duress, because a threatened breach of contract cannot constitute duress
There was duress; the discount store had not affirmed the contract by making payment without protest
There was duress but the discount store had affirmed the contract by making payment without protest
There was duress, because the manufacturer had acted in bad faith
There was no duress, because the discount store had no other choice but to submit to the manufacturer's demands

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. There was economic duress, but the discount store did not protest at the time. The Atlantic Baron [1979] is authority for the principle that payment can be recovered on the ground of economic duress. In that case, the buyers had lost their right to rescind, however, because they had already paid the money without protest, until several months after taking delivery of the goods. The court held that this was sufficient to constitute affirmation of the contract. Lead case: North Ocean Shipping Co Ltd v Hyundai Construction Co Ltd (The Atlantic Baron) [1979] QB 705 (The Atlantic Baron [1979]).

stem: A man owns the fee simple in a property. He grants a lease to a woman for ten years using a document which is not executed as a deed. The woman subsequently grants a lease to a farmer for eight years by deed.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The farmer will have a legal sub-lease which must be registered at Her Majesty's Land Registry (HMLR) with its own title number
The farmer will have an equitable sub-lease which must be registered at HMLR with its own title number
The farmer will have a legal sub-lease which cannot be registered at HMLR With its own title number
The farmer will have an equitable sub-lease which cannot be registered at HMLR with its own title number
The farmer has no interest in the property at all

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The farmer will have an equitable lease and this cannot be registered at HMLR with its own title number. Because his lease was not made by deed, the woman only has an equitable lease (s.52 (1) Law of Property Act 1925). It follows that the woman cannot grant a legal lease out of his equitable lease and therefore the farmer's lease will exist in equity only even though it has been made by deed. As it is not a legal estate, the farmer cannot register it with its own title number.

stem: After leaving his wife to live in an extra-marital relationship with another woman, a man received damages of £1,000 for a work related injury. The man and his mistress subsequently opened a bank account, set up in the man's sole name, with the £1,000 damages forming the bulk of the money held in it.
ask: Just before he died suddenly, the man said to his mistress "this money is as much yours as mine." Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The money in the account will pass to the man's widow, not his mistress, under the Intestacy Rules
The money in the account will pass to the mistress as the sole surviving beneficiary under the trust through which the man held the money in the account
The money in the account will be split between the widow and the mistress
The money in the account will pass to the mistress who will hold it on trust for the widow
The money in the account will pass to the widow who will hold it on trust for the mistress

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. Although the man has left his wife, until they are divorced she will inherit all of his estate on his death under the Intestacy Rules. Property that the man holds on trust does not form part of his estate. The words "the money is as much yours as it is mine" have been held to demonstrate an intention that the money would be held on trust for the man and the mistress as joint tenants (see Paul v Constance [1977]). Therefore when the man dies, the money does not pass into his estate (and thereafter to the widow under the Intestacy Rules) because he was holding it on trust for himself and his mistress. Instead, the mistress becomes solely entitled to the money under the Doctrine of

stem: Two women and a man run a property development business under a formal partnership agreement which stipulates that all transactions over £500,000 must be authorised by all partners, a copy of which has been lodged with BankCo, the firm's bank. The three people inform their bank manager that they intend to apply for funding to acquire a new property for £600,000. One woman is actually on holiday when the other woman and the man subsequently sign the loan documents on behalf of the firm. When the woman returns from holiday, she claims that her business partners had no authority to bind her into the loan.
ask: Which of the following best states the correct legal position?

options.en: The woman and man had actual authority to bind the other woman whilst she was on holiday; all partners would be jointly liable for the loan
The woman and man had implied authority to bind the other woman whilst she was on holiday; all partners would be jointly liable for the loan
The woman and man had apparent authority to bind the other woman whilst she was on holiday; all partners would be jointly liable for the loan
The woman and man had no authority to bind the other woman whilst she was on holiday; however, all partners would nevertheless be jointly liable for the loan
The woman and man had no authority to bind the other woman whilst she was on holiday; she would not be liable for the loan

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The terms of the partnership agreement dictate the authority of the partners to bind each other and where the agreement expressly limits this authority, transactions over that limit will not bind the other partners. Whilst the conversation with their bank manager would seem to give rise to an apparent authority to transact at £600,000, the fact that the partnership agreement expressly limits the authority to £500,000 and the fact that BankCo was aware of this limit would mean that BankCo would know that the woman and man in fact had no authority to transact at £600,000.

stem: Your clients are a married couple of advanced years. They wish to arrange their financial affairs so that their estate attracts less Inheritance Tax (IHT) when they die.
ask: They ask whether there are types of gifts that are exempt from IHT and allow people to pass on large parts of their estate to friends and loved ones without attracting IHT Which option best advises the couple with regards to gift money?

options.en: They can gift up to £3,000 per year
They can gift up to £1,000 per year
They can gift up to £250 per person
They can gift up to £5,000 per year
There are no limits on gifts, provided they are bona fide gifts

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. They can gift up to £3,000 a year (although it can roll over for a year, offering a total of £6,000 in one year). Anything over will still potentially fall into part of the estate.

stem: An electrical company agreed to carry out maintenance work for a computer company. The computer company alleges that the electrical company's maintenance was shoddy and substandard and is refusing to pay the electrical company for its work. The electrical company contests the computer company's claim and intends to issue proceedings for recovery of the £17,000 it claims is owed by the computer
ask: Which option best states the most appropriate forum for the electric company's?

options.en: Since the value of a claim is less than £100,000, the claim must be commenced in the county court
Since the value of a claim is less than £25,000, the claim must be commenced in the county court
Since the value of a claim is more than £15,000, the claim may be commenced in the High Court
Since the value of a claim is more than £15,000, the claim may be commenced in the county court
Since the value of a claim is less than £100,000, the claim may be commenced in either the county court or the High Court

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. Civil cases generally commence in the county court or the High Court. Part 7 of the Civil Procedure Rules (CPR) stipulates that where the value of a claim is less than £100,000, the claim must commence in the county court. wwwI

stem: A husband and wife jointly shared their matrimonial home, until the husband left to live with another woman. They both signed an agreement that the husband would pay the wife a £900 monthly sum, and eventually transfer the house to her, if she kept up the monthly mortgage payments. When the mortgage was paid the husband refused to transfer the house.
ask: Can the wife sue the husband over his refusal to transfer the house to her?

options.en: Yes; despite the presumption that domestic agreements are not intended to be legally binding, once they began to haggle, it may safely be presumed that they intended to create legal relations
Yes; despite the presumption that domestic agreements are not intended to be legally binding, the presumption does not apply when the parties are not living in harmony but are separated
Yes, because, in accordance with the presumption involving married couples, their domestic arrangement was intended to create legal relations
No, because it runs counter to public policy that domestic agreements are intended to be legally binding
No, because, in accordance with the presumption involving married couples, their domestic arrangement was not intended to create legal relations

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. Although there is a presumption in the context of domestic or social agreements that married couples do not intend to create legal relations, the presumption involving a married couple is not made when the married couple are separated. The agreement having been made when the parties were not living together in amity is unenforceable. There is no sustainable argument that there was no consideration, since the payment of the balance of the mortgage was a detriment to the wife and the husband had received the benefit of being relieved of liability to the bank. Lead case: Merritt v Merritt [1970] 2 All ER 760.

stem: In the course of purchasing a house, a client seeks advice and follow-up arrangements in relation to a mortgage and collateral life policy.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position?

options.en: The advice and arrangements for the mortgage are permitted, because mortgages of land do not constitute specified investments
The advice and arrangements for the mortgage are permitted, because they do not constitute specified investment activities
The advice on the merits of an endowment policy and mortgage when compared to a repayment mortgage is permitted, because they are not specified investments
Advice on a particular endowment policy and advice on the arrangement of an endowment policy are prohibited, and the exclusion for necessary advice will not apply
Advice on a particular endowment policy and advice on the arrangement of an endowment policy are prohibited; however, the exclusion for necessary advice will apply

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is D. Advising a client or arranging for a client to enter into a regulated mortgage contract is prohibited under Article 25A of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities Order). Moreover, the exclusion for necessary advice or arrangements will not be available, because the firm could carry out the conveyancing work without performing the investment activities. While general advice on the merits of an endowment policy and mortgage may be given, when compared to a repayment mortgage, this is not because mortgages and/or life policies do not constitute specified investments (answer C).

stem: A man is charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm on a woman, but denies he committed the offence. The man's solicitor discovers that a new witness who says the man committed the crime is one of his former clients.
ask: The solicitor knows that the new witness has previous convictions, but the prosecution does not know Which of the following statements best describes what the solicitor should do?

options.en: The solicitor must continue to act for the man, because the witness is a former client
The solicitor must cease acting for the man, due to confidentiality
The solicitor must cross-examine the witness about his previous convictions
The solicitor may not cross-examine the witness about his previous convictions, but may continue to act for the man
The solicitor may continue to act for the man

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is B. The solicitor must cease acting for the man, due to confidentiality. On one hand, the solicitor must do everything possible to represent the man's interests. This will require the witness to be cross-examined about his previous convictions to shake the witness' credibility. However, the solicitor cannot do this on the facts as set out without breaching confidentiality towards his former client. Accordingly, the solicitor must stop acting for the man, because he cannot do the best job possible for the man without breaching confidentiality to his former client (the duty of confidentiality lasts forever). This is a clear conflict of interest.

stem: A worker at a manufacturing company did not join the trade union, but has been told by a shop steward on the factory floor that the manufacturing company is a 'closed shop"; trade union membership is compulsory. He has therefore been suspended and told he must join the trade union or face dismissal.
ask: Which right under the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention) has potentially been breached?

options.en: The right to be free from slavery or forced labour has potentially been breached
The right to liberty has potentially been breached
The right to respect for private and family life, home and correspondence has potentially been breached
The right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion has potentially been breached
The right to right to freedom of assembly and association has potentially been breached

explanation.en: E is correct. Compulsion to join a trade union or be dismissed may be contrary to rights under Article 11 of the Convention (Freedom of Assembly and Association). Everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and to freedom of association with others, including the right to form and to join trade unions for the protection of their interests. HR; ECHR; Young, James and Webster v UK (App nos 7601/76, 7806/77) Judgment of 13 August 1981. Article 11 ECHR.

stem: You are instructed by a foreign national, who is the sole director of a UK-based import/export limited company, in respect of drawing up a contract for delivery of goods with a supplier based in Sicily. The client pays in £500,000 into your account and asks you to pay the supplier on his behalf for the goods. You learn from the media that your client may have links to organised crime in Sicily. You suspect that the transaction is to facilitate money laundering and make a disclosure to your MLRO, who makes an external disclosure to National Crime Agency (NCA).
ask: Your client demands an explanation for the delay in proceeding with payment to the foreign Which of the following best describes the answer you can give?

options.en: You tell him that all foreign nationals' transactions are subject to anti-money laundering checks and that the delay is just part of the standard checks
You tell the client a specific report has been made, as you suspect money laundering, and are waiting for the all-clear
You tell the client a specific report has been made, as you suspect money laundering, and urge him not to proceed with the transaction
You cannot give an answer and must cease acting for the client
You apologise for the delay and explain that internal accounting policies and external banking systems for international transactions take some time

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. You apologise for the delay and explain that internal accounting policies and external banking systems for international transactions take some time. Under s333A POCA, It is an offence to disclose to [i.e. to "tip off"] a third person that a suspicious activity report has been made by any person to the police, HM Revenue and Customs, NCA or a nominated officer, where that disclosure might prejudice any investigation that might be carried out as a result of the Suspicious Activity Report. For the ottence to be committed, the tollowing three conditions must be met: A disclosure must have already been made; You know or suspect that, by disclosing the information, you are likely to prejudice any investigation elating to the Suspicious Activity Report. Therefore, no offence will be committed if you did not know or suspect that the disclosure was likely to prejudice any investigation; and The information upon which the disclosure is based came to you in the course of business in the regulated sector. If you cannot be absolutely sure, you must not tip off *haslant Anriminr Cir an innaeant aunlonstinn which 9-3--. If you cannot be absolutely sure, you must not tip off the client. Answer E is an innocent explanation which is not likely to tip off the client or prejudice any investigation, and you would reasonably be able to give this explanation without knowing or suspecting that it would amount to tipping off. Answers A and B are wrong. You are quite clearly tipping off the client, whatever the follow-up explanation to him for the delay occasioned by the disclosure. Answer C is wrong. The 'dissuading' exception under $333D (2) won't apply here - the disclosure of the to explain the delay, rather dissuading the client from engaging in criminal conduct. It is still likely to be considered as tipping off. Answer D is wrong because, in and of itself, a request for an explanation of a delay occasioned by a disclosure is not sufficient grounds to cease acting for the client. You should only cease to act for a client for good reason and with reasonable notice (IB 1.26 SRA Code of Conduct). stem: Iwo men are the trustees ot a private tamily will trust. The trust instrument provides that the trustees may advance income or capital to any of the grandchildren of the testator and that, at the expiration of 10 years from the date of the testator's death, the capital shall be paid to the testator's son. The testator's son asks the trustees to advance 25% of his share of the capital to him before the expiration of the 10 years, so that he can establish a business.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The trustees may not advance any of the capital to the testator's son
The trustees can only advance capital to the testator's son if they obtain the consent of all of the testator's grandchildren
The trustees can only advance capital to the testator's son if authorised to do so by an order of the court
The trustees have an absolute discretion as to whether to advance capital to the testator's son; the consent of the testator's grandchildren is not required
The trustees can only advance capital to the testator's son if authorised in writina to do so bv the testator

explanation.en: The best answer is D. The trustees have an absolute discretion as to whether to advance capital to the testator's son; the consent of the testator's grandchildren is not required. Before advancing capital to a beneficiary, the trustees must obtain the consent of any beneficiaries with a prior interest. However, this proviso does not apply where the prior beneficiaries constitute a discretionary class of beneficiaries. stem: Two men and a woman are in partnership together, importing products from abroad and selling them on domestically at a profit. The partnership is very informal and when starting the business the partners did not want a formal partnership agreement or deed in place. The partnership owns a warehouse and inventory. The female partner is killed whilst on a buying trip in Thailand.
ask: On hearing this, one of the male partners quickly and quietly enters into a contract to sell part of the partnership's inventory, hoping to keep the profits of that sale Which of the following best describes the legal position in respect of the partnership, its assets and the transaction entered into by the partner?

options.en: The partnership will automatically continue, with the deceased's share of the assets automatically vesting in the remaining partners. The contract remains valid but the profits form part of the partnership assets

The partnership will automatically continue, but the remaining partners will need to purchase the deceased's share of the assets from her estate. The contract is valid but the profits form part of the partnership assets

The partnership was automatically dissolved on the death of the female partner. All partnership assets will be sold, but the profits from the subsequent transaction can be retained by the contracting partner personally

The partnership was automatically dissolved on the death of the female partner. The female partner's share of the assets form part of her estate and the remaining partnership assets will be sold. The transaction entered into after her death is void for illegality

The partnership was automatically dissolved on the death of the female partner. The woman's share of the partnership assets will be sold as part of the dissolution process. Any profit made by the transaction entered into after the female partner's death will be held on trust for the partnership as a whole

explanation.en: - - The correct answer is E. The partnership was automatically dissolved on the death of the female partner. The woman's share of the partnership assets will be sold as part of the dissolution process. Any profit made by the transaction entered into after the female partner's death will be held on trust for the partnership as a whole. The death of a partner will automatically dissolve a partnership, unless otherwise agreed by the partners. On dissolution, all assets of a partnership are sold.
