stem: A tenant claims that her landlord has failed to repair a broken window, resulting in further damage to the property due to dampness. The cost of repairs is estimated at £3,880.
ask: The tenant seeks a court order for the landlord to carry out the necessary Which is the most appropriate venue for the tenant to seek the court order?

options.en: ) The most appropriate court for any claim by the tenant is the county court (small claims track)
The most appropriate court for any claim by the tenant is the county court (fast- track)
The most appropriate court for any claim by the tenant is the county court (multi-track)
The most appropriate court for any claim by the tenant is the High Court (Queen's Bench Division)
The most appropriate court for any claim by the tenant is either the magistrates' court or the crown court

explanation.en: You did not select the best answer. The best answer is B. Landlord and tenant disputes worth more than £1,000 but less than £25,000 will usually be allocated to the fast track of the county court. The case would only be allocated to the small claims track if the claimant is a tenant, and is claiming against her landlord because she wants her landlord to carry out repairs or other work to the premises and the cost of the repairs or work is £1,000 or less. While it may be appropriate to try the case in the small-claims track if the parties agree, and the court consents, option B is the most appropriate and therefore is the best answer.

stem: A local authority invited tenders to run a concession to operate pleasure flights from its airport and sent invitations to the existing operator and 6 others. The terms required submission of tenders no later than 12pm on a specified date. An airline company submitted a tender by 11am on the required date, but the post box at the local authority's office was not cleared until later, meaning the airline company's tender was mistakenly marked as being late and was thus not considered.
ask: Can the airline company claim a breach of contract?

options.en: Yes, because the local authority was contractually obligated to consider the airline company's tender
Yes, because it was an offer made to an individual, group or the whole world and the local authority is therefore bound
No, because a tender is not an offer to sell to the person making the highest offer, but merely an invitation to treat
No, because the local authority could decide the terms on which the tenders were to be considered, and the basis on which the selection of the successful tender would be made
No, because there was nothing explicit in the invitation by the local authority to indicate that all tenders meeting the deadline would be considered

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is correct. In this context, a reasonable invitee would understand the invitation to clearly say, that if the tender was timely submitted, it would be considered, along with other tenders. Lead case: Blackpool and Fylde Aero Club Ltd v Blackpool Borough Council [1990] 3 All ER 25.

stem: Two men own and live in a property. They have a means of accessing the property via a track which crosses a field owned by a woman (in relation to which they have the benefit of an express easement); however, they find it easier, when going to the shop, to climb the fence and cut across the woman's orchard, which separates their house from the shop. The woman has not spoken to the two men about this for 25 years and has just put up with what they are doing.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The two men's use is without permission and without force and is capable of taking place as of right
The two men's use is without permission but with force and is not capable of taking place as of right
The two men's use is with permission and without force and is not capable of taking place as of right
The two men's use is with permission and with force and is not capable of taking place as of right
The two men's use is without permission and without force and is not capable of taking place as of right

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The two men's use is without permission but with force and is not capable of taking place as of right. The fact that the two men must climb the woman's fence to gain access to the orchard means that their use is forcible and is therefore not capable of taking place as of right.

stem: A person commences proceedings against a local authority for breaching its statutory duty to provide adequate day care for dementia sufferers. The question of whether one can bring a claim for breach of statutory duty depends upon whether the statute creates such a duty, which is a question of compliance
The question of whether one can bring a claim for breach of statutory duty depends upon whether the statute creates such a duty, which is a question of regulation

The question of whether one can bring a claim for breach of statutory duty depends upon whether the statute creates such a duty, which is a question of policy

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best option. The question of whether one can bring a claim for breach of statutory duty depends upon whether the statute creates such a duty, which is a question of construction. The result of any such lacuna in statutory language means that it is generally left to the courts to interpret what might be the consequences where the terms of legislative requirements or statutory prohibitions are contravened. Where a claim is based on breach of statutory duty, the main issue is, whether from the provisions and construction of the statute, the intention can be understood to create a private law remedy. stem: A husband and wife entered into a suicide pact and each fed sleeping tablets to the other. The husband died, but the wife did not and is now concerned that she will be held legally responsible.
ask: What do you advise her?

options.en: Involvement in suicide pact does not constitute a criminal offence
If she can prove that her husband wanted to die, she won't face charges
Where there is a suicide pact, the charge is reduced from murder to manslaughter
As she also tried to kill herself, she faces no charges
As the victim fed himself some of the tablets, the wife is not responsible

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. Section 4 of the Homicide Act 1957 reduces an offence of murder to one of manslaughter in the case of ges a survivor of a joint suicide pact, who took part in the killing of another person in the pact. The defendant must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that they were acting in the course of the suicide pact.

stem: A book was publisned by a tormer close triend of the claimant, a television personality. The book revealed deep and personal information about the claimant. The claimant believes that the information was private in the sense it is protected by the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention).
ask: How does the court determine whether the information was private and protected by the Convention?

options.en: Courts determine whether the information was private and protected by the Convention by applying a subjective test of 'reasonable expectation of privacy"
Courts determine whether the information was private and protected by the Convention by applying an objective test of 'reasonable expectation of privacy'
Courts determine whether the information was private and protected by the Convention by applying an objective test of 'realistic prospect of privacy"
Courts determine whether the information was private and protected by the Convention by applying a subjective test of 'genuine belief in privacy'
Courts determine whether the information was private and protected by the Convention by applying an objective test of 'a balance of probability of privacy"

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. In a breach of confidence action concerning disclosure of private information, the first question that should be asked is: was the information private in the sense protected by Article 8 of the Convention? This is determined by applying an objective test of 'reasonable expectation of privacy'. Lead case: McKennitt v Ash [2006] EWCA Civ 1714.

stem: A woman is the treehold owner of a property. She executes a transter of the legal and equitable title to the property to a man and delivers the transfer deed to him. The man does not register the transfer and puts it away in a bank safe deposit box and therefore the property remains registered in the woman's name. Two years later, the woman dies. The personal representative of the woman's estate claims that the transfer of the property was not valid and therefore the property belongs to the estate.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Legal and equitable title to the property has passed to the man and the property does not form part of the woman's estate
The woman holds the property on an express trust for the man and the property does not form part of the woman's estate
The woman holds the property on a resulting trust for the man and the property does not form part of the woman's estate
The woman holds the property on a constructive trust for the man and the property does not form part of the man's estate
Legal and equitable title to the property have remained with the woman and the propertv forms nart of her estate

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The woman holds the property on a constructive trust. The transfer of the legal title fails, because the transfer must be registered at HM Land Registry in order to make the transfer effective at law. However, the common intention of the woman and man was that the property would be transferred to the man; therefore, although the woman retains the legal title due to a failure of the transfer, equitable title has nevertheless been conveyed to the man. An express trust could not arise in these circumstances, as any express trust contained in the transfer would have been on the basis that the legal title would vest in the man. A constructive trust is imposed by the court as a personal representative who holds the legal title through the estate to assert their legal interest to the exclusion of the man who claims the beneficial interest of the property. This is so because of a common intention formed between the woman and the man that the beneficial interest would be held in a certain way.

stem: A woman executes a will in which she leaves a legacy of £50,000 to her friend absolutely. When the woman who executed the will returns home, she writes a letter to her friend stating that the £50,000 is to be used to pay for the education of her friend's daughter, who is aged five, but that the woman did not want to include this in the will as it would have made their other friends jealous.
ask: The woman dies five Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The friend holds the £50,000 on trust for her daughter
The trust is invalid as it is a testamentary disposition and it violates s.9 of the Wills Act 1837 by not being made in writing
The trust is invalid as there is no certainty of intention
The trust is invalid as there is no certainty of subject matter
The trust is invalid as there is no certainty of objects

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Although testamentary dispositions should generally be made by deed to be valid, where a secret trust is created, the trust is said to be declared during the testator's lifetime (when they communicate its terms to the trustee) with the testamentary disposition only constituting the transfer of the trust asset to the trustee and not the declaration of trust itself. It is therefore a valid trust, even though its terms are not included in the will (Re Young [1951]). The trust would have certainty of intention, which could clearly be inferred from the letter, certainty of subject matter (the specific legacy under the will) and certainty of objects, being the education of the friend's daughter.

stem: Opposing counsel made submissions to the court in regard to a disabled couple who are facing eviction from a local authority housing department for non-payment of rent. stem: An energy company suggested to a petrol station that they should formalise the existing agreement between them in which the energy company supplied a tanker of petrol to the petrol station on a weekly basis. A draft agreement was drawn up and before signing and returning it to the petrol station, the energy company inserted several new clauses into the draft and introduced the name of an arbitrator who would decide upon any differences which might arise. The petrol station's manager simply put the signed agreement into a drawer, continuing to accept a weekly supply of the petrol on the terms specified in the draft. A dispute has now arisen between the parties, and the energy company argues that there was no contract, because it was not formally executed.
ask: Which option best states the legal position?

options.en: A binding contract arose out of the parties' conduct; as soon as the petrol station's manager put the draft agreement into his drawer, a contract was made, even though none was formally entered into
A binding contract arose out of the parties' conduct; they had indicated by their conduct that they had waived the execution of the formal document and agreed to act on the basis of the draft
A binding contract did not arise from the parties' conduct; the signed and returned agreement was merely an invitation to treat
A binding contract did not arise from the parties' conduct; there must have been some act on the part of the petrol station to indicate its acceptance
A binding contract did not arise from the parties' conduct; for an offer to have been accepted there must be a promise, either by words or in writing, which must be clear and unambiguous

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. While the draft was not binding on the parties (the energy company having inserted new terms), the parties had indicated by their conduct that they had waived the execution of the formal document and agreed to act on the basis of the draft. The fact is that the petrol station had placed orders on the basis of the agreement, and the energy company should therefore be taken to be bound by its terms. The arbitration clause is not a red herring; it illustrates that when the draft was offered by the petrol station and approved by the energy company, everything was agreed to, except the name of the arbitrator, yet both parties acted upon the draft and treated it as binding. stem: Two men would like to incorporate a private limited company for their business. They are unsure if they need to appoint a company secretary.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: Public companies must have a company secretary whilst private companies may, at their discretion, have a company secretary or not
Both public and private companies must have a company secretary
Both public and private companies must have a company secretary unless the articles of association state otherwise
Neither private nor public companies must appoint a company secretary
Private companies must have a company secretary whilst public companies may, at their discretion, have a company secretary or not

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. Section 270 of the Companies Act 2006 states that a private company is not required to have a secretary, whereas section 271 of the Companies Act 2006 states that a public company must have a secretary.

stem: Upon the Queen's handing over of the throne in favour of Prince Charles, now King Charles, a backlog of Parliamentary matters needs attending to. An advisor informs him that he is required to obey the will of his Ministers by the granting of Royal Assent. New to his role, the King requests advice as to what his adviser is referring to.
ask: Which option best advises the King?

options.en: Royal Assent refers to the Monarch formally approving an Act of Parliament to become a Parliamentary Bill, thus making it a law
Royal Assent refers to the role the Monarch plays in the annual ceremonial opening of Parliament
Royal Assent refers to the Monarch's annual State Opening of Parliament ceremony where the Queen opens Parliament, in person, and addresses both Houses in The Queen's Speech
Royal Assent refers to the Monarch formally approving a Parliamentary Bill to become an Act of Parliament, thus making it a law
Royal Assent refers to the Monarch formally approving a Parliamentary Bill to become an Act of Parliament, thus making it a law, which then cannot be overturned by Parliament

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best option. When a Bill has completed all its parliamentary stages in both Houses, it must have Royal Assent before it can become an Act of Parliament (law). Royal Assent is the Monarch's agreement to make the Bill into an Act and is a formality. There is no set time period between the consideration of amendments to the Bill and Royal Assent - it can even be a matter of minutes after the process whereby the Bill has passed back and forth between the two Houses debating amendments to the Bill has been completed.

stem: A foreign student seeking naturalisation in the UK has had her naturalisation application refused. The (fictional) British Naturalisation Act provides that the Home Secretary "shall not be required to assign any reason for the grant or refusal of any application" and that his decision "shall not be subject to appeal to, or review in, any '. She is seeking judicial review of the decision.
ask: Which of the following statements best captures the courts' stance in such a?

options.en: The doctrine of Parliamentary sovereignty does not allow for the judicial review of primary legislation (Acts of Parliament)

Decisions taken under the Royal Prerogative, (Royal Prerogative is the term given to the formal powers of the Crown within the executive process of British politics), are not amenable to judicial review
Since the courts in the UK may strike down offensive Parliamentary legislation, the Home Secretary could not refuse Leila's naturalisation application

If the court considers that Parliament could not have intended the decision maker to be enabled to act unfairly and in breach of natural justice, this may take the decision-maker outside his or her jurisdiction and be challenged
Parliamentary Acts, that have duly received Royal Assent, explicitly and implicitly oust the court's jurisdiction of judicial review

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Ouster clauses do not oust jurisdiction of the courts for the purpose of procedural judicial review. The rules of natural justice apply and any breach of those rules would make the Home Secretary ultra vires and hence subject to review notwithstanding the statute. Lead case: Rv Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Fayed [1998] 1 WLR 736.

stem: A man borrows his brother's car to go to the seaside. The brother, who is away for the weekend, had allowed him to borrow the car previously in one occasion, but the man had not asked his brother's permission this time.

Consent is irrelevant to appropriation
While consent may be relevant to dishonesty, it is irrelevant to appropriation

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. E is correct. The man has assumed a single right of the owner of the car by borrowing it and so has thus appropriated it. While consent is irrelevant to appropriation, it may be relevant to dishonesty. Criminal Law; Theft; Statute: s.2 (1) Theft Act 1968.

stem: A merchant bank gave a reference to another bank concerning the financial position of a potential client, which sought to borrow money to finance an advertising campaign. ask: What are the advertising agent's prospects of success?

options.en: Slim, because the law will not imply a duty of care when a party looking for information from a party possessed of a special skill trusts it to exercise due care, even if that party knew or ought to have known that reliance was being placed on its skill and judgment

Although the law will imply a duty of care when a party seeking information from a party possessed of a special skill trusts it to exercise due care, and that party knew or ought to have known that reliance was being placed on its skill and judgment, since here there was an express disclaimer of responsibility, however, no such duty was implied. In Hedley Byrne v Heller, the respondents' disclaimer was adequate to exclude an assumption by them of the legal duty of care, but in the absence of a disclaimer, the circumstances would have given rise to a duty of care, despite the absence of a contract or fiduciary relationship. 1*2

stem: A man owns two shops in a small inland village, which are on opposite sides of the street. The restrictive covenant would be protected by a Notice in the Charges Register of the fishmonger's title and a Notice in the Property Register of the owner's title

stem: A man had given biometric samples during police investigations. explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. stem: Two women have formed a partnership through which they intend to trade as estate agents. They intend to call the partnership "HM Estates" and have had stationary produced showing this name, the partnership's office address and stating that a list of partner names can be inspected at its offices.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The two women will have to reconsider the partnership's name and change their stationary
The two women will have to reconsider the partnership's name but the stationary would be acceptable
The two women will have to change their stationary but the partnership's name would be acceptable
The partnership's name and stationary are acceptable

explanation.en: i ting that a list of You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is E. A business cannot be called anything that would give the impression that it is connected with the UK Government and, therefore, "HM" would not be likely to be acceptable for the purposes of the Business Names Act 1985. stem: A woman is a used car dealer who contracts with a client to sell them 20 cars for a total amount of £100,000. She agrees that the client can select the cars from her stock from time to time over the following six months. After two months, the woman is made bankrupt, with the client only having taken ten cars.
ask: The client claims that the ten most valuable cars held by the woman at the time of her bankruptcy do not form part of her bankruptcy estate and are held on trust for it under the terms of the Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The ten most valuable cars are held on trust for the client and are therefore out of the reach of the woman's other creditors
There is no trust in favour of the client because there is no certainty of intention
There is no trust in favour of the client because there is no certainty of subject matter
There is no trust in favour of the client because there is no certainty of objects
There is no trust in favour of the client because there was no written trust deed

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. The other two certainties would exist- there would be a certainty of intention to create an interest on the part of the client in some of the cars that the woman had in stock, and there would be a certainty of objects (the client). However, there would be no certainty of subject matter, since the cars are all different and distinct from each other (see Re London Wine Co (Shippers) Ltd [1986] and Hunter v Moss [1994]). It is not strictly necessary for an express written declaration of trust to be made, and in circumstances such as this, the court would be prepared to infer a trust.

stem: The two sole partners of a firm of solicitors approach another solicitor for advice. One partner wishes to leave the partnership, while the other partner has agreed to buy his interest in the partnership. Both have the same aim, they say, and they would like to use the same solicitor to act for them to be as cost effective as possible.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes what the solicitor consulted by the partners is allowed to do?

options.en: Act for both partners, as there is no conflict of interest between the two clients
Act for both partners, as both clients have a common interest
Act for both partners, provided both clients consent
Act for either partner, but not both
Act for neither partner

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Superficially, the two clients have a common interest - the partner who wishes to leave desires to sell, while the partner who wishes to stay wants to buy - enabling them to rely on the 'common interest' exception in 03.6. However, they are very much in a situation requiring negotiation between them: the partner who remains will desire to pay as little as possible for his share in the partnership, while the partner who stays will desire to receive as high a price as possible for his partnership interest. Other areas for potential conflict may arise regarding such issues as the liability for the debts of the partner who remains. The two cannot, therefore, be said to have a common interest, due to their conflicting issues..11 indicates that solicitors should not act for two or more clients in a conflict of interest under Outcome 3.6 (substantially common interest) where the clients' interests in the end result are not the same, for example, one partner buying out the interest of the other partner in their joint business.

The offence can be committed in a public or private place, except when the persons involved are inside a dwelling

A person is guilty of an offence if, with intent to cause a person harassment, alarm, or distress, he uses threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour, or disorderly behaviour, or displays any writing, sign or other visible representation which is abusive or insulting, thereby causing that or another person harassment, alarm or distress, or physical damage. The offence can be committed in a public or private place, except when the persons involved are inside a dwelling

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. The offence of intentional harassment, alarm or distress is as set out in section 4A of the Act. A person is guilty of the of an offence if, with intent to cause a person harassment, alarm, or distress, he uses threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour, or disorderly behaviour, or displays any writing, sign or other visible representation which is abusive or insulting, thereby causing that or another person harassment, alarm or distress. The offence can be committed in a public or private place, except when the persons involved are inside a dwelling. Causing damage is not required.

stem: A man aged 35 has been convicted of racially aggravated murder of a woman 19 years ago and is due to be sentenced following a pre-sentence report. The starting point by which the judge must set a minimum term before an adult may be considered for parole for racially aggravated murder is 30 years. The starting point for an offender under 18, however, is 12 years, even if the offence is racially motivated.
ask: Which option best advises the man?

options.en: The starting point for the man is 12 years, and he must serve his sentence in an adult prison
The starting point for the man is 12 years, and he must serve his sentence in a young offender's institute

The starting point for the man is 12 years, and he must serve the period prior until he would have attained 18 years of age when committing the offence in a young offender's institute; the remainder in an adult prison
The starting point for the man is 30 years, and he must serve his sentence in an adult prison
The starting point for the man is 30 years, since he cannot rely on his evading justice as an adult and then claim juvenile status, and he must serve his sentence in an adult prison

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. A is the best answer. The man was 16 when he committed the offence. Since he is now an adult, he can expect to serve his sentence in adult prisons. The starting point for an offender under 18 years, however, is 12 years, even if the offence is racially motivated. C cannot be correct because, as the fact pattern clearly illustrates, the man is no longer a minor having attained the age of majority. By a basic subtraction, it's quite obvious that the man was a sixteen year-old juvenile when he committed the offence, and must therefore be sentenced as a sixteen year-old offender (despite being now an adult). This does not mean, of course, that he would be allowed to serve the first part of his sentence F

stem: A firm of third party stevedores negligently damaged barrels of chemicals. The stevedores then claimed immunity offered by a limitation clause contained in the bill of lading which governed the relationship between the shipping company and the carrier.
ask: The stevedores were under contract with the shipping company, which contained an exclusion clause, but the exclusion clause did not explicitly mention the Would the stevedores be able to rely on the exclusion clause under the common law doctrine of privity of contract?

options.en: Yes, because under the doctrine of vicarious immunity, the stevedores would be able to rely upon any exemption clause in the contract, even though they were not a party to it

Yes, because the 'commercial reality' approach allows the stevedores to rely upon any exemption clause in a contract, provided it was the intention of all concerned, that the benefit should be extended to them
No, because the doctrine of privity means that the stevedores, as a third party, are denied the effectiveness of a contract, even where that is the expressed intention of the parties
No; although the stevedores were not parties to the contract of carriage, they would be able to rely on the limitation clause, even though the limitation clause did not mention the stevedores by name

No; since the stevedores were not parties to the contract of carriage, they would not be able to rely on the limitation clause, especially since the limitation clause did not mention the stevedores by name

explanation.en: E is correct. The common law doctrine of privity of contract affirms in the absence of a trust or agency, a person cannot rely on a term in a contract to which he is not a party, even if he is the person whom the contract is intended to benefit. Lead case: Scruttons Ltd v Midland Silicones Ltd [1962] AC 446; [1962] 1 AIl ER 1.

stem: You are assisting a client who is buying a house to find a suitable endowment mortgage. You therefore introduce your client to an authorised third person (ATP) and then make arrangements for him to acquire the policy recommended by the ATP. Your client asks your opinion concerning the policy recommended by the ATP.
ask: Which of the following best explains the legal position in order to avoid making an unlawful financial promotion?

options.en: You will be exempt from making an unlawful financial promotion, because you can rely on the ATP exemption
You will be exempt from making an unlawful financial promotion, because you can rely on the 'introducers' exemption
You will be exempt from making an unlawful financial promotion, because you can rely on the 'professional firms' exemption
You will be exempt from making an unlawful financial promotion, because you can rely on the exemption for one-off financial promotions
You cannot provide an opinion on the policy, because no exemption against the prohibition on unlawful financial promotion is available

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. One client buying one property and being advised about one endowment policy is a one-off financial promotion. Further, each property purchase for separate client is likely to be a one-off financial promotion. It will only cease to be "one-off" if the solicitor regularly or frequently performs restricted activities such as advising about or arranging endowment policies. The one-off financial promotion exemption will exempt the solicitor from making an otherwise unlawful financial promotion. -- - The 'introducers' exemption would not be available to follow-up advice concerning the policy recommended by the ATP. The 'professional firms' exemption is available only where either the exclusion for reasonably necessary work performed in the course of the solicitor's profession applies or where the incidental exemption applies. The ATP exclusion from regulated activities is the most appropriate exclusion - however, this does not exist as an exemption in respect of financial promotions.

stem: A seven year old child died after eating poisonous berries in a council run park. The berries looked like cherries or blackcurrants. The council knew of the berries, and there were no warning signs, but the plot was enclosed by a wooden fence.
ask: How would you describe the council's legal position regarding liability?

options.en: Even if the council had been negligent, the child contributed to his own injuries, so any damages would be reduced on grounds of contributory negligence
The council would not be liable, because the duty resting upon an occupier does not include an obligation of protection against dangers which are by themselves familiar and obvious
Since the child was a trespasser, having climbed over or through the wooden fence, the council would not be liable

The council is not liable, because it was the parents' own responsibility in respect that they either had not effectively taught the child not to take what did not belong to it, or that they had not arranged for proper adult supervision of the child whilst it was in a public park
An occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults, so the council would be liable

explanation.en: E is correct. If an occupier admits children to the premises, the child visitor must be reasonably safe. Lead case: Glasgow Corp v Taylor [1922] 1 AC 44. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 2(3)(a) Occupiers' Liability Act 1957.

stem: A woman is the owner of the fee simple of a property.
ask: She transfers her interest to a man and inserts a provision in the transfer that the man can hold the fee simple "until he qualifies as a solicitor" Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The woman has transferred the fee simple absolute in possession to the man and he has a legal estate in the property
The woman has not transferred the fee simple absolute in possession to the man and he has a legal estate in the property
The woman has transferred the fee simple absolute in possession to the man and has an equitable interest in the property
The woman has not transferred the fee simple absolute in possession to the man and he has an equitable interest in the property
The transfer does not operate at law or in equity and the man has neither a legal nor equitable interest in the property

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The woman has not transferred the fee simple absolute in possession to the man and he has an equitable interest in the property. The estate that the woman has transferred to the man will not necessarily last forever as the man may one day qualify as a solicitor. The woman has attempted to create a "determinable fee" which, by virtue of s.1 of the Law interest.

stem: A woman was watching a football match in the main stand of the stadium when the roof behind one of the goals collapsed due to shoddy construction. The woman's fiancé was also at the match, and although she could not recognise him in the large crowd, she reasonably feared that he was one of those reportedly killed or injured. Seven hours later she identified the body of her fiancé after making her way to the mortuary, and is now suffering from nervous shock.
ask: Which of the following statements most accurately reflects the law concerning the woman's prospects for a successful claim for psychiatric injury in such circumstances?

options.en: connection for the woman to qualify as a secondary victim

Since the woman was so close in space and time to the accident, had to identify her fiancé's body in the mortuary, and met the requirement of having close ties of love and affection with the principal victim, there was a sufficiently direct connection for the woman to qualify as a secondary victim

By viewing the disaster at the stadium, and seeing her fiancé's body in the mortuary, the woman would be entitled to recover damages as a secondary victim, since taken together these constituted a single incident

The woman would not be entitled to recover damages as a secondary victim, because the requirement of having close ties of love and affection with the principal victim of the trauma applies to close family members only, and does not stretch to fiancé and fiancée

Although there was a sufficiently close relationship of love and affection between the woman and her fiancé to make it reasonably foreseeable that she would suffer psychiatric injury in the circumstances, she was neither sufficiently proximate to the event, nor the immediate aftermath, nor in the immediate zone of danger

explanation.en: E is correct. Even though there was a sufficiently close relationship of love and affection between the woman and her fiancé, watching the event from a position of safety in another part of the stadium and only identifying her fiancé's corpse in the mortuary several hours after his death was too far removed from the shocking events to be within the "immediate aftermath" or the "zone of danger". In Alcock v. Chief Constable of South Yorkshire, the House of Lords confirmed that only the parents and spouses of the victims could recover damages for nervous shock and only then if they had actually witnessed the scene of the accident or identified bodies immediately afterwards.

stem: Your client was dismissed from her job as a prison guard for whistle-blowing about gender discrimination against staff at the private prison where she worked. Her appeal against dismissal was unsuccessful and her father is so concerned that he is seeking judicial review of the prison Board of Governors' decision. He argues that, despite a recommendation by an official inquiry to tackle gender discrimination in the prison five years ago, and which the Board of Governors had publicly agreed to implement, it is still not being implemented.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes your client's father's legal situation concerning any application for judicial review?

options.en: An application for judicial review would probably fail, because your client's father neither has locus standi, nor can the prison be considered a public body
Even though the prison could be considered a public body, an application for judicial review would probably fail, because your client's father does not have locus standi
Even though your client's father has locus standi, an application for judicial review would probably fail, because the prison cannot be considered a public body
An application for judicial review would probably succeed, because your client's father has locus standi, and the prison can be considered a public body
An application for judicial review would probably succeed, because your client's father has locus standi, and it is irrelevant whether the prison can be considered a public body

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. To be entitled to apply for judicial review of a decision in principle, a person must have a "sufficient interest" (or standing), and it would appear that your client's father lacks this requirement. It can be argued that the private prison agency is a 'hybrid' public authority and that therefore the prison is carrying out a public function. Lead case: Aston Cantlow v Wallbank [2003] UKHL 37. Comment: In a modern, developed state, governmental functions extend far beyond maintenance of law and order and defence of the realm. Further, the manner in E varies considerably. In the interests of efficiency and economy, and for other reasons, functions of a governmental nature are frequently discharged by non-governmental bodies. Sometimes this will be a consequence of privatisation, sometimes not. One obvious example is the running of prisons by commercial organisations. Parochial Church Council of the Parish of Aston Cantlow and Wilmcote with Billesley, Warwickshire v. Wallbank & Anor [2003] UKHL (26 June 2003).

stem: The Minister for Consumer Affairs has briefed her Parliamentary Private Secretary (PPS) on the drafting of legislation that is being prepared for Parliamentary approval. She asks her PPS for advice regarding what impact, if any, the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA) will have if the legislation is challenged in the courts.
ask: Which option best states the impact the HRA has on judicial interpretation of?

options.en: The HRA requires legislation to be interpreted unconditionally in a way which is compatible with the rights contained in the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention)
The HRA requires legislation to be interpreted in some measure which is compatible with Convention rights
The HRA requires legislation to be interpreted unreservedly in a way which is compatible with Convention rights
The HRA requires legislation to be interpreted as far as possible in a way which is compatible with Convention rights
The HRA requires legislation to be interpreted to a certain extent in a way which is compatible with Convention riahts

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Section 3 of the HRA mandates that statutes must be read, and given effect, in a way that is, as far as possible, compatible with Convention rights. Courts must seek to interpret primary and secondary legislation, as defined by Section 21, so as to be compatible with the HRA. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 3 HRA 1998.

stem: An entertainer agreed to perform at a club for the entire month of June. One of the contract terms states that 'the entertainer undertakes not perform at any other club during the entire month of June'. The club owner has discovered that the entertainer will be appearing at a rival club between those dates.
ask: Which equitable remedy would be most appropriate if the club owner wished to stop the entertainer from appearing at the rival venue?

options.en: Restitutionary damages
Prohibitory injunction
Quantum Meruit
Specific performance
Declaratory injunction

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. As the term imposes upon the entertainer a negative obligation, the injunction sought will be a prohibitory injunction. Lead case: Lumley v Wagner (1852) 1 De GM & G 604.

stem: A driver suffers a sudden and unforeseen loss of consciousness whilst driving his car. The car subsequently passes through a red traffic light and collides with another vehicle, causing severe damage to the other vehicle and killing its driver.
ask: Which option best advises the driver as regards his criminal liability, if any?

options.en: The driver is liable to be charged with relevant offences concerning the incident because the standard required of any driver is the standard of the reasonably competent and experienced driver
The driver is liable to be charged with the offences of criminal damage (to the other vehicle) and causing death by careless or inconsiderate driving
The driver is liable to be charged with causing death by careless or inconsiderate driving because involuntary incapacity is not a defence to such strict liability offences
No offence had been committed because the driver reacted instinctively to a stimulus that results in him committing a criminal breach of the law
No offence had been committed because involuntariness or automatism is always a complete defence to any criminal charge

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. D is the best option. A person will not be criminally liable where he reacts instinctively to a stimulus that results in him committing a criminal breach of the law. The classic example of this is where a person "...became unconscious while driving; for example, if he were struck by a stone or overcome by a sudden illness; or the car was temporarily out of control by his being attacked by a swarm of bees...". E is not the best option because, although involuntariness or automatism is ordinarily a complete defence to any criminal charge, the use of that defence is limited by a number of considerations. Lead Case: Kay v Butterworth (1945) 61 TLR 452, 453.

stem: A woman executes a declaration of trust, by which she places £100,000,000 in trust for her niece, who is 19. The woman appoints a solicitor as the trustee of the trust and the terms of the deed give the solicitor an unrestricted power to invest the fund however she sees fit. The solicitor's husband is starting out as an independent investment consultant and, although he has no experience in managing a fund so large, she places the fund at his disposal to be invested. The fund fails to generate as much income as it should.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The solicitor is under no duties as to how she should exercise her powers as trustee, as neither the trust nor common law impose any duties upon her
The solicitor is under no duties as to how she should exercise her powers as trustee, as the beneficiary is over the age of 18

The common law implies additional restrictions into the trust deed as to how a trustee should exercise their powers which apply in all cases, except where a trustee has delegated management of the fund to another
Regardless of the contents of the trust deed, the solicitor has an absolute duty to act in the best interests of the niece as beneficiary at all times

Regardless of the contents of the trust deed, the solicitor has an absolute duty to act in the best interests of the niece as beneficiary, except where to do so would diminish the capital value of the trust

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is D. Regardless of the contents of the trust deed, the solicitor has an absolute duty to act in the best interests of the niece at all times. This duty arises by virtue of the fact that she is in a fiduciary relationship with her as trustee and beneficiary. A fiduciary relationship can arise regardless of the ages of the parties and regardless of the contents of any instrument governing their relationship. The duties exist at the very heart of the parties' relationship with each other and consequently should not be regarded as having been implied into any document.

stem: A man and woman are friends who purchase a large town house together which they hold on trust for themselves as joint tenants. Some years later, the man decides that he wants to go travelling with his fiancée and agrees with the woman that she will buy his interest in the property. However, they agree that she will pay the money to the man when he returns from his travels so that he can buy his own house with his fiancée. While they are in Australia, the man and his fiancée are bitten by a venomous spider and die.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: At the time of the man's death, he and the woman held the property as joint tenants. The woman has inherited the man's share in the property according to the Doctrine of Survivorship
At the time of the man's death, he and the woman held the property as tenants in common. The woman has inherited the man's share in the property according to the Doctrine of Survivorship
At the time of the man's death, he and the woman held the property as joint tenants. The man's share passes to his estate
At the time of the man's death, he and the woman held the property as tenants in common. The man's share passes to his estate

The agreement between the man and the woman operated to transfer the man's beneficial interest to the woman and, at the time of the man's death, he and the woman held the property on trust for herself

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: cording to You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is D. At the time of the man's death, he and the woman held the property as tenants in common. The man's share passes to his estate. It is possible for a joint tenancy to be severed by the mutual agreement of all joint tenants, and specifically where one joint tenant agrees to buy the other out (Burgess v Rawnsley [1975] Ch 429) and therefore, once the agreement was made, the joint tenancy was severed, even though the agreement was never actually completed.

stem: An Act of Parliament confers a power on local authorities to make delegated legislation in the form of by-laws. Donfield Borough Council is seeking to make a by- law controlling the number of dogs walked by a person in parks and open spaces.
ask: The council seeks advice with regards to its competence, if any, to make such a Which option best describes the nature and status of delegated legislation?

options.en: Delegated legislation is made by the general public, rather than Parliament itself passing the delegated legislation
Delegated legislation is made by a person to whom authority is delegated, rather than Parliament itself passing the delegated legislation
Delegated legislation is made by Parliament itself passing the delegated legislation, rather than the Ministers to whom authority is delegated
Delegated legislation is made by Parliament itself passing the delegated legislation, rather than a person to whom authority is delegated
Delegated legislation is made by private Members of Parliament (MP's) and Peers who are not Government Ministers, rather than Parliament itself passing the delegated legislation

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is the best answer. Delegated or subordinate legislation is made by ministers (regulations in the form of so-called 'statutory instruments') and other bodies outside of central government (e.g. local authority bye-laws). Its primary use is to supplement Acts of Parliament by prescribing the detailed and technical rules required for their operation. Unlike an Act, it has the advantage that it can be made, and later amended if necessary, without taking up parliamentary time.

stem: On the last day of a business trip to London, a man orders a meal at an expensive restaurant. The meal takes longer than expected, so as soon as he finishes the meal, he rushes out of the restaurant and to the airport to catch his flight. He left his business card with his UK and international contact details on the table at the restaurant. On the back of the card he has handwritten:
ask: "Call me for CC details 2 Which criminal offence has the man committed, if any?

options.en: The man has committed no criminal offence - it is a civil matter between the parties
The man has committed no criminal offence or breach of civil law
The man has committed the offence of fraud by false representation
The man has committed the offence of theft
The man has committed the offence of making off without payment

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is B. The man has committed no criminal offence or breach of civil law. The offence of making off without payment is defined under Section 3 of the Theft Act 1978 as where: "... a person who, knowing that payment on the spot for any goods supplied or service done is required or expected from him, dishonestly makes off without having paid as required or expected and with intent to avoid payment of the amount due...". The prosecution must prove that the man made off from the spot without having paid when payment was due (actus reus) and that the man knew that payment was due, and dishonestly intended to avoid payment (mens rea). The prosecution will be unlikely to succeed in showing the man's dishonest intention to avoid payment. In this case, the man was in a rush and left his business card with contact details and a written request for the restaurant to call him for credit card details so as to pay the bill. The man has merely deferred payment, as opposed to avoiding it. The dishonest intention not to pay for the goods or services after having received them was never formed in the man's mind. In Rv Allen [1985] AC 1029, it was held that a mere intention to defer payment would not meet the mens rea requirement for the offence to be complete. civil law (i.e. breach of a contractual agreement) and is therefore not a civil law matter between the parties. The man isn't claiming he doesn't owe the money nor refusing to pay nor inviting civil recovery proceedings; he acknowledges he owes the money but is paying in a slightly different manner than cash immediately on completing the meal. There is a debt but not incurred in breach of civil law.

stem: The building of an oil refinery was authorised by an Act of Parliament. Local residents brought an action against the refinery due to the subsequent smell and noise caused by the refinery once it began operating. The company's defence is that the nuisance is an inevitable result of operating the refinery, which they have been given statutory authority to do and been carried on reasonably.
ask: Which option best describes the legal position?

options.en: Clear statutory authority excuses all nuisances
Clear statutory authority excuses private nuisances
Clear statutory authority excuses public nuisances
Clear statutory authority excuses nuisances born out of necessity
Clear statutory authority excuses nuisances if the activities are carried on reasonably

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. E is the best option. Where Parliament has authorised the doing of a particular act, any right of action in nuisance based on that act is barred as long as the statutory powers are exercised without negligence (i.e. with all reasonable regard and care for the interests of others). In the context of the fact pattern, it would be a good defence to the company if it is able to prove that the activities are carried on reasonably.

stem: A private company limited by shares, has issued 100 fully paid up £1 shares, all of which are held by a holding company. The holding company is a private company limited by shares and has issued two fully paid up shares, one to a man and one to a woman. The man dies, leaving no will and no heirs.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Both companies must be wound up
The holding company must be wound up, but the subsidiary company will continue to exist
The subsidiary company must be wound up but the holding company will continue to exist
Both companies will continue to exist, with the man's share in the holding company passing to the woman
Both companies will continue to exist, with the man's share in the holding company remaining in his estate

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is E. The man, woman, holding and subsidiary companies all have distinct legal personalities and, therefore, the death or winding up of one of them will not affect the rights and constitution of the others. The man's shareholding in the holding company will remain in his estate which, if he has left no heir, will become bona vacantia and pass to the Crown to be administered by the Treasury Solicitor. However, the holding company will remain fully constituted and benefits from perpetual succession, despite the death or winding up of its members. As the holding company is the only member of the subsidiary company, it follows that if the holding company continues in

stem: After reading the warning on the label of a tampon packet, which warned of the risk of toxic shock from tampons, a female complainant proceeded to use the product. She suffered toxic shock syndrome as a consequence, but because she did not comprehend the symptoms she was suffering from, her injuries were exacerbated and she eventually had to be hospitalised.
ask: Is the manufacturer liable under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 (CPA) in such an?

options.en: A warning label on toxic shock syndrome would be sufficient to warn the consumer of the risks of using the product; therefore, the manufacturer would not be liable
Liability is strict, so it is not necessary to prove that the manufacturer was at fault in causing the defect and the presence of a warning has no impact whatsoever

The manufacturer would not be liable, because while warnings provided directly to consumers with a product are a factor in measuring liability under the CPA, they have no relevance unless they are delivered by a professional intermediary, such as the Chief Medical Officer
The manufacturer would be liable on the basis that it owed a continuing duty to warn of any faults. The warning was not sufficient, so they should have modified or withdrawn the product
The manufacturer would not be liable, because the warning label served to completely exclude the manufacturer's liability by contract term or notice

explanation.en: A warning label on toxic shock syndrome would be sufficient to warn the consumer of the risks of using the product; therefore, the manufacturer would not be liable. A product is defective if it is not as "safe as persons generally are entitled to expect", considering such factors as instructions or warnings supplied with the product and the products marketing method. "Defect" does not require the ultimate level of safety. Products will not be defective so long as they meet a minimum standard fixed by the defectiveness standard, regardless of whether the product could have been made safer in some way. Lead case: Worsley v Tambrands Ltd (2000) PIQR 95.

stem: A trader challenged legislation imposing a tax on financial transactions conducted by the London Stock Exchange. A High Court judge noted she was under an obligation imposed by the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA) to detect potential breaches of the European Convention on Human Rights (the Convention). The judge was satisfied that the legislation was incapable of being interpreted compatibly with Convention rights and made a declaration of incompatibility (DOI).
ask: Which option best states how DOl's affect legislation, if at all?

options.en: The continuing validity and enforcement of any legislation is affected by a DOI
The continuing validity and enforcement of any legislation is not affected by a DOI
The respective parties to High Court proceedings are bound by a DOI
A DOI does not affect the validity, continuing operation or enforcement of the provision but is binding on the parties to the proceedings
A DOl affects the validity, continuing operation or enforcement of the provision but is not binding on the parties to the proceedings

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. A declaration of incompatibility will not affect the validity of the Act of Parliament and a public authority will not be acting unlawfully in applying the legislation. But it confirms that the Convention rights have been breached and provides the UK Government with the power to use a special procedure to amend the conflicting Act of Parliament quickly. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 4 HRA 1998.

stem: A man became a barrister in 1987, and became a Queen's Counsel in 2002. He has been a noted human rights advisor to government and is generally seen as supportive of the Prime Minister in his out.
ask: He has been sounded out for appointment as head of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and asks you what his What is the official title of the head of the CPS?

options.en: The Attorney-General
The Queen
The Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP)
The Lord Chief Justice
The Lord Chancellor

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The DPP is head of the CPS and statutorily required to issue guidance to crown prosecutors on, for example, when to institute or continue proceedings and which charges should be preferred. The Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 provides the statutory framework for the duties and powers of the DPP and The CPS. Criminal Law; CPS; DPP; Prosecution of Offences Act 1985.

stem: You are acting for a property developer who is the owner of the fee simple in a property. The owner has granted a tenant a lease of the property for a term of two years and six months, to take effect in four months' time. To be on the safe side, you have insisted that the property owner grant the lease by deed.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The lease takes effect in law and does not need to be registered at HM Land Registry
In order to take effect in law, the lease must be registered at HM Land Registry, due to the length of its term
In order to take effect in law, the lease must be registered at HM Land Registry, due to the start date
In order to take effect in law the, lease must be registered at HM Land Registry, as it is made by deed
A lease for less than three years will always operate in equity only

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is C. In order to take effect in law the lease must be registered at HM Land Registry, due to the start date. The lease is a reversionary lease, meaning that it is not granted to give possession to the tenant immediately. Reversionary leases which grant possession to the lessee more than three months from the date of grant must always be registered in order to take effect at law, regardless of their term.

stem: An experienced dairy farmer sold milk to a man who was visiting the countryside from London. The milk turned out to be infected with typhoid, and killed the man's wife, who had been feeling unwell, due to her pregnancy. The farmer can show, however, that he had used all reasonable care to prevent such an infection.
ask: With reference to the Sale of Goods Act 1979, can the farmer escape liability from claim for damages from the man whose wife was poisoned?

options.en: Yes, because in the context of fitness for the purpose, the Act does not apply to business sales, only to private sales
Yes, because the man did not rely on the farmer's skill and judgement when buying the milk from him
Yes, because the man's wife was unusually sensitive due to her pregnancy, as the milk would not have harmed a normal person
No, the milk was not reasonably fit for the man's purpose; because the duty is absolute, the farmer has no answer to the man's claim
No, because even if the man's wife was found to be unusually sensitive to milk, and the milk would not have harmed a normal person, the farmer is still liable

explanation.en: = You did not select the correct answer. D is correct. Plainly, this milk was not reasonably fit for the buyer's purpose; it was no answer to the buyer's claim that the sellers had used all reasonable care to prevent such an infection. Lead case: Frost v Aylesbury Dairy Co [1905] 1 KB 608.

stem: Your client wishes to draw up a will for distribution of his assets. Whilst he has been married for 30 years, he has a mistress whom he has been seeing for the last 3 years. Your client wishes to leave some of his assets to the mistress in the event of his death, however he does not want his family - particularly his wife - to know about it.
ask: Can your client create a secret trust?

options.en: No, because a secret trust is at odds with the formalities requirements of the Wills Act 1837 and so is not capable of being effective
Yes, as long as he establishes the secret trust by placing a moral obligation on the trustee and communicating that intention to the trustee, who accepts that obligation

Yes, as long as he has the intention to establish a secret trust by obliging the trustee to receive the property; passes the property to the trustee; communicates his intention to the trustee; and the trustee accepts that obligation
Yes, as long as he names a trustee and states that the purposes of the trust are to follow
Yes, as long as he leaves the trust property in his will and communicates the terms of that trust to the trustee in private

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is C. Yes, as long as he has the intention to establish a secret trust by obliging the trustee to receive the property; passes the property to the trustee as beneficiary; communicates his intention to the trustee; and the trustee accepts that obligation. A secret trust requires the intention of the testator to establish a secret trust by obliging the trustee to receive the property then pass it to the beneficiary; communicate that intention to the trustee; and for the trustee to accept that obligation. These requirements were set out in Ottaway v Norman [1972] 2 WLR 50. Per Re Snowden, a settlor cannot simply impose a moral obligation on a trustee to create a secret trust. 2.

stem: A company limited by shares has issued 100 ordinary shares of £1 each to three people ("the Members"), who each paid £100 to the company when the shares were issued to them. While travelling together to their annual meeting with the directors of the company, the Members are killed in a rail accident.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: All of the company's assets now vest automatically in the directors and the company ceases to exist
All of the company's assets now vest automatically in the personal representatives of the Members and the company ceases to exist
All of the company's assets now vest automatically in the directors, but the company continues to exist
All of the company's assets now vest automatically in the personal representatives of the Members, but the company continues to exist
All of the company's assets remain in the ownership of the company and the company continues to exist

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. As the company has its own legal personality which is separate from that of its members and directors, it retains ownership of all of its assets, even if all of its members die. The Members' shareholdings would pass to their personal representatives, who would be able to exercise each Member's rights in relation to the company.

stem: A person dug up roots from a neighbour's tree that were encroaching on to his land. The person neither gave notice to the neighbour, nor entered on to the neighbour's

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is the best option. Abatement is a form of self - help whereby the claimant takes autonomous remedial measures to alleviate the nuisance. stem: A woman is the fee simple owner of a property, which she has divided into flats which her estate agent tells her will yield £600 per month rental income. She agrees orally with a man that he can occupy one of the flats on payment of £650 per month for one year to take effect in possession. The woman sells her fee simple (which is registered at HM Land Registry) to her friend.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman's friend will be bound by the man's lease, provided that the woman's friend is a bona fide purchaser for value without notice
The woman's friend will be bound by the man's lease, provided that the man has registered it as a Land Charge
The woman's friend will be bound by the man's lease provided that the man has registered it against Jake's title
The woman's friend will be bound by the man's lease in any event
The woman's friend will never be bound by the man's lease

explanation.en: *hich is You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. The woman's friend will be bound by the man's lease in any event. The man's lease is an overriding interest within the meaning of the Land Registration Act 2002. It does not require registration to make it operate at law and will bind all registered dispositions of the fee simple.

stem: A woman paid a flower company £300 to supply 5,000 tulip bulbs, but because the bulbs were of a lesser species than the one she requested, her entire crop failed and the woman suffered a loss of £33,000. The flower company points to an exclusion clause contained in the contract limiting its liability to the price of the bulbs.
ask: Considering the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (UCTA), which test would the flower company's exclusion clause likely fail?

options.en: The 'common law duty of skill and care' test
The ' the standard term' test
The 'requirement of reasonableness' test
The 'plain, intelligible language' test
The 'enforceability' test

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. The - Jibs. restrictive approach to the appellate courts' powers in relation to a decision on the 'requirement of reasonableness' stems from George Mitchell (Chesterhall) Ltd v Finney Lock Seeds Ltd [1983] 2 AC 803. In relation to a contract term, the requirement of reasonableness is that the term shall have been a fair and reasonable one to be included, having regard to the circumstances which were, or ought reasonably to have been, known to or in the contemplation of the parties when the contract was made. It would not be fair and reasonable for the flower company to limit their liability to the cost of the seeds when they provided a lesser species of seeds than that which the that the lesser species would cause the crop to fail. Lead case: George Mitchell (Chesterhall) Ltd v Finney Lock Seeds Ltd [1983] 2 AC 803. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 11(1) UCTA.

stem: A case comes before the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) in 2010. There is a previous decision by the Supreme Court (previously the House of Lords) in 1971.

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. B is correct. The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is bound by the Supreme Court's previous decisions under the doctrine of stare decisis. stem: A man and woman have agreed to act as trustees of a trust which contains a range of property, including land. Under the trust, the beneficiary is entitled to the income of the trust for 15 years, after which time the remainder will pass to her two children. The trustees have no experience in administering and managing a trust, and are keen to delegate as many functions as they can to more experienced individuals. Under the Trustee Act 2000, which of the following powers
ask: are the trustees not permitted to?

options.en: The powers of advancement
The management of the land held on trust
The maintenance of the land held on trust
The power to insure the trust property
The powers of investment

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The best answer is A. Section 11(1) of the Trustee Act 2000 allows for trustees "[to] authorise any person to exercise any or all of their delegable functions as their agent," with s. 11(2) defining "delegable functions" as any function other than the powers to distribute or dispose of trust assets; allocating fees or other payments; appointing a trustee; or further delegating duties. Thus the distribution (including the advancement of capital to beneficiaries) of trust assets (e.g. under a discretionary and non-charitable trust) is a function which must be exercised by the trustee in person and cannot be delegated.

stem: A newspaper had published a story about a famous footballer's treatment for baldness. What he had objected to was publication of the fact that he had been receiving treatment at a clinic and details of where, when, how and how often his treatment was running, as well as intrusive photos of him taken with a long lens outside the clinic. The UK Supreme Court had agreed with him by a majority ruling of three to two and awarded him damages for the breaching of his right to privacy.
ask: Has the newspaper any further avenue of appeal or other form of application against the Supreme Court's decision?

options.en: The newspaper has no further avenue of appeal, because it is no longer possible to go to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) if a remedy is unsatisfactory
The newspaper has no further avenue of appeal, because the UK Supreme Court is the court of last resort since the introduction of the Human Rights Act 1998

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. C is correct. An individual can still take his or her case to the ECtHR in Strasbourg as a last resort, if they exhausted their rights within the English legal system. CASE OF MGN LIMITED v. THE UNITED KINGDOM (Application no. 39401/04).

stem: Two people are the members of a small private company limited by shares. They receive an email communication from the director of the company, proposing to dispense with the company's annual general meeting and requesting that the two members approve the company's accounts for the previous year, fix the director's remuneration for the coming year and approve the appointment of a man as the company's auditor.

options.en: All companies are required to have at least one annual general meeting and the matters proposed by the director must be approved by a resolution at that meeting
All companies are required to have at least one annual general meeting, but the matters proposed by the director can be approved by way of a written resolution
Companies can dispense with the requirement to have an annual general meeting, but the matters proposed by the director must be approved by a resolution at a formal meeting

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. There is now no requirement for a private company to have an annual meeting of its members and all matters which fall to be decided by way of a resolution of the members can be decided by way of a written resolution.
