stem: A man has mortgaged his leasehold estate in a property to BankCo. The lease has 90 years left to run, however the term of the mortgage is such that the capital balance of the loan and all associated interest will be repaid when the man's lease will only have 10 years left to run. The man is concerned that the lease will be worthless at the end of the mortgage and borrows some money from his father to redeem BankCo's mortgage. BankCo refuses to allow the man to redeem the mortgage early, on the basis that it will lose out on a large proportion of interest over the term of the loan.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: BankCo's refusal to allow the man to redeem the mortgage early amounts to an unreasonable clog on his equity of redemption and this would be unlikely to be allowed by the courts
BankCo's refusal to allow the man to redeem the mortgage early amounts to an unreasonable clog on the equity of redemption but this would be likely to be allowed by the courts
BankCo's refusal to allow the man to redeem the mortgage early does not amount to an unreasonable clog on his equity of redemption and this would be unlikely to be allowed by the courts
BankCo's refusal to allow the man to redeem the mortgage early does not amount to an unreasonable clog on the equity of redemption and would be likely to be allowed by the courts
It is not possible for the man to redeem the mortgage early

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is A. BankCo's refusal to allow the man to redeem the mortgage amounts to an unreasonable clog on his equity of redemption and this would be unlikely to be allowed by the courts. The man's leasehold estate is a wasting asset and, therefore, the estate that he will recover following natural redemption will be of very little value and of a very different character to the one that he mortgaged. The court would likely refuse to allow BankCo to place such a restriction on the man's right to redeem. See Fairclough v Swan Brewery Co. Ltd [1912] AC 565.

stem: A patient went to an acupuncturist appointment. After being examined by the acupuncturist, the patient refused to pay. The acupuncturist claims that as a matter of fact the parties had an implied contract, which the patient has breached.
ask: Which option best when the courts will imply a term as a matter of fact, if at all?

options.en: The court will imply a term in fact where it considers that it is giving effect to the reasonable expectations of the obligations as between the parties
The court will imply a term in fact where it considers that it is giving effect to the practise of a particular trade or business, market or locality
The court will imply a term in fact where it considers that it is giving effect to a term that the parties would not, in fact, have considered
The court will imply a term in fact where it considers that it is giving effect to the normal expectations of the obligations as between the parties
The court will imply a term in fact where it considers that it is giving effect to the presumed intention of the parties

explanation.en: E is the best option. The court will imply a term in fact where it considers that it is giving effect to the presumed intention of the parties. The courts will imply a term if they consider that it represents the true intention of the parties on a particular issue. The term is implied on the basis that, as a matter of fact, this was the intention of the parties, even though the agreement was implicit rather than explicit. The courts will not imply a term just because a particular clause would appear to be "reasonable". Lead case: Shirlaw v Southern Foundries [1939] 2 KB 206 (CA)

stem: Two women and a man set up a business together as an LLP. The two women are the designated members and the partnership deed provides that in the event of the LLP going into insolvent liquidation, the partners will not be required to make any contribution. The two women leave the partnership at a time when its debts amount to £100,000. Six months later, the partnership goes into insolvent liquidation with debts of £150,000 and assets of £100,000. Which of the following statements
ask: is?

options.en: All three people are jointly liable to the LLP for £50,000
All three people are jointly liable to the LLP's creditors for £50,000
The remaining partner is liable to the LLP for £50,000
The remaining partner is liable to the LLP's creditors for £50,000
The partners who left are liable to the LLP's creditors for £50,000

explanation.en: You did not select the correct answer. The correct answer is D. When membership of an LLP becomes less than two, the benefits of limited liability cease and the remaining member becomes jointly liable with the LLP for any debts incurred after that. Outgoing members are not directly liable to the creditors. The LLP's assets would meet the first £100,000 of the LLP's debts, and the remaining £50,000 could be claimed directly from the partner who remained, as they were incurred after she became the sole member of the LLP and therefore jointly liable for that debt.

stem: A majority of the UK Supreme Court held that once a local authority had a contractual and proprietary right to possession of a property, there was nothing further to investigate. That decision was flatly contradicted by a subsequent decision of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).
ask: In light of this statement, what approach must domestic lower courts adopt where domestic binding precedent conflicts with an ECtHR ruling?

Domestic lower courts must follow apparently inconsistent authority from the ECtHR

Domestic lower courts which would ordinarily be bound to follow the decision of another court higher in the domestic hierarchy are no longer bound to follow that decision if it appears to be inconsistent with a later ruling of the ECtHR

Domestic lower courts are bound to follow a later ECtHR ruling where the ECtHR has established a clear and authoritative interpretation of Convention rights based on an accurate understanding of UK law

Lower courts must follow binding domestic precedent and not apparently inconsistent authority from the European Court of Human Rights. Lead case: Kay & Ors v.
